      "@type": "Question",
      "name": "1. Introduction",
      "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/drafting-bills-for-parliament/2024-03-19-drafting-guidance#introduction",
      "acceptedAnswer": {
        "@type": "Answer",
        "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/drafting-bills-for-parliament/2024-03-19-drafting-guidance#introduction",
        "text": "\u003cp\u003eThis guidance has been produced by the Drafting Techniques Group of the Office of the Parliamentary Counsel.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe guidance is for members of the office. It is meant to help them in their task of making it as easy as possible for readers to understand the Bills that we produce.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIt is tailored to our particular needs. So it is not meant to be a comprehensive guide to legislative drafting or to clarity in legal writing. For example, some things which assist clarity such as layout or typography are outside our control and so are not discussed. Nor is this document meant as a guide to statutory interpretation or past drafting practice.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eMembers of the office are asked to have regard to the guidance. But everything in the guidance is subject to the fundamental requirement that drafts must be accurate and effective, and drafters will need to take their particular requirements into account. It follows that there will be departures from what is said here.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf you have any suggestions or comments to make on the guidance, the Drafting Techniques Group will be grateful to receive them.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn this edition of the guidance the following are new or changed:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eParts 2.1 and 2.2 (gender neutrality and sex-specific language);\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ePart 5 (citation);\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ePart 6.8 (amending uncommenced material);\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ePart 9.3.11 (made affirmative procedure);\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ePart 9.5 (amending subordinate legislation).\u003c/p\u003e"
      }

    {
      "@type": "Question",
      "name": "2. PART 1 CLARITY",
      "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/drafting-bills-for-parliament/2024-03-19-drafting-guidance#part-1-clarity",
      "acceptedAnswer": {
        "@type": "Answer",
        "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/drafting-bills-for-parliament/2024-03-19-drafting-guidance#part-1-clarity",
        "text": "\u003ch3 id=\"telling-the-story\"\u003e2.1 1.1 TELLING THE STORY\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"telling-the-story-1\"\u003eTelling the story\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.1.1 Take readers by the hand and lead them through the story you have to tell. Imagine that you are trying to explain something orally to interested listeners. Where would you start? What will they want to know first?\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.1.2 It may help to give readers an overview of the whole story at the outset, so that they can understand each part in the light of the whole. Readers are more likely to understand something if they know why you are telling them.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.1.3 Sometimes the table of contents can give a suitable overview. Or you could have an overview clause.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.1.4 Of course, a finished Act will have many different readers with different interests (those who are subject to its provisions, professional advisers, the courts). And the readers of a Bill (as opposed to an Act) will be different again — Ministers, members of the two Houses of Parliament, as well as lobby groups and other interested parties. These competing interests need to be balanced and given due weight in what we write.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"find-a-logical-order-and-structure\"\u003eFind a logical order and structure\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.1.5 Finding a clear order in which to tell your story is fundamental. This goes for a story which is spread across a whole Bill or for a story contained in a single clause.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.1.6 The material in your Bill should be set out in a logical order, so that later propositions build upon earlier ones.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.1.7 Cross-references can prove hard work for the reader, so it is helpful to minimise their use. This can sometimes be done by re-ordering the material.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.1.8 Similarly, find a Bill structure which shows how your provisions fit together. Let the divisions in your Bill reflect the divisions of thought.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"get-to-the-point\"\u003eGet to the point\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.1.9 Get to the point as quickly as you can. Ideally the opening subsection of a clause will contain the main proposition or at least give the reader some idea of what the clause is about. Don’t bury the main proposition away in the middle of the clause if you can possibly avoid it.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.1.10 So if the clause produces a particular legal effect if conditions are met, it may be more helpful to state the effect before listing the conditions.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA notice must be given if… (several conditions)…\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eis probably easier to understand than—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf…(several conditions)… a notice must be given.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"keep-propositions-short\"\u003e2.2 Keep propositions short\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.1.11 Clarity is helped by the use of short sentences. A long sentence may require the reader to keep too much in the mind. So on the whole it’s best to try to stick to one idea per sentence.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.1.12 That said, a single complex proposition is sometimes best expressed in a single sentence, rather than as a series of short sentences in successive subsections which then have to be put back together again to make sense.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"the-medium-is-not-the-message\"\u003eThe medium is not the message\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.1.13 A Bill should not draw any more attention to its own structure and mechanics than it needs to. The reader is likely to be interested in how a Bill changes the law; drafting in a way that draws more attention to the structure and mechanics of the Bill itself than to its effect is likely to be unhelpful.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.1.14 In particular, don’t create more artificial structure, such as Chapters and Parts, than you need to.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.1.15 See also Part 3.8, Lists of conditions and exceptions, and Part 3.10, Cross-references.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"tone\"\u003eTone\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.1.16 Tell your story in a moderate, level tone. Legislation should speak firmly but not shout.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.1.17 While brevity may be good, brusqueness is not. Avoid excessive emphasis, which may be distracting (for example, unnecessary use of “But” at the beginning of a sentence).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"syntax\"\u003e2.3 1.2 SYNTAX\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"sentence-structure\"\u003eSentence structure\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.2.1 Sentences should be simply and logically constructed. The classic structure is subject-verb-object. If possible, avoid inserting words between the subject and the main verb.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eInstead of—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Secretary of State may, if the required conditions are met, issue a licence to the applicant.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eyou could say—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Secretary of State may issue a licence to the applicant if the required conditions are met.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"positive-and-negative\"\u003ePositive and negative\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.2.2 The positive is often easier to understand than the negative.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSpeak after the tone\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eis easier to understand than—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eDo not speak until you hear the tone\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.2.3 This is of course not a universal rule. A prohibition may be best expressed in the negative (“do not walk on the grass” as opposed to “walk on the path”).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.2.4 Express quantities positively rather than negatively.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e25% or more\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003erather than\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003enot less than 25%\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.2.5 Avoid double negatives wherever it is not impossible to do so.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"active-and-passive\"\u003eActive and passive\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.2.6 The active voice is generally understood more readily than the passive.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Secretary of State must give a notice\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003erather than\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA notice must be given by the Secretary of State\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.2.7 The passive may be appropriate if the agent is unimportant, universal or unknown.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf a notice is given to the Authority…\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003emight be appropriate if the same rule applies whoever gave the notice.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"verbs-and-nouns\"\u003eVerbs and nouns\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.2.8 A verb is often easier to understand than a noun.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA person may apply\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eis crisper and more instantly intelligible than—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA person may make an application\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"shall\"\u003e“Shall”\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.2.9 Office policy is to avoid the use of the legislative “shall”.\u003csup id=\"fnref:1\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:1\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 1]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e There may of course be exceptions. One reason for using “shall” might be where the text is being inserted into an Act that already uses it.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"vocabulary\"\u003e2.4 1.3 VOCABULARY\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"which-words-to-choose\"\u003eWhich words to choose?\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.3.1 Write in modern, standard English using vocabulary which reflects ordinary general usage. So avoid archaisms and other words or phrases which can give rise to difficulty. Equally, it is not our role to be in the vanguard of linguistic development.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.3.2 Sir Ernest Gowers proposed three principles as to “how best to convey our meaning without ambiguity and without giving unnecessary trouble to our readers”.\u003csup id=\"fnref:2\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:2\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 2]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• use no more words than are necessary;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• use the most familiar words;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• use precise and concrete words rather than vague and abstract words.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.3.3 These three principles are hard to beat as a starting-point.\u003csup id=\"fnref:3\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:3\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 3]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e They do of course overlap with and support each other.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"use-no-more-words-than-necessary\"\u003eUse no more words than necessary\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.3.4 This principle takes on additional force in legislative drafting for obvious reasons to do with avoiding confusion and ambiguity.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.3.5 We should prefer the single word to what Gowers describes as the “roundabout phrase”. It is easy to slip into saying “for the purpose of” when very often we could just say “to”; or “in accordance with” when we could use “by” or “under”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"use-the-most-familiar-words\"\u003eUse the most familiar words\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.3.6 Avoid words that are not found in standard modern writing in English. In the first place, avoid archaisms (for example, “here-” and “there-” words such as “herewith” or “thereby”).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.3.7 The novel and modish can be as “far-fetched” and unfamiliar as the archaic. We should try not to use language that calls attention to itself.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.3.8 We should also avoid jargon, whether legal jargon or policy jargon. It may of course sometimes be necessary to use technical legal expressions.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.3.9 This principle, though, does not merely filter out archaisms, neologisms and jargon. There are degrees of familiarity. You may have two words neither of which is “far-fetched” or incomprehensible but one of which may be more familiar or everyday than the other. In that case, it is worth considering using it. For example, confer is a perfectly unobjectionable word, but this principle might suggest giving thought to the more familiar give. You might require particulars to be given, but if all you mean is information, why not say that?\u003csup id=\"fnref:4\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:4\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 4]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.3.10 There is of course a caveat. Only use the more familiar word if it conveys the meaning equally well.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"use-precise-and-concrete-words\"\u003eUse precise and concrete words\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.3.11 Drafters are used to drawing on words with a broad range of meanings such as “affect” or “in relation to”. These can be very useful, if a broad range of meaning is intended, as it often is. But if a more precise word can be used, it is more likely to get the actual intention across.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.3.12 Text with a lot of opaque words may cause readers’ eyes to glaze over. While it is not our job to spice things up, we are failing our readers if we produce text that is impenetrable or unnecessarily turgid.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.3.13 Here are some examples of potentially vague words. Sometimes their breadth of meaning is just what a drafter needs. But if in the context it is possible to be more precise, that may be more helpful to the reader.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• affect (limit, restrict)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• prescribe (specify, set out)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• provide for (specify, make, enable, authorise)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• make provision about (what exactly?)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• in relation to, in respect of (for, about)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• subject to (limited or restricted by)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• without prejudice (does not limit or restrict)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e1.3.14 These are considered in more detail in Part 11.1, Words and phrases.\u003c/p\u003e"
      }
    },
    {
      "@type": "Question",
      "name": "3. PART 2 LANGUAGE AND STYLE",
      "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/drafting-bills-for-parliament/2024-03-19-drafting-guidance#part-2-language-and-style",
      "acceptedAnswer": {
        "@type": "Answer",
        "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/drafting-bills-for-parliament/2024-03-19-drafting-guidance#part-2-language-and-style",
        "text": "\u003ch3 id=\"gender-neutrality\"\u003e3.1 2.1 GENDER NEUTRALITY\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"government-policy\"\u003eGovernment policy\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.1.1 It is government policy that primary legislation should be drafted in a way that avoids reinforcing gender stereotypes.\u003csup id=\"fnref:5\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:5\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 5]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e In practice, this means two things—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• avoiding pronouns such as “he” where a reference to men and women is intended;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• avoiding nouns that might appear to assume that only a man, or only a woman, will do a particular job or perform a particular role (eg “chairman”).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.1.2 This does not mean that sex-specific language should never be used and there are times when its use remains appropriate. Part 2.2 discusses how to give effect to the government’s policy on that separate issue. The government’s policies on both gender neutral drafting and when it is appropriate to use sex-specific language were confirmed by Written Ministerial Statement in the House of Commons on 23 May 2022, HCWS 47.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.1.3 The need to draft in a gender-neutral way applies not only when drafting freestanding text in a Bill but also when inserting text into older Acts which are not genderneutral. This is unlikely to cause difficulties. However, in very limited circumstances, exceptions may be made when amending an older Act where it might be confusing to be gender-neutral.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"drafting-techniques-to-avoid-sex-specific-pronouns\"\u003eDrafting techniques to avoid sex-specific pronouns\u003c/h4\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"introduction-1\"\u003eIntroduction\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.1.4 There are a number of techniques that may be used. They fall into three principal categories—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• repeat the noun\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• change the pronoun\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• rephrase to avoid the need for a pronoun or noun\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"repeat-the-noun\"\u003eRepeat the noun\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.1.5 You can repeat the noun each time rather than using a pronoun.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e…earnings, in relation to a person, means sums payable to the person in connection with the person’s employment…\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.1.6 Constant repetition of a noun or phrase in a way which would not occur in speech can jar and might detract from readability.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.1.7 Sometimes, rather than repeating a long compound noun, it might be possible to use a defined term.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e… may give a youth conditional caution to a child or young person (“the offender”) if the offender….\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.1.8 A defined term reduces, but does not entirely eliminate, the awkwardness of a repeated noun, and requires the reader to substitute the actual wording intended for the defined term. It may only be worthwhile if the actual wording is long and would have to be repeated a lot.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.1.9 A variant technique is to replace the noun with a letter.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf a person (“P”) who is registered in respect of a regulated activity carries on that activity while P’s registration is suspended, P is guilty of an offence.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.1.10 Using a letter in place of a noun or pronoun does not reflect normal English usage. It requires the reader to go through the mental hoop of substituting the actual noun being referred to and may thereby decrease readability. In a House of Lords debate in 2013 concerns were expressed about the technique.\u003csup id=\"fnref:6\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:6\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 6]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.1.11 The technique of using a letter in place of nouns and pronouns is seldom, if ever, likely to be appropriate solely for the purposes of securing gender neutrality. It is, however, sometimes useful for other reasons, such as to distinguish between two or more people (A and B and so on). Even in that context, though, the technique should be used judiciously.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"change-the-pronoun\"\u003eChange the pronoun\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.1.12 They (singular). In common parlance, “they” is often used in relation to a singular antecedent which could refer to a person of either sex. 2.1.13 Whether this popular usage is correct or not is perhaps a matter of dispute. OED (2nd ed, 1989) records the usage without comment; SOED (5th ed, 2002) notes “considered erron. by some”. It is certainly well-precedented in respectable literature over several centuries.\u003csup id=\"fnref:7\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:7\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 7]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e In a House of Lords debate in 2013\u003csup id=\"fnref:8\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:8\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 8]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e a number of peers expressed concern about the use of “they” as a singular pronoun.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.1.14 It may be that “they” as a singular pronoun seems more natural in some contexts (for example, where the antecedent is “any person” or “a person”) than in others.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.1.15 Many examples can be found of the use of the singular “they” in legislation.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA person commits an offence if they provide false or misleading information to the regulator… (Building Safety Act 2022, section 24)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.1.16 They (plural). It may be possible to turn the noun into a plural noun and then to use “they” (relying on section 6(c) of the Interpretation Act 1978).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eParticipants may only carry on [particular activities]… if they hold a permit\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.1.17 Take care to ensure that the plural does not create an ambiguity that would be avoided if the singular were used.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.1.18 He or she. Although “he or she” has sometimes been used in legislation to refer to individuals, it is best avoided. The expression can be awkward, particularly if frequently repeated, and it uses words denoting sex or gender in contexts where they are not relevant.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"rephrase-to-avoid-the-need-for-a-pronoun-or-noun\"\u003eRephrase to avoid the need for a pronoun or noun\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.1.19 Use the passive.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eexplaining why the regulations have not been laid\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003erather than\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eexplaining why he has not laid the regulations.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.1.20 Excessive use of the passive detracts from readability (see 1.2.6).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.1.21 Use “who” instead of “if he”\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLES\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eInstead of\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA person commits an offence if he….\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eperhaps\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA person who… commits an offence\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.1.22 One danger of the approach in the example is that it postpones the operative words to the end. That can detract from readability, especially if the relative clause is long.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.1.23 Impersonal constructions. Other impersonal constructions are possible. Again, care needs to be taken not to produce an unnatural dislocation between the person and the thing or event being spoken of.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE (1)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIt is an offence for a person to….\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eas opposed to\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA person commits an offence if he….\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE (2)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA member may… be removed from office on any of the following grounds—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) failure to discharge the functions of membership;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) failure to comply with the terms of appointment;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(c) conviction of a criminal offence.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eas opposed to\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA member may be removed from office if he—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) fails to discharge the functions of membership;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) fails to comply with the terms of appointment;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(c) is convicted of a criminal offence.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE (3)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eDropping litter is an offence (rather than “A person commits an offence if he drops litter”)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eBefore giving guidance….(rather than “Before he gives guidance”)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.1.24 Substitute “the” or “that”\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLES\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ethe reasonableness or otherwise of that belief (not “his belief”)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Secretary of State may remove a member from office if satisfied that the member…. has failed to discharge the functions of the office (not “his office”)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.1.25 This approach on occasion may risk losing the link between the noun and the person being spoken of and thereby lose clarity, or at least may give the reader an unexpected jolt.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.1.26 Omit the pronoun. Sometimes it is not necessary to use a pronoun at all.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLES\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ecircumstances which justify doing so (not “circumstances which justify him doing so”)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eimmediately before death (rather than “immediately before his death”)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.1.27 This technique relies on the reader using the context to supply the word omitted. Care is needed to ensure that resulting proposition does not become uncertain.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.1.28 Omit the phrase with the pronoun. It might be worth asking whether the phrase requiring the personal pronoun is really worth having.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ethe Secretary of State may\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003erather than\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ethe Secretary of State may, if he thinks fit\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.1.29 This of course involves taking a view as to the redundancy of the words omitted.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"avoiding-sex-specific-nouns\"\u003eAvoiding sex-specific nouns\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.1.30 The sex-specific noun most likely to be encountered is “chairman”. “Chair” is now widely used in primary legislation as a substitute. It may also be possible to use a different word entirely, such as “convenor” or “president”, but these might perhaps have different connotations.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.1.31 Some English words denoting a particular occupation, role or activity exist in a form with a feminine suffix, the obvious example being -ess (manager/manageress). In many cases the feminine form has fallen or is falling out of use and the suffixless form is or can be used for a woman as well as for a man. Where that is the case, drafters should prefer the suffixless form.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"sex-specific-language\"\u003e3.2 2.2 SEX-SPECIFIC LANGUAGE\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"government-policy-1\"\u003eGovernment policy\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.2.1 It is government policy that the use of sex-specific language is appropriate in some circumstances. This is likely to be relevant where legislation is concerned only or mainly with people of one sex. Examples include legislation relating to pregnancy, childbirth or breastfeeding. The government’s policies on this issue were announced by Written Ministerial Statement, House of Commons, 23 May 2022, HCWS 47. A failure to use sex-specific language in this kind of context has been the subject of debate in Parliament.1\u003csup id=\"fnref:9\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:9\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 9]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.2.2 The guidance below is also likely to be relevant in any circumstances where the policy is for legislation to distinguish between people on the basis of sex. Examples in existing legislation include the old state pension and the provision of toilet facilities.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"background\"\u003eBackground\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.2.3 Within the United Kingdom the law treats sex as binary, with a person’s legal sex generally being determined by what is recorded on their birth certificate.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"gender-recognition-act-2004\"\u003eGender Recognition Act 2004\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.2.4 When using sex-specific language consideration needs to be given to the Gender Recognition Act 2004, which allows people to change their legal sex.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.2.5 Section 9(1) provides:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e“Where a full gender recognition certificate is issued to a person, the person’s gender becomes for all purposes the acquired gender (so that, if the acquired gender is the male gender, the person’s sex becomes that of a man and, if it is the female gender, the person’s sex becomes that of a woman).”\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.2.6 The effect is that (for example) a reference to a “woman” will generally include someone who is a woman by virtue of a gender recognition certificate but not someone who is a man by virtue of a gender recognition certificate.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"variations-in-sex-characteristics-or-intersex\"\u003eVariations in sex characteristics (or intersex)\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.2.7 When drafting in certain areas, consideration may need to be given to people who are registered as male or female but who have variations in sex characteristics (or are intersex) and whose physical development is different to that generally expected of a person of the sex in question. Where relevant, policy decisions need to be made about how legislation is to apply to such a person, and drafting then needs to give effect to that policy.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"interpretation-act-1978\"\u003eInterpretation Act 1978\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.2.8 Section 6 of the Interpretation Act 1978 provides that, unless the contrary intention appears, “words importing the masculine gender include the feminine” and “words importing the feminine gender include the masculine”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.2.9 It is sometimes suggested that where sex-specific language is used section 6 can be relied upon to cover people of the opposite sex or people of the opposite sex to whom the legislation is relevant (so that, for example, in legislation about pregnancy a reference to a woman would include a person who is a man by virtue of a gender recognition certificate).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.2.10 Drafters should not, as a matter of course, rely on section 6 in this way. First, because it is often unclear whether “the contrary intention appears” in this context (especially in Acts drafted since the Gender Recognition Act 2004 and the adoption of gender-neutral drafting). Secondly, because it is not a clear or transparent way to draft.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"drafting-approaches\"\u003eDrafting approaches\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.2.11 Where sex is relevant, a range of different drafting approaches can be used. Different approaches produce different policy results. The drafting options available in any given case will therefore necessarily depend, in the first instance, on the underlying policy.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"using-sex-specific-language-without-more\"\u003eUsing sex-specific language without more\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.2.12 Legislation sometimes uses sex-specific language without more.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.2.13 As mentioned above, the starting point is that (for example) a reference to a woman would include a person who is a woman by virtue of a gender recognition certificate under the Gender Recognition Act 2004 but not a person who is a man by virtue of a gender recognition certificate.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.2.14 It is possible to envisage contexts where the courts may be prepared to adopt a strained construction so that (for example) in legislation about pregnancy a reference to a woman is read as including a person who is a man by virtue of a gender recognition certificate. But where, in this example, the policy is to include a person who is a man by virtue of a gender recognition certificate, drafters should strive to make that clearer.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.2.15 That said, the drafting approach in any case will need to take account of the preexisting legislative context. An amendment of an existing Act that uses sex-neutral nouns might need to do the same; and an amendment of an older Act that uses sex-specific nouns in a way that would be interpreted as covering both sexes might need to adopt the approach of the older Act (especially taking into account section 6 of the Interpretation Act 1978).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"using-sex-specific-language-with-additional-wording-to-deal-with-other-cases\"\u003eUsing sex-specific language with additional wording to deal with other cases\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.2.16 This approach involves using sex-specific language to deal with the main case in the main proposition (for example “women”), and including a further proposition to achieve the desired policy outcome for the less common case.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSubsection (1) applies in relation to a person who is a man by virtue of a full gender recognition certificate issued under the Gender Recognition Act 2004 as it applies in relation to a woman.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"refer-to-both-sexes\"\u003eRefer to both sexes\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.2.17 An alternative is to deal with the main case and the less common case on an equal footing (eg “a woman or man”). However, this approach is not appropriate where it gives undue prominence to what is a very rare case.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"modifying-the-effect-of-the-gender-recognition-act-2004\"\u003eModifying the effect of the Gender Recognition Act 2004\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.2.18 This approach involves using sex-specific language and including provision to modify the effect of section 9 of the Gender Recognition Act 2004 (as contemplated by section 9(3)).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE (1)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSection 9(1) of the Gender Recognition Act 2004 is to be disregarded for the purposes of construing subsection (1).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE (2)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe reference in subsection (1) to a woman includes a man who would be a woman but for section 9(1) of the Gender Recognition Act 2004.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.2.19 Note that these examples would produce different policy outcomes:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(1) Example 1 would ensure that a reference to “a woman” includes a person who is a man by virtue of a gender recognition certificate but not a person who is a woman by virtue of a gender recognition certificate.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(2) Example 2 would ensure that a reference to “a woman” includes a person who is a man by virtue of a gender recognition certificate as well as a person who is a woman by virtue of a gender recognition certificate.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"anatomical-terms\"\u003eAnatomical terms\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.2.20 It is natural in some contexts to draft using anatomical terms, possibly with a defined expression to indicate that the provision is mainly concerned with people of one sex.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE (from section 136 of the Health and Care Act 2022)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(1) It is an offence under the law of England and Wales for a person to carry out virginity testing.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(2) “Virginity testing” means the examination of female genitalia, with or without consent, for the purpose (or purported purpose) of determining virginity.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e…\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(5) In subsection (2), “female genitalia” means a vagina or vulva.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.2.21 In this example the definition in subsection (5) would include the vagina or vulva of a a person who is a man by virtue of a gender recognition certificate.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"nouns-that-are-not-sex-specific\"\u003eNouns that are not sex-specific\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.2.22 Even in contexts in which sex is relevant, a noun that is not sex-specific may still be appropriate. For example, it is natural to refer to someone undergoing a medical procedure as a “patient” or to refer to someone who is employed by another as an “employee”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"omitting-the-noun\"\u003eOmitting the noun\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.2.23 It is sometimes possible to structure the draft in a way that does not use the sexspecific noun. This is fine so long as the draft does not become contrived.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn this Chapter references to a child include a child stillborn after twenty-four weeks of pregnancy.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"numbers-and-dates\"\u003e3.3 2.3 NUMBERS AND DATES\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"numbers\"\u003eNumbers\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.3.1 Generally, for references to the quantity of something—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• use words where the number is between 1 and 10 inclusive\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLES The Commission is to consist of six members.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e…the period of two months…\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• use figures where the number is greater than 10\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLES\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Commission is to consist of 20 members.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e…the period of 12 months…\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.3.2 But for sums of money, ages, measurements and terms of imprisonment, use figures.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.3.3 For references to a number as an abstract quantity (ie as a noun), use figures.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf the emissions figure is not a multiple of 5, round it down to the nearest multiple of 5.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.3.4 Zero is a special case. It is usually best to say “zero” or “nil” rather than “0”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.3.5 Avoid mixing figures and words in the same context.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE (to avoid)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Commission is to have at least three members and no more than 12 members\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn that case it would be better to use either “3” and “12” or “three” and “twelve”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.3.6 For ordinal numbers, use “first”, “second” etc up to and including “tenth” and figures after that (11th, 12th etc). This does not apply to dates (see below).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"dates\"\u003eDates\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.3.7 Use figures but without the endings -st, -nd, -rd, -th.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis Act comes into force on 1 January 2020.\u003csup id=\"fnref:10\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:10\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 10]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"percentages\"\u003ePercentages\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e2.3.8 Use “%” rather than “per cent”.\u003c/p\u003e"
      }

        "text": "\u003ch3 id=\"headings\"\u003e4.1 3.1 HEADINGS\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"choice-of-headings\"\u003eChoice of headings\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.1.1 Headings help people to find what they are looking for.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.1.2 It helps if your clause headings give as full an indication of the contents of the clause as reasonably possible, consistent with keeping the heading reasonably short. But a clause heading may not need to repeat the work done by a Chapter or Part heading.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.1.3 The ideal is to draft headings in such a way that the reader can see the overall story from the arrangement of clauses. Re-read the contents page regularly to ensure it still all hangs together.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.1.4 Try to ensure that a clause heading does not go into a second line.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"overviews\"\u003e4.2 3.2 OVERVIEWS\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"what-is-an-overview\"\u003eWhat is an overview?\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.2.1 An “overview” is a brief summary of an Act, Part, Chapter, group of sections or Schedule. Its purpose is to help the reader to navigate through the legislation.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.2.2 An overview is not usually intended to have any operative effect of its own. It may be contrasted with a purpose clause intended to affect the interpretation of other provisions.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.2.3 The fact that an overview is included for one part of an Act does not mean that one has to be included for every other part. Use your judgment to decide what is likely to be helpful.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"advantages\"\u003eAdvantages\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.2.4 The contents pages at the beginning of an Act or headings are often enough to give the reader an overview of what is to come. An overview that merely repeats the headings is unlikely to be helpful.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.2.5 Overviews can, however, be helpful when used appropriately.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• In a large Act the contents can be long (running to tens of pages). An overview may be a good way to provide a pithy summary.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• An overview can be more descriptive and can draw out themes and relationships between provisions. See, for example, section 1 of the Corporation Tax Act 2009.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• An overview can explain how the new legislation fits into the legislative landscape, for instance by including signposts to other relevant provisions. See, for example, section 35 of the Corporation Tax Act 2010.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"risks-to-watch-out-for\"\u003eRisks to watch out for\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.2.6 The main risk of an overview is that it will be given some unintended effect by the courts. Risks may be minimised by ensuring the overview is accurate and drafting in a way that makes it clear that it is intended merely as a signpost.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.2.7 An overview will often have a clause to itself. If it is included alongside substantive provision, make sure that the section heading is not misleading.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.2.8 When amending legislation that contains an overview, consider whether the overview also requires amendment.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"clauses\"\u003e4.3 3.3 CLAUSES\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"clause-length\"\u003eClause length\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.3.1 Try to avoid clauses containing more than ten subsections or so.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.3.2 However, this is again a matter of judgment: if you have a self-contained story to tell, it may be more convenient for the reader to have it all in one clause which is a bit longer, rather than in two or more shorter clauses.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.3.3 It may also help if the division into clauses follows the division of thought. If, for example, you have to make separate provision for three different cases, but one case requires more provision than the other two, it might still be easiest to have only one clause for each case, even if that means that one of the clauses is longer than you would otherwise wish.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"subsections\"\u003e4.4 3.4 SUBSECTIONS\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"second-sentences-in-a-subsection\"\u003eSecond sentences in a subsection\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.4.1 The starting point is that each sentence in a clause should be a separate numbered provision. But there is no absolute rule against having more than one sentence in a numbered provision. The logical connection between subsections is likely to be closer in some cases than others. A second sentence enables the drafter to distinguish two levels of connection between subsections in the same section; or to deal with cases where putting a second thought in a separate provision would place undue emphasis on it.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(1) A party to a construction contract has the right to refer a dispute arising under the contract for adjudication under a procedure complying with this section. For this purpose “dispute” includes any difference.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(2) The contract must include provision in writing so as to—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) enable a party to give notice at any time of his intention to refer a dispute to adjudication;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) provide a timetable [etc].”\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.4.2 In this example, there are only two main propositions — the right to refer disputes to adjudication and what the contract must say about referrals. The point about the meaning of “dispute” is just an afterthought to the first, and it might be unhelpful to treat it as equal in weight to the other two. This is an example of form following function.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"alternatives-to-subsections\"\u003eAlternatives to subsections\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.4.3 Part 3.5 considers some alternatives to a traditional sentence-by-sentence narrative: formulae, method statements and tables.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"formulae-method-statements-tables\"\u003e4.5 3.5 FORMULAE, METHOD STATEMENTS, TABLES\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.5.1 There are alternatives to a subsection-by-subsection, sentence-by-sentence narrative.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"formulae\"\u003eFormulae\u003c/h4\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"when-to-use-a-formula\"\u003eWhen to use a formula\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.5.2 A formula may be the neatest way to express a relationship between various quantities.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE I\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003en this Part, “scheme transfer factor” means the amount of any sums transferred on the scheme transfer reduced by the relevant relievable amount and then divided by the standard lifetime allowance at the time when the scheme transfer took place.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis might be better expressed as a formula.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn this Part, “scheme transfer factor” means—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eT - R / S\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ewhere—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eT is the amount of any sums transferred on the scheme transfer,\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eR is the relevant relievable amount, and\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eS is the standard lifetime allowance at the time when the scheme transfer took place.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.5.3 However, sometimes a sequence of written instructions may be more accessible than a formula: see, for example, the “method statement” (below).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.5.4 If the proposition is very simple (for example, the sum of two quantities) using a formula may make it look more complicated than saying the same thing in words.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.5.5 A formula may be more accessible to, say, an actuary or accountant than to a general reader. So be guided by the expected readership.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"how-to-express-a-formula\"\u003eHow to express a formula\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.5.6 It is generally preferable for everything to be dealt with in the formula itself, so that each element represents a single thing, rather than, say, the sum or product of two things.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE (to avoid)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn this Part, “scheme transfer factor” means—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA / B\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ewhere—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA is the amount of any sums transferred on the scheme transfer minus the relevant relievable amount, and\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eB is the standard lifetime allowance at the time when the scheme transfer took place.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn this example the complete story has to be stitched together from the formula and the narrative (see the “minus” in the description of A).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.5.7 Use a single letter for each element, rather than a cluster of letters.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE (to avoid)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn this Part, “scheme transfer factor” means—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eST — RRA / SLA\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ewhere—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eST is the amount of any sums transferred on the scheme transfer,\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eRRA is the relevant relievable amount, and\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSLA is the standard lifetime allowance at the time when the scheme transfer took place.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn this example, although the compound abbreviations more obviously suggest the terms for which they stand, they make the formula look more complicated than necessary. Those mathematically inclined might also start off on the wrong foot assuming that “RRA” means R x R x A.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.5.8 An exception might be made for well-known abbreviations (eg “RPI”).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"method-statements\"\u003eMethod statements\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.5.9 A “method statement” may be the neatest way to set out the various steps in a process.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE (Pensions Act 2014, Schedule 1, para. 2)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA person’s amount for pre-commencement qualifying years is calculated as follows.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eStep 1 - calculate the person’s pension under the old system\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eCalculate the weekly rate based on the old state pension and graduated retirement benefit (see paragraph 3 for more about this).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eStep 2 - calculate a pension based on the new system\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eCalculate the weekly rate based on the new state pension (see paragraph 4 for more about this).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eStep 3 - take whichever rate is higher (the foundation amount)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eTake whichever of the rates found under Steps 1 and 2 is higher.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eStep 4 - revalue to date when the person reached pensionable age.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eRevalue the amount of that rate in accordance with paragraph 6.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe amount for the person’s pre-commencement qualifying years is the amount as revalued under Step 4.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"tables\"\u003eTables\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.5.10 A table is often a neat and clear way of setting out a number of cases with the rule that applies to each of them. As with anything else, they can be overdone. Beware of creating a table when you could express the idea just as well in a couple of sentences.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"paragraphs\"\u003e4.6 3.6 PARAGRAPHS\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"use-of-paragraphs\"\u003eUse of paragraphs\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.6.1 A large slab of unbroken text is difficult to understand. Many drafters try to avoid subsections or undivided clauses of more than, say, half-a-dozen unbroken lines.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.6.2 Paragraphs are a way to break material up and can help to make it clear how the ideas in the paragraphs are linked to one another.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.6.3 However, paragraphing can be overdone. It is distracting to the reader if the paragraphs are too short or break up the flow of the sentence. So just because text can be turned into paragraphs doesn’t mean it has to be. In some cases it may be better to have continuous text with appropriate punctuation, and not to separate out the items at all.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.6.4 An alternative to paragraphs is to split off exceptions and conditions into freestanding propositions. See Part 3.8, Lists of conditions and exceptions.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.6.5 Sub-paragraphs (numbered (i), (ii) etc.) may add complexity and make things harder to follow.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"two-sets-of-paragraphs\"\u003eTwo sets of paragraphs\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.6.6 The use of a structure which involves two or more sets of paragraphs in the same sentence (eg in the same subsection) has for some time been discouraged.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf the minister considers that—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) the authority is not likely to achieve the target, or\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) the authority is not likely to achieve the target in a reasonable time, the minister may after consulting the authority—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(i) revise the target, or\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(ii) require the authority to explain.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.6.7 In general, it remains the case that such a structure is best avoided. Instead, split the proposition into two so that there is one set of paragraphs in each part (assuming the paragraphing is preserved).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.6.8 That is not to say that the above layout cannot be used where it is thought to be a clear and logical way of presenting material (and one might argue that those criteria are satisfied in the above example). If using such a layout, make sure to use a different lettering system in the second set of paragraphs (eg (i), (ii), as above), rather than using the same lettering system in both sets. Otherwise it will be difficult to distinguish between the two sets of paragraphs when referring to one or the other.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"sandwiches\"\u003e“Sandwiches”\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.6.9 The following structure is a sandwich—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf an inspector reasonably believes that-\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) premises falling within this Part are unfit for human occupation,\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) the premises are nevertheless occupied, and\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(c) the life or health of the occupants is at risk,\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ethe inspector may serve a notice under this section.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.6.10 This structure does not always help the reader, especially if the main proposition is at the end.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.6.11 To avoid a sandwich, try moving the proposition in the words at the end so that it appears in the opening words. So instead of the text above, you could say this—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAn inspector may serve a notice under this section if the inspector reasonably believes that-\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) premises falling within this Part are unfit for human occupation,\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) the premises are nevertheless occupied, and\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(c) the life or health of the occupants is at risk.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.6.12 That said, in some cases a “sandwich” may be helpful, especially in the case of relatively short propositions where no more than two or three paragraphs separate the opening words from the final words.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"punctuation\"\u003ePunctuation\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.6.13 Paragraphs which are linked by a conjunction should end with commas.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis Act applies to—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) cats,\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) dogs, and\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(c) rabbits.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.6.14 Paragraphs which are not linked by a conjunction should end with semicolons.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe authority may require the applicant to supply any or all of the following—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) a driving licence;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) a passport;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(c) a birth certificate.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"unnumbered-paragraphs\"\u003eUnnumbered paragraphs\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.6.15 Paragraphs need not have numbers or letters, especially in a case where the list is short and so are the individual entries.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn this section “award for bravery” means—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ethe Victoria Cross;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ethe George Cross;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ethe Albert Medal.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"conjunctions-between-paragraphs\"\u003e4.7 3.7 CONJUNCTIONS BETWEEN PARAGRAPHS\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"and-and-or\"\u003e“And” and “or”\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.7.1 Ensure that it is clear whether paragraphs are intended to operate cumulatively or instead as alternatives.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.7.2 Often it will be sufficient to put the appropriate conjunction at the end of the penultimate paragraph and rely on the implication (in the absence of a contrary indication) that each of the preceding paragraphs is separated by the same conjunction.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.7.3 However, this makes the reader wait until then to know whether the paragraphs are cumulative or alternative and may be unhelpful with a long list of paragraphs.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.7.4 It is of course possible to say “and” or “or” at the end of each paragraph. That can however be cumbersome.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.7.5 Do not mix conjunctions, ie put different conjunctions at the ends of different paragraphs in the same provision.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"or\"\u003e“Or”\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.7.6 “Or” can have an inclusive and an exclusive sense: so “A or B” can mean “A or B or both” or “A or B but not both”. Dickerson suggests that: “Observation of legal usage suggests that in most cases “or” is used in the inclusive rather than the exclusive sense”.\u003csup id=\"fnref:11\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:11\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 11]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e This construction may be bolstered, or alternatively excluded, by the context.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe regulator may require the employer to—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) produce any relevant document, or\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) provide any relevant information.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.7.7 In that example, it seems very unlikely that the powers are intended to be mutually exclusive. But in other cases it may be less clear.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE Where an animal is taken into possession, a magistrates’ court may order—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) that specified treatment be administered to the animal, or\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) that the animal be sold or destroyed.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eHere, it seems unlikely the court should have to choose between (a) and (b). So the “or” at the end of (a) should probably be read in an inclusive sense.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOn the other hand, in (b), it would make no sense for the court to order both sale and destruction, so “or” should no doubt be read in an exclusive sense.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.7.8 It may be tempting to omit “or” from provisions in order to avoid any suggestion of exclusivity and perhaps to make it clear from the opening words what is intended. But where it is obvious from the context that the provisions would be read in an inclusive sense, it may be better from the point of view of clarity or consistency across the statute book to follow normal English and use “or”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.7.9 Sometimes it will be desirable to spell out that both of two alternatives are a permissible option. For example, in a provision allowing for the imposition of a fine or a term of imprisonment it is probably best to make it clear that the imposition of both is permitted (for example, by adding “or both”).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"and\"\u003e“And”\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.7.10 Similar issues can arise with “and”. If, in the example above, the court were given power to order that treatment be given to the animal and that it be sold or destroyed, would it have to do both? Again, though, the context will probably supply the answer.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"neither-and-nor-or\"\u003eNeither “and” nor “or”\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.7.11 It is possible to avoid a single conjunction by making it clear in the opening words whether the paragraphs are cumulative or alternative.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA person who applies for a licence must send with the application a copy of [all] [at least one] of the following documents—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) the person’s birth certificate;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) the person’s passport;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(c) the person’s driving licence.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.7.12 This can be heavy-handed in simple propositions, when “and” or “or” may be better.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.7.13 When setting out what can be done by subordinate legislation, the conjunction is often omitted. It is also common practice not to expand the opening words so as to say “any or all of the following”, but instead to rely on the context to supply the right answer.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Secretary of State may by regulations make provision about—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) the form of an application;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) the procedure for making an application;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(c) the fee to be paid by an applicant.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn this example, it seems sufficiently clear that the Secretary of State may make provision about any or all of the things mentioned.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"lists-of-conditions-and-exceptions\"\u003e4.8 3.8 LISTS OF CONDITIONS AND EXCEPTIONS\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"separate-lists-of-conditions-and-exceptions\"\u003eSeparate lists of conditions and exceptions\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.8.1 A list of conditions or exceptions can make a sentence long and unwieldy. It is often possible to break it up by using paragraphs. As an alternative, conditions and exceptions can be split off into separate propositions, either as separate subsections or in a single subsection with sub-headings. This kind of approach may be especially useful where each condition or exception is a complex proposition in its own right. This approach may, of course, be used in relation to conditions whether they are cumulative or alternative.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE (using separate subsections)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(1) The FCA may, in writing, cancel the registration of a registered society if any of conditions A to E is met.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(2) Condition A is that—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) the society has requested the cancellation of its registration,\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) the request is evidenced in such way as the FCA from time to time directs, and\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(c) the FCA considers it appropriate to cancel the registration.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(3) Condition B is that…\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE (using a single subsection with sub-headings)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(2) But this treatment does not apply to any income within any of the following exceptions.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eException A\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIncome to which neither of the individuals is beneficially entitled.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eException B\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIncome consisting of a distribution arising from property consisting of—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) shares in or securities of a close company to which one of the individuals is beneficially entitled to the exclusion of the other, or\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) such shares or securities to which the individuals are beneficially entitled in equal or unequal shares.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e“Shares” and “securities” have the same meaning as in section 254 of ICTA.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eException C\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIncome to which one of the individuals is beneficially entitled so far as it is treated as a result of any other provision of the Income Tax Acts as-\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) the income of the other individual, or\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) the income of a third party.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.8.2 Consider whether the conditions or exceptions need to be in separate subsections. Having a single subsection with headings, as in the second example, means avoiding using a mixture of numbers (for subsections) and letters (for conditions), a mixture that some readers might find confusing or at any rate unattractive.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.8.3 Where ordinal numbers are used for a list of conditions (first, second, third etc) it is not obvious what to call a new condition that needs to be inserted into the middle of the list in future. The use of cardinal numbers (1, 2, 3 etc) or letters (A, B, C etc) is preferable. Future conditions can then be added as 1A, 2A, 3A or AA, BA, CA etc.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.8.4 As with other techniques, the listing of things as conditions or exceptions can be overdone. Bear in mind also that the labelling of a proposition as a “condition” may draw too much attention to its status rather than its effect. Readers may come to the Bill with the question “what are the conditions?”. They are unlikely to be asking “what is condition A?”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"schedules\"\u003e4.9 3.9 SCHEDULES\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"when-to-use-schedules\"\u003eWhen to use Schedules\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.9.1 Schedules can assist clarity by providing a home for material that would otherwise interrupt and distract from the main story you are trying to tell.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.9.2 Examples where a Schedule might be useful include—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• technical provision that is unlikely to be of interest to many readers;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• lengthy material that is at something of a tangent to the main story;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• repeals;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• long series of minor textual amendments;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• large tables and very long lists.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.9.3 Bear in mind that relegating text to the end of the Bill may not always help the reader. It may break up the story you are telling; or make the structure of the Bill more complicated than it needs to be. So don’t dispatch material to Schedules without good reason.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"how-to-introduce-schedules\"\u003eHow to introduce Schedules\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.9.4 Some Schedules consist of lists which directly continue a proposition in a clause. So, for example, a clause might say that it is an offence to kill the animals listed in Schedule 1, and Schedule 1 will then list the animals. This kind of Schedule needs no further introduction.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.9.5 However, other Schedules consist of free-standing propositions (for example, a Schedule of consequential amendments to other Acts). This kind of Schedule still needs to be “introduced” in the body of the Bill so that readers know it is there and what it does.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.9.6 There are many different ways to do this.\u003csup id=\"fnref:12\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:12\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 12]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLES\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSchedule 1 makes further provision about….\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSchedule 1 contains amendments of the [title of Act].\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSchedule 1 amends the [title of Act] to provide for….\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor further provision about…, see Schedule 1.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.9.7 It is important to ensure that the description of the Schedule is accurate and covers everything in the Schedule.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.9.8 The “introductory words” should be in the clause to which the Schedule most closely relates or, if it doesn’t relate to any particular clause, in a separate one.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.9.9 If your Schedule consists of free-standing provision, the section or subsection of the Act which introduces it will need to come into force at the same time as the Schedule. And if different parts of the Schedule come into force at different times, the section or subsection introducing it should come into force, so far as relating to any particular provision of the Schedule, at the same time as that provision.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.9.10 Where a Bill is divided into Parts, a Schedule will be regarded as being in the same Part as the section which introduces it. So, where two or more sections refer to a Schedule, it is important to be clear which section is the one which introduces it. Clarity on this point is also important when it comes to commencement.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"cross-references\"\u003e4.10 3.10 CROSS-REFERENCES\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"no-cross-reference-needed\"\u003eNo cross-reference needed\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.10.1 A legislative proposition must be read in context. Where the connection between different propositions is clear, no cross-reference is needed.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eInstead of the following—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(1) A person may apply to the council for a permit to play music.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(2) An application under subsection (1) must contain the prescribed information.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(3) On receiving an application made by a person under subsection (1), the council may issue a permit to the person.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(4) A permit issued under subsection (3) must be in the prescribed form.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(5) A permit issued under subsection (3) authorises the holder to play music as indicated in the permit.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eyou might say—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(1) A person may apply to the council for a permit to play music.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(2) An application must contain the prescribed information.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(3) The council may issue a permit to an applicant.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(4) A permit must be in the prescribed form.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(5) A permit authorises the holder to play music as indicated in the permit.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"refer-to-the-idea-not-the-provision\"\u003eRefer to the idea, not the provision\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.10.2 It is helpful to refer to a substantive rule or proposition, rather than the statutory provision containing it (in which readers are unlikely to be interested).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSuppose subsection (1) says—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(1) A company must pass a resolution before [doing something].\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou want to make an exception for small companies.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eYou could say—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(2) Subsection (1) does not apply in the case of a small company.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eBut rather than telling readers about “subsection (1)”, it might be more helpful to say—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(2) No resolution is required in the case of a small company.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"forward-references\"\u003eForward references\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.10.3 Forward references (referring to something you haven’t yet introduced) may well be a sign that the order isn’t quite right. That said, it can be helpful to give a signpost to later material which is relevant but which does not necessarily need to be understood now (eg “For more about fines, see section x”).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"parenthetical-descriptions\"\u003eParenthetical descriptions\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.10.4 If you refer to a provision of another Act, it is generally helpful to give a description of it in brackets. And it is sometimes helpful to give such a description when you are referring to a provision of the same Act. But consider the usefulness of the descriptive words against the disadvantage of interrupting the flow of text.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.10.5 The parenthetical description is a description, not a quotation. It will often be the heading of the section or Schedule referred to, but it does not have to be. For example, the heading may have been devised in the context of other headings in the Act in question, but may not be particularly helpful taken in isolation.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.10.6 When including a parenthetical description that names the provision and the Act, the parenthesis should generally appear after the reference to the Act.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003esection 2 of the Limitation Act 1980 (time limit for actions founded on tort)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003erather than\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003esection 2 (time limit for actions founded on tort) of the Limitation Act 1980\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.10.7 For parenthetical descriptions in textual amendments, see Part 6.10.1, Minor points of amendment style.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"above-and-below\"\u003e“Above” and “below”\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.10.8 On the whole, do not use “above” and “below”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.10.9 However, it may sometimes be appropriate to do so for the purposes of achieving certainty: for example, if you are referring in one breath to a provision of the Bill and a provision of another Act.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.10.10 If inserting material into an existing Act which uses “above” and “below” you do not necessarily have to follow suit, particularly in the case of substantial insertions of new text.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"of-this-act-etc\"\u003e“of this Act” etc\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.10.11 As a general rule, expressions such as “of this Act” and “of this section” should also be avoided.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.10.12 They may serve a useful purpose in some cases—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• in contexts where “above” or “below” might otherwise be used (see above): there may be reasons of symmetry or emphasis that mean that, for example, “of this Act” is to be preferred to “above” or “below”;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• in a Schedule divided into Parts in a Bill which is also divided into Parts, it may help to make it clear whether you are referring to a Part of the Schedule or a Part of the Bill;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• where there is a reference to a Chapter of the Part in which the reference occurs and another Part of the Bill is also divided into Chapters: it may be desirable to add “of this Part” to the reference in the interests of clarity.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"arabic-and-roman-numerals-in-pre-2001-acts\"\u003eArabic and Roman numerals in pre-2001 Acts\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.10.13 Since 2001 Acts switched from Roman to Arabic numerals for Parts and Chapters of Acts and for Parts of Schedules.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.10.14 Arabic numbers should be used when referring to Parts and Chapters of pre-2001 Acts and Parts of Schedules to such Acts, even though the original Act will have used Roman numerals.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.10.15 When inserting or substituting text in a pre-2001 Act use Arabic numerals even if that leads to a mixture of Arabic and Roman in the text of the Act.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e3.10.16 But if you are quoting text in which Roman numerals appear (for example, for the purposes of amending it), quote the text as it is.\u003c/p\u003e"
