        "text": "\u003ch3 id=\"definitions\"\u003e5.1 4.1 DEFINITIONS\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"different-kinds-of-definition-and-their-function\"\u003eDifferent kinds of definition and their function\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e4.1.1 There are two main kinds of definition—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(1) Exhaustive definitions that replace the meaning that the defined term would otherwise have. It is usual to use “means” for this kind of definition.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(2) Inclusive/exclusive definitions that adapt the meaning that the defined term would otherwise have by clarifying potential doubt or expanding or limiting the meaning. It is usual to use “includes/does not include” for this sort of definition.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e4.1.2 Exhaustive definitions are sometimes used as drafting devices to break material up or make it easier to follow. A complex concept can be given a short label or “tag” that can be referred to instead. The potential benefits of using a definition in this way need to be weighed against the additional complexity that can be caused by the reader having to piece the story back together again. This is especially likely to be an issue if the meaning of the defined term is not particularly intuitive.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"choosing-labels\"\u003eChoosing labels\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e4.1.3 The natural meaning of a defined term may influence the way that the definition is interpreted so it is important to ensure that an appropriate label is used.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e4.1.4 Avoid labels that are misleading.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE (to avoid)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn this Act, “child” means a young person in care.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e4.1.5 Where possible avoid bland terms such as “the relevant person” or “the principal Act”. Try instead to use a label that gives the reader some clue as to what it means (but be careful not to use a tag that might colour the meaning in unwanted ways).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e4.1.6 Think carefully before using acronyms or other initials unless you are confident that they are commonly understood or commonly understood in the particular context (for example, RPI for the retail prices index). Initials may be shorter but this often comes at a cost to the reader who has to decode what they stand for.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e4.1.7 Using the same label to denote different things in the same Bill may be confusing.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"dont-make-a-definition-do-too-much\"\u003eDon’t make a definition do too much\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e4.1.8 It is usually best to avoid using a definition to make operative provision since one would not usually expect to find operative provision in a definition.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE (to avoid)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e“information notice” means a notice, issued by the Regulator to a registered person, requiring the registered person to send, within the period of 30 days beginning with the day on which the notice is issued, a return to the Regulator containing such information as is specified in the notice.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e4.1.9 In this example the definition ought to be restructured as a series of operative provisions: (1) conferring power on the Regulator to require a person to provide information, and (2) imposing a duty on a recipient to comply within 30 days. An “information notice” could then be defined as a notice issued by the regulator under (1).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"referential-definitions\"\u003eReferential definitions\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e4.1.10 Where a term in a Bill is intended to have the same meaning as in an earlier Act consider whether it is most helpful to set it out again or attract the earlier definition.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e4.1.11 One reason for attracting an earlier definition is to pick up case law on its meaning. Another reason is to attract future changes to the definition. However, it is important to note that neither of these results follow automatically. It will ultimately be a question of construction. Much depends on context.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e4.1.12 Try to help the reader by being specific about where the earlier definition is.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e4.1.13 A simple way to attract an earlier definition is—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn this Act, “health care” has the meaning given by section 98 of the Health Act 2006.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e4.1.14 In this kind of context it makes no difference whether “given in” or “given by” is used.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e4.1.15 An alternative approach that may be particularly useful where a word or phrase has to be constructed from a number of different provisions of an Act is—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn this Act, “health care” has the same meaning as in the Health Act 2006 [(see sections 98, 102 and 105 of that Act)].\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"identifying-the-purposes-for-which-a-definition-applies\"\u003eIdentifying the purposes for which a definition applies\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e4.1.16 Be clear about the purposes for which a definition applies.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e4.1.17 Use “in this Act”, “in this section” and so on unless there is no reasonable doubt. Where a definition is in the form ““X” means/includes/does not include” this is usually preferable to “for the purposes of this Act/section/etc”, if only because it is shorter.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e4.1.18 Defining terms “unless the context otherwise requires” is generally unhelpful. If there are circumstances where the context otherwise requires it is far better to identify them rather than leaving the reader guessing. The same result is, in any event, likely to be achieved by leaving out the words “unless the context otherwise requires”: see Meux v Jacobs (1875) LR 7 HL 481 at 493.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"where-to-put-definitions\"\u003eWhere to put definitions\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e4.1.19 There are no hard and fast rules when it comes to deciding where to put a definition: what will work best for the reader is necessarily a matter of judgement.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e4.1.20 A definition that is key to understanding a provision will often be best up front, either where it is first used or in introductory material.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e4.1.21 A definition that is merely clarificatory will often be left to the end so that the reader can get on with reading the main story before getting bogged down in the definitional detail (for example, “bank holiday”).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e4.1.22 Definitions that are used in more than one provision and defined in the first of them should generally be signposted by including a reference to them in a general definition section (eg “[In this Act]… X has the meaning given in section 1”) or in an index of defined terms. An index of defined terms is a provision that simply lists terms defined elsewhere, and indicates where the definitions can be found.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e4.1.23 Avoid prospective definitions in the form: “In this section and the next section, x means y”, which are easily missed by the reader of the next section. Alternatives include putting the definition in both sections or including a cross-reference in the second section.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"ordering-of-definitions\"\u003eOrdering of definitions\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e4.1.24 In most cases definitions should be listed alphabetically, with numbers coming first. When determining the alphabetical order ignore “the” (eg in “the regulator”).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e4.1.25 It some cases, however, it may make sense to list the definitions in conceptual order (for example, where each definition builds on a previous one).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e4.1.26 In a list of definitions, each entry should end with a semicolon. There should be no conjunction.\u003c/p\u003e"

One approach is to refer to the instrument “as it has effect [from time to time] in EU law”. The words in square brackets should be included only if the policy is to cover future amendments.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"instruments-made-between-1968-and-2014\"\u003eInstruments made between 1968 and 2014\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e5.2.3 Regulations and directives. The title of a regulation or directive made between 1968 and 2014 will look like this—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eCouncil Regulation (EEC) No 1462/86 of [date] [subject]\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eCommission Regulation (EU) No 495/2010 of [date] [subject]\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eRegulation (EU) No 439/2010 of the European Parliament and of the Council [date] [subject]\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eCouncil Directive 86/609/EEC of [date] [subject]\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eCouncil Directive 2010/24/EU of [date] [subject]\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eDirective 2010/13/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of [date] [subject]\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e5.2.4 Note that up to and including 1998, the year was written with two digits (eg “98”); for 1999-2014 four digits are used (eg “2002”).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e5.2.5 When referring to a 1968 - 2014 regulation or directive for the first time, use the full title. For subsequent references, the date and subject-matter may be omitted.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e5.2.6 Decisions. The title of a Decision made between 1968 and 2014 will be “Council Decision [date] [subject]”. This is then followed by a number such as “(2010/299/EU)”, but the number is not formally part of the title. Use the full title, including the number in brackets, for the first reference. For second and subsequent references, use the form “Council Decision 2010/299/EU”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"instruments-made-from-2015-onwards\"\u003eInstruments made from 2015 onwards\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e5.2.7 As from 1 January 2015 the numbering system of EU instruments changed. The title of an instrument made on or after that date will look like this—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eCommission Regulation (EU) 2015/140 of [date] [subject]\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eDirective (EU) 2015/2 of the European Parliament and of the Council of [date] [subject]\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eCouncil Decision (EU) 2015/3 of [date] [subject]\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eCommission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/5 of [date] [subject]\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eCommission Implementing Directive (EU) 2015/6 of [date] [subject]\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eDecision (EU) 2015/7 of the European Parliament of [date] [subject]\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eDecision (EU, Euratom) 2015/8 of the European Parliament of [date] [subject]\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e5.2.8 Again, for the first reference use the full title including the date and subject-matter.       "acceptedAnswer": {

        "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/drafting-bills-for-parliament/2024-03-19-drafting-guidance#part-6-amendments",
        "text": "\u003ch3 id=\"repeals\"\u003e7.1 6.1 REPEALS\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"operative-words\"\u003eOperative words\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.1.1 To repeal a whole Act, use the formula—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e“The [Act] is repealed”\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.1.2 For repeals of less than a whole Act, use “omit”—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn section 10(2) of the [Act] omit the words from “except” to “below”;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn section 10 of the [Act] omit subsection (3);\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn the [Act] omit section 10;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn the [Act] omit Part 2.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.1.3 For a repeal Schedule, or any other list of enactments to be repealed, there is no single recommended form of words, but a fairly standard form of words is—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e“( ) The provisions/enactments specified/mentioned in Schedule X are repealed [or revoked] to the extent specified/shown.”\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.1.4 A reference to “or revoked” is needed, of course, where a repeal Schedule includes revocations of subordinate legislation. In such a case “provisions” might be better than “enactments”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"where-repeals-should-go\"\u003eWhere repeals should go\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.1.5 The office no longer does “double entry” repeals (considered in Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis v Simeon [1982] 2 All ER 813 HL). Accordingly, a repeal should appear either in the body of a Bill or in a repeal Schedule, as clarity dictates, but not both.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"repeal-of-amendments\"\u003eRepeal of amendments\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.1.6 Where amendment is completely superseded. Where the amending provision is completely superseded (for example by repeal or complete substitution of the provision amended), it is good practice to repeal it.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.1.7 Where amendment is not completely superseded. Do not repeal amendments which are not completely superseded.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.1.8 Textual amendments, so far as Westminster legislation is concerned, are sometimes said to be “always speaking”. So the first enactment is regarded as having effect subject to a continuing amendment by the second.\u003csup id=\"fnref:15\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:15\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 15]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e This view differs from that taken in a number of other  jurisdictions, where textual amendments are considered to have a “once-and-for-all” effect, and are therefore regarded as spent as soon as they have done their job.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.1.9 Where the repeal of an amendment that is in force is not accompanied by a repeal of the amended enactment, questions may arise as to the intended effect. Bennion, Bailey and Norbury on Statutory Interpretation states that in this case “one might ordinarily expect the repeal to be intended to do no more than tidy up the statute book by stripping away the machinery by which the amendment was made. Absent other considerations, it would be surprising if a substantive change to the law were intended to be made by such indirect means.”\u003csup id=\"fnref:16\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:16\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 16]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.1.10 Nevertheless, the safest and most convenient approach is to leave the amendments alone.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"repeal-of-uncommenced-amendments\"\u003eRepeal of uncommenced amendments\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.1.11 See paragraphs 6.8.10 to 6.8.13.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"repeal-of-repeals\"\u003eRepeal of repeals\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.1.12 We do not routinely repeal earlier repealing enactments. But where the earlier repeal is part of an Act the whole of the rest of which is repealed, it will usually be tidier, and less confusing to the reader, to remove the whole Act rather than to carve around the repeal provision. If savings were made on the earlier repeal, consideration needs to be given to the effect of the later repeal on those savings.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.1.13 The repeal of a repeal does not of course revive the enactment originally repealed. See section 15 of the Interpretation Act 1978 (which is subject to the savings in section 16).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"repeal-of-paragraphs-with-conjunctions\"\u003eRepeal of paragraphs with conjunctions\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.1.14 If you are repealing a paragraph which ends with a conjunction, make it clear whether or not you are repealing the conjunction. You might do that, for example, by adding words such as “(together with the final “and”)” or “(but not the final “or”)”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"substitutions\"\u003e7.2 6.2 SUBSTITUTIONS\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"operative-words-1\"\u003eOperative words\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.2.1 The recommended form is—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003efor x substitute y\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"how-much-text-to-substitute\"\u003eHow much text to substitute\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.2.2 The starting point is that the minimum amount of text should be replaced. This will usually make it easier for the reader of the Bill to identify the bit that is actually changing. It also avoids the risk of missing a cross-reference, non-textual modification or old saving.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.2.3 However, in some cases it will be helpful to the reader of the Bill, or the reader of the Act being amended, to substitute more text than is strictly necessary. For example—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• where a number of related changes are being made to a single provision,\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• where the end result of a group of amendments would be to alter the whole basis of an existing provision or to leave very little of the previous text,\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• where the passage to be amended has previously been amended non-textually (so that there may be some doubt about which words remain),\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• where it is otherwise helpful to the reader to substitute a few extra words, and • where doing so enables the text substituted to be identified more readily.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"substitutions-include-words-quoted\"\u003eSubstitutions include words quoted\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.2.4 Section 20(1) of the Interpretation Act 1978 states: “Where an Act describes or cites a portion of an enactment by referring to words, sections or other parts from or to which (or from and to which) the portion extends, the portion described includes the words, sections or other parts referred to unless the contrary intention appears.”\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.2.5 Note that this is the opposite of the practice with House amendments.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"substitution-or-insertion\"\u003eSubstitution or insertion?\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.2.6 If you have new text that is in substance a replacement for the existing text, then put it by way of substitution, re-using the number of the existing text.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.2.7 But if you want to repeal text and, at the same time, have new text to put in at the same place, where the new text is not a direct replacement for the existing text, it is better not to substitute. Instead, repeal the old text and insert the new text, without re-using the number. That way it is clearer that you are doing two separate things (so let form follow function).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"insertions\"\u003e7.3 6.3 INSERTIONS\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"operative-words-2\"\u003eOperative words\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.3.1 Use the imperative form—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eafter x insert y\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"after-or-before\"\u003eAfter or before\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.3.2 It is usual to specify that a new provision is to be inserted “after” another one.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.3.3 If you are inserting something as the very first section or Schedule, you will of course need to insert it “before section 1” or “before Schedule 1”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.3.4 “Before” can also be useful in other circumstances where the new section is to be inserted at the beginning of a Part, Chapter or group of sections, where a reference to “after” the preceding section would tend to suggest that the intention was that the new section should appear at the end of the preceding Part etc.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"at-the-beginning\"\u003eAt the beginning\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.3.5 The usual form is to say—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eat the beginning insert x\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003erather than to say that x is inserted “before” particular words.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"at-the-end\"\u003eAt the end\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.3.6 The usual form is to say—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eat the end insert x\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.3.7 This is in contrast to House amendments to Bills, which just say “at end”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.3.8 Say “insert” rather than “add”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"in-a-list\"\u003eIn a list\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.3.9 Where an amendment is made to insert an entry into a list, such as a list of definitions or statutory bodies, it is sometimes framed as an amendment to insert the text “at the appropriate place” (instead of “after” something). This is appropriate where, for example, a list runs in alphabetical order.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"next-to-an-unnumbered-provision\"\u003eNext to an unnumbered provision\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.3.10 To add a subsection or sub-paragraph to a section or paragraph which is not already subdivided, proceed as follows—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• renumber the existing text—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn [section] [paragraph] N the existing text becomes [subsection] [sub-paragraph] (1).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• make any amendments to the existing text—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn that [subsection] [sub-paragraph], after ”x” insert…\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• insert the new subsection or sub-paragraph—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAfter that [subsection] [sub-paragraph] insert—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e“(2) [Text of new provision]”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"numbering-of-inserted-provisions\"\u003e7.4 6.4 NUMBERING OF INSERTED PROVISIONS\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"at-the-beginning-of-a-series\"\u003eAt the beginning of a series\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.4.1 Number as follows when inserting a new whole provision at the beginning of an existing series of provisions (eg a subsection at the beginning of a section or a Schedule before the first Schedule).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• New sections inserted before the first section of an Act are preceded by a letter, starting with “A” (A1, B1, C1 and so on).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• The same approach is taken in relation to all other divisions of text (other than lettered paragraphs).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThus the Insolvency Act 2000 inserted a Schedule A1 before Schedule 1 to the Insolvency Act 1986, and the Enterprise Act 2002 inserted a new Schedule B1 after Schedule A1.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• A provision inserted before “A1” (or “ai”) is “ZA1” or (“zai”).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• In the case of lettered paragraphs, new paragraphs inserted before paragraph (a) are (za), (zb) etc.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• And paragraphs inserted before (za) are (zza), (zzb) etc.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"at-the-end-of-a-series\"\u003eAt the end of a series\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.4.2 Where adding a provision at the end of an existing series of provisions of the same kind (eg a subsection at the end of a section or a Schedule at the end of the Schedules), the numbering should continue in sequence.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"between-existing-provisions\"\u003eBetween existing provisions\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.4.3 The following applies when inserting whole provisions between existing provisions.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• New provisions inserted between 1 and 2 are 1A, 1B, 1C etc.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• New provisions inserted between 1A and 1B are 1AA, 1AB, 1AC etc.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• New provisions inserted between 1 and 1A are 1ZA, 1ZB, 1ZC etc. (and not 1AA etc.)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• New provisions inserted between 1A and 1AA are 1AZA, 1AZB, 1AZC etc.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.4.4 Do not generate a lower level identifier unless you have to.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• A new provision between 1AA and 1B is 1AB not 1AAA.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• But a new provision between 1AA and 1AB is 1AAA.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.4.5 The above recommendations apply equally to sub-paragraphs with roman numerals and lettered paragraphs.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• New sub-paragraphs between sub-paragraphs (i) and (ii) are (ia), (ib), (ic) etc.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• New paragraphs between paragraphs (a) and (b) are (aa), (ab), (ac) etc.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• New paragraphs between paragraphs (a) and (aa) are (aza), (azb), (azc) etc.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"series-of-more-than-26\"\u003eSeries of more than 26\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.4.6 After Z use Z1, Z2, Z3 etc. For example, after section 360Z insert sections 360Z1, 360Z2 and so on; after paragraph (z) insert paragraphs (z1), (z2), (z3).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"re-using-numbers\"\u003eRe-using numbers\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.4.7 If you are inserting new text at a place where there has previously been a repeal, do not re-use the number.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"identifying-text\"\u003e7.5 6.5 IDENTIFYING TEXT\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"opening-or-closing-words-of-a-subsection-with-paragraphs\"\u003eOpening or closing words of a subsection with paragraphs\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.5.1 A subsection with paragraphs will have words before the paragraphs, and may have words after the paragraphs.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf an inspector reasonably believes that—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) premises falling within this Part are unfit for human occupation,\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) the premises are nevertheless occupied, and\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(c) the life or health of the occupants is at risk,\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ethe inspector may serve a notice under this section.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.5.2 The words before the paragraphs start should be referred to as “The words before paragraph (a)” (or whatever the first paragraph is).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.5.3 The words after the paragraphs should be referred to as the words “after paragraph (c)” or whatever the last paragraph is.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.5.4 If you are amending words that only appear once there is no need to specify whether they appear before or after the paragraphs, but it is sometimes helpful to do so (for example, if the provision is particularly long).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"words-which-occur-more-than-once\"\u003eWords which occur more than once\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.5.5 Where words occur more than once in a provision, and you want to identify one instance of them, the recommended form is as follows—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003efor “x”, in the first place it occurs, substitute “y”\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eafter “x”, in the second place it occurs, insert “y”\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eomit “x” in the third place it occurs.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.5.6 In some cases it may be simpler to replace a slightly bigger chunk of text so as to avoid having to refer to the “first” or “second” instance of the word or phrase.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.5.7 Where words occur twice and you want to catch both instances the recommended form is—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003efor “x”, in both places it occurs, substitute “y”\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eafter “x”, in both places it occurs, insert “y”\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eomit “x” in both places.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.5.8 Where words occur three or more times and you want to catch all instances, the recommended form is —\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003efor “x”, in each place it occurs, substitute “y”\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eafter “x”, in each place it occurs, insert “y”\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eomit “x” in each place.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.5.9 Note that it is unnecessary to refer to “the words” x or y; or to use brackets.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.5.10 If an amendment is intended to be made in a heading as well as in the body of a provision it is worth making this clear by adding “(including the heading)”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"english-and-welsh-language-text\"\u003eEnglish and Welsh language text\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.5.11 It is possible, if unusual, for a Bill to amend an Act of Senedd Cymru or an instrument made by the Welsh Ministers. Such an Act or instrument will exist in both English and Welsh. If amending both versions, refer to the “English language text” and the “Welsh language text” as opposed to the “English text” and “Welsh text” (so as not to suggest that one part of the law is “English” or “Welsh” in terms of nationality).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"amendment-of-headings\"\u003e7.6 6.6 AMENDMENT OF HEADINGS\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"when-to-amend-headings\"\u003eWhen to amend headings\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.6.1 It is acceptable to amend the heading to a provision, and it may be helpful to do so - for example, if the provision is falsified by a textual amendment you are making.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.6.2 There is no need to amend a heading merely because the existing heading is not quite what you would have chosen for the amended text.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"how-to-amend-headings\"\u003eHow to amend headings\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.6.3 The wording used to amend a heading should be the same as the wording used to make other amendments (so, for these purposes, do not treat headings as different from other statutory text).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.6.4 The recommended practice is not to mimic typography when amending or substituting a heading (ie do not use bold or italic font or small capitals).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.6.5 However, use the appropriate typography when inserting a completely new heading (for example, a new italic heading before an existing group of sections).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"what-to-call-headings\"\u003eWhat to call headings\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.6.6 Parts and Chapters. A heading of a Part or Chapter in the body of an Act should be referred to as the “Chapter heading” or “Part heading” or “the heading of Chapter/Part X”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.6.7 Groups of sections. An italic cross-heading which precedes a group of sections in the body of an Act should be called the “italic heading before section x”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.6.8 Sections. A section heading should be referred to simply as the “heading” of the section. This applies to pre-2001 Acts as well as later Acts, even though the headings for pre2001 Acts took the form of marginal sidenotes.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.6.9 Schedules. The heading of a Schedule should be referred to as such.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.6.10 The heading of a Part of a Schedule should be referred to as the “Part heading” or “the heading of Part X”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.6.11 An italic heading within a Schedule should be called “the italic heading before paragraph x”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.6.12 As a matter of house style a heading is a heading “of” something, not “to” something.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"schedules-and-other-series-of-amendments\"\u003e7.7 6.7 SCHEDULES AND OTHER SERIES OF AMENDMENTS\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"series-of-amendments\"\u003eSeries of amendments\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.7.1 Although individual amendments are drafted as instructions (“insert”), series of amendments should start with “is amended”—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(1) The Kangaroos Act is amended [as follows] [as specified in subsections…].\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(2) After section 1 insert….\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(3) Omit section 2.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.7.2 If you say Act X is amended “as follows”, what follows shouldn’t include an amendment to Act Y.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"format-of-amendment-schedules\"\u003eFormat of amendment Schedules\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.7.3 Where amendments to an Act are arranged under an italic heading giving the name of the Act, the recommended style is—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e“Counter-Terrorism Act 2008 (c. 28)\u003c/p\u003e\u003col\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eIn the Counter-Terrorism Act 2008, after section N….”\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.7.4 Note in particular—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• the short title of the Act needs to be given in the text of the amendment as well as in the heading;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• the chapter number should be given in the heading but does not need to be repeated in the text of the amendment.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"format-of-repeal-schedules\"\u003eFormat of repeal Schedules\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.7.5 The format of a repeal Schedule is now fairly standard. Any repeal Schedule, or any other table of repeals, should be in that standard form.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.7.6 Within each part of a Schedule or other table of repeals, the provisions affected should continue to be arranged chronologically (with chapter numbers).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.7.7 Repeals and revocations may be dealt with together or in separate parts of a repeal Schedule.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"uncommenced-material\"\u003e7.8 6.8 UNCOMMENCED MATERIAL\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.8.1 Uncommenced legislation should be kept in a state in which it can be brought into force. So it needs to be catered for when legislating to implement new policy.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.8.2 The discussion below deals with the following topics—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• amending uncommenced provisions;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• repealing uncommenced amendments;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• amending provisions subject to uncommenced repeals;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• drafting provisions that need to work with existing and prospective provisions.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"amending-uncommenced-provision\"\u003eAmending uncommenced provision\u003c/h4\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"amending-uncommenced-free-standing-provisions\"\u003eAmending uncommenced free-standing provisions\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.8.3 An amendment can be made to an uncommenced free-standing provision in an earlier Act in the usual way. For considerations relating to commencement, see below.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"amending-an-act-that-is-the-subject-of-earlier-uncommenced-amendments\"\u003eAmending an Act that is the subject of earlier uncommenced amendments\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.8.4 In the interests of simplicity, where a Bill amends an Act that is already the subject of earlier uncommenced amendments, it should operate directly on that Act (not on the intervening amending Act).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• Act 1 is in force.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• Act 2 inserts a new section 7A and the insertion is not yet in force.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• A Bill needs to insert a new subsection (1A) into section 7A. The amendment in the Bill should be expressed as an amendment to section 7A of Act 1 (not as an amendment to the provision of Act 2 which inserts it).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.8.5 It may be helpful to include a signpost to indicate where the provision came from—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn section 7A of Act 1 (as inserted by section 2 of Act 2) after subsection (1) insert…\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.8.6 If a provision is subject to an uncommenced substitution, it may be necessary to amend the provision both in its original and in its substituted form.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE In Act 1—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) in section 1 (before its substitution by section 2 of Act 2), after “or dogs” insert “or cats”;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) in section 1 (as substituted by section 2 of Act 2), after “or dogs” insert “or cats”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"commencement-issues\"\u003eCommencement issues\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.8.7 To avoid confusion, amendments should not be brought into force before the provision they amend.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.8.8 The recommended approach when drafting an Act that amends earlier uncommenced provision is to—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) confer a fresh power, in the amending Act, to govern the amendments made by it (rather than expanding any power in the amended Act so that it can be used to commence the amendments), or\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) if the policy is that the amended Act should never be in force without the amendments, provide for linked commencement (eg “X comes into force at the same time as Y”).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.8.9 The approach in paragraph 6.8.8(a) allows flexibility as the amendments can be brought into force at the same time as or later than the provisions that they amend.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"repealing-uncommenced-amendments\"\u003eRepealing uncommenced amendments\u003c/h4\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"repeal-of-part-of-uncommenced-amendment\"\u003eRepeal of part of uncommenced amendment\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.8.10 Where a Bill repeals part only of an uncommenced amendment to an earlier Act, it should operate directly on that Act (not on the intervening amending Act). This is the same as the approach discussed above for amending uncommenced amendments.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• Act 1 is in force.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• Act 2 inserts a new section 7A and the insertion is not yet in force.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• The policy underlying a Bill is to repeal subsections (3) to (6) of section 7A. The repeal should be expressed as a repeal of subsections (3) to (6) of section 7A of Act 1 (not as a partial repeal to the provision of Act 2 which inserts it).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.8.11 The commencement of the repeal should be governed by the commencement provision made by the Bill; and the repeal should not be brought into force before the provision of Act 2 which inserts section 7A into Act 1.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"repeal-of-whole-of-uncommenced-amendment\"\u003eRepeal of whole of uncommenced amendment\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.8.12 The position is different where the policy is to repeal an uncommenced amendment in its entirety and without it ever having been brought into force. Then the repeal should operate on the Act making the uncommenced amendment (rather than the amended Act).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• Act 1 is in force.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• Act 2 inserts a new section 7A and the insertion is not yet in force.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• The policy underlying a Bill is to repeal section 7A. The repeal in the Bill should be expressed as a repeal of the uncommenced provision in Act 2 that inserted the new section 1A into Act 1.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.8.13 The reason for adopting this approach is that the aim is to stop section 7A from operating at all, rather than altering the way in which it operates. Expressing the proposition as a repeal of section 7A of Act 1 would necessitate commencing the amendment (so that there is something to repeal) and then repealing it immediately afterwards, which is unnecessary and potentially misleading.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"amending-provisions-subject-to-an-uncommenced-repeal\"\u003eAmending provisions subject to an uncommenced repeal\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.8.14 A provision in an Act subject to an uncommenced repeal may need to be amended if the policy of the Bill demands a change before the repeal is to be commenced. In that case, consideration needs to be given to what will happen to the amendment.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.8.15 In some cases it will be obvious that the amendment is not intended to have any effect following the commencement of the repeal (for example, where the amendment inserts a single word). An express repeal is nonetheless helpful to tidy things up.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.8.16 In other cases, the intended effect may be less clear. For example, if a new section is inserted into a Part of an Act that is subject to an uncommenced repeal and the section is capable of operating in its own right, it might not always be clear to the reader that the section is intended to be repealed at the same time as the Part into which it is inserted. An express repeal of the amendment should be made to put the point beyond doubt.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.8.17 An alternative approach that can sometimes be used to tackle these issues is to make transitory provision that has effect only until the repeal is commenced.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e“Until section 2 of Act 2 (which repeals section 1 of Act 1) is brought into force, section 1 of Act 1 has effect as if, after “dogs” there were inserted “and cats”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.8.18 This is likely to be of particular use in cases where the commencement of the repeal is imminent.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"drafting-a-provision-that-needs-to-work-with-existing-and-prospective-provisions\"\u003eDrafting a provision that needs to work with existing and prospective provisions\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.8.19 Below are examples of techniques that may be useful when drafting a provision that needs to take account of prospective amendments as well as working with the existing law.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.8.20 The examples assume that—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• Act 1 is in force\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• Act 2 inserts a new section 1A and is not yet in force.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• A Bill is inserting a new section 3A into Act 1, referring to an Authority’s functions under sections 1 and 1A.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE 1\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(1) After section 3 of Act 1 insert—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e“3A The Authority must publish an annual report on the exercise of its functions under section 1.”\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(2) In section 3A of Act 1 (as inserted by subsection (1)), for “section 1” substitute “sections 1 and 1A”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE 2\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(1) After section 3 of Act 1 insert—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e“3A The Authority must publish an annual report on the exercise of its functions under sections 1 and 1A.”\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(2) Until section X of Act 2 comes [fully] into force, section 3A of Act 1 (as inserted by subsection (1)) has effect as if the reference to section 1A of Act 1 were omitted.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE 3\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAfter section 3 of Act 1 insert—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e“3A (1) The Authority must publish an annual report on the exercise of its functions under sections 1 and 1A.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(2) Until section X of Act 2 comes [fully] into force, subsection (1) has effect as has effect as if the reference to section 1A were omitted.”\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.8.21 When considering the approaches in Examples 2 and 3 consideration should be given to the trade-off between the advantages of bringing the reader’s attention to the transitional provision and the disadvantages of cluttering up the statute book in the long term.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"non-textual-modifications\"\u003e7.9 6.9 NON-TEXTUAL MODIFICATIONS\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"distinguishing-between-textual-amendments-and-non-textual-modifications\"\u003eDistinguishing between textual amendments and non-textual modifications\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.9.1 A “non-textual modification” is a modification of an enactment that is not intended to result in a change to the text of the modified enactment when the enactment is next printed (in contrast to a textual amendment, which is).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.9.2 There have been occasions where it has not been clear to departments, or to those who produce and edit statutory text, whether something is a textual amendment or a non-textual modification. Sometimes non-textual modifications have even been printed as textual amendments.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.9.3 The potential for confusion arises because the word “modification” is sometimes used simply to refer to a change, whether textual or non-textual. It is therefore important to make it clear what is intended.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.9.4 Sometimes non-textual modifications are drafted in essentially the same form as a textual amendment, the only difference being in the opening wording—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE (to avoid)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(1) Section 3 applies to fine defaulters as to offenders but with the following modifications—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) in subsection (1) for “offence” substitute “default”, and\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) in subsection (2) for “6 months” substitute “3 months”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.9.5 This might readily be mistaken for a textual amendment. The opening words indicate that something other than a textual amendment is intended, but the rest is exactly the same as a textual amendment. It would be particularly easy to lose sight of the opening words if the list of substitutions and other changes were very long.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.9.6 It would be clearer, in the first place, if the subjunctive mood were used to indicate that there is no intention actually to substitute the text—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE (in a simple case involving few modifications)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(1) Section 3 applies to fine defaulters as to offenders but as if—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) in subsection (1) for “offence” there were substituted “default”, and\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) in subsection (2) for “6 months” there were substituted “3 months”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE (in a complex case involving more modifications)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(1) Section 3 applies to fine defaulters as to offenders but as if it were modified as follows.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(2) In subsection (1) for “offence” substitute “default”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(3) In subsection (2) for “6 months” substitute “3 months”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(4) …\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.9.7 Another approach which is clear is to avoid the reference to substitution altogether—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(1) Section 3 applies to fine defaulters as to offenders but as if—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) in subsection (1) the reference to an offence were to a default; and\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) in subsection (2) the reference to 6 months were to 3 months.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"amendments-other-minor-points\"\u003e7.10 6.10 AMENDMENTS: OTHER MINOR POINTS\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"parenthetical-description-of-provision-amended\"\u003eParenthetical description of provision amended\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.10.1 It is common practice to give a brief description in brackets of the provision that is being amended, to give the context of the amendment and perhaps its significance. It may be particularly helpful to do so in the case of an important substantive amendment. Sometimes parenthetical descriptions may enable a reader to see exactly what an amendment is doing, though it is hard to achieve this consistently in a Bill of any length.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.10.2 Include a parenthetical description only if it is useful. It may not be useful in a Schedule of consequential amendments, where there is no important substantive effect to be described (and fewer readers to describe it to). For example, if you are simply changing the name of a body in all existing legislation, there may be little point in describing every provision where you are making the change.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.10.3 It is also unlikely to be worthwhile to give the description of a section after which a new section is inserted, unless there is a very close connection between the two.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.10.4 The parenthetical description will often match the heading of the section or Schedule to which it relates, but it does not have to do so. It may be better, for readers of the Bill, to describe the section in a different way.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.10.5 Be careful about whether you are describing a whole section or a particular provision in it. The heading of a section may be unhelpful as a description of an individual subsection. For example, if section 1 is called “cases to which Part 1 applies”, and specifies those cases, but subsection (3) sets out some exceptions, it would be misleading to say “In section 1(3) (cases to which Part 1 applies)….”\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.10.6 For the location of parenthetical references, see paragraph 3.10.6.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"punctuation-1\"\u003ePunctuation\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.10.7 Where inserted or substituted words end with a full stop before the closing quotes, do not add a further full stop after the closing quotes.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"no-need-to-amend-spent-provisions\"\u003eNo need to amend spent provisions\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e6.10.8 There is no need for amendments to update a provision that is spent, whether or not subject to an uncommenced repeal. But be sure that the provision is spent — the fact that a repeal has not been commenced might indicate that the repealed provision is not (or not yet) spent.\u003c/p\u003e"

        "text": "\u003ch3 id=\"bodies-corporate\"\u003e8.1 7.1 BODIES CORPORATE\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"form-of-words-to-establish-statutory-corporation\"\u003eForm of words to establish statutory corporation\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e7.1.1 When drafting a proposition that itself creates a statutory corporation or office, use the form of words “[Name] is established” in preference to alternatives such as “there is to be”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e7.1.2 This does not prevent drafters from using “there continues to be” when consolidating or re-enacting a provision that sets up a statutory corporation or office or when turning an existing non-statutory body into a statutory one.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"singular-or-plural\"\u003eSingular or plural?\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e7.1.3 Statutory corporations and other bodies corporate should be treated as singular nouns.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf the authority is satisfied that the conditions are met, it may….\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e7.1.4 When textually amending an Act that uses the plural, it may be necessary to follow suit in order to avoid confusion.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"senedd-cymru\"\u003e8.2 7.2 SENEDD CYMRU\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"renaming-of-welsh-legislature\"\u003eRenaming of Welsh legislature\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e7.2.1 The Senedd and Elections (Wales) Act 2020 (“SEWA”) changed the name of the Welsh legislature (originally called the “National Assembly for Wales”).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e7.2.2 Section 1 of the Government of Wales Act 2006 (“GOWA”), as amended by SEWA, provides that “There is to be a parliament for Wales to be known as Senedd Cymru or the Welsh Parliament (referred to in this Act as “the Senedd”)”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e7.2.3 Office practice for Westminster legislation is to refer to the body by its Welsh name only. This is consistent with the practice for legislation passed in Wales.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e7.2.4 The starting point then is that the body should be referred to as “Senedd Cymru”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e7.2.5 Where you are referring to the body a number of times you might choose to use the form “the Senedd”, and then define that to mean “Senedd Cymru”.         "text": "\u003ch3 id=\"periods-of-time-introductory\"\u003e9.1 8.1 PERIODS OF TIME Introductory\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"this-part-is-about-how-to-express-a-period-of-time-where-you-need-to-know-exactly-when-the-period-begins-or-ends17\"\u003e8.1.1 This Part is about how to express a period of time where you need to know exactly when the period begins or ends.\u003csup id=\"fnref:17\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:17\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 17]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\n\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eBeginnings\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e8.1.2 An unambiguous formulation is to describe the period as beginning “with” a particular day. This makes it clear that the day itself is counted within the period.\u003csup id=\"fnref:18\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:18\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 18]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe taxpayer must be resident in the United Kingdom throughout the period of two years beginning with the day on which the asset is acquired.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e8.1.3 Avoid referring to a period beginning “on” a particular day. This may leave open the question of the exact time on the day in question when the period begins — and, accordingly, if the period is a whole number of days, months or years, exactly when it ends.\u003csup id=\"fnref:19\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:19\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 19]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e8.1.4 Also avoid referring to a period running “from” or “after” a particular event. This will usually be taken to exclude the day on which the event takes place.\u003csup id=\"fnref:20\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:20\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 20]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e But that is not invariably the case — it will depend on the context. So you will not necessarily get a certain result.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"endings\"\u003eEndings\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e8.1.5 Periods determined by reference to their end should be expressed to end “with” a particular day as opposed to “on” it, for the reasons given above.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE The taxpayer must have been resident in the United Kingdom throughout the period of two years ending with the day on which the asset was disposed of.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"within\"\u003eWithin\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e8.1.6 A requirement to do something within a period is not necessarily the same as a requirement to do it before the end of the period.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLES\u003c/p\u003e\u003col\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eAn appeal may be brought at any time within the period of 14 days beginning with the day after that on which the decision was made.\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003e\n    \u003cp\u003eAn appeal may be brought at any time before the end of the period of 14 days beginning with the day after that on which the decision was made.\u003c/p\u003e\n  \u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003cp\u003e8.1.7 If “within” is used (example 1), an appeal may not be brought on the day of the decision, because that is not within the period beginning the following day.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e8.1.8 But “before the end of” (example 2) appears to leave open the possibility of action being taken on the day of the decision, because that is, literally, before the period ends. However, there is a possibility that such a proposition might be interpreted by the courts as preventing action from being taken before the day by reference to which the period is calculated (and so “before the end of” might then come to the same thing as “within”).\u003csup id=\"fnref:21\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:21\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 21]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"periods-triggered-by-events\"\u003ePeriods triggered by events\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e8.1.9 If an event triggers a period for something to happen — such as a decision after which there is a period for an appeal — it is a question of policy whether the day of the event should be included or not.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e8.1.10 If you do not want to include the day of the event, it is probably best to start the period with the day after the event, and say that the action must take place within the period (as in example 1 in paragraph 8.1.6).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e8.1.11 If you do want to include the day of the event, while following example 2 might work, it carries the risk referred to in paragraph 8.1.8. So a safer way of doing it is like this—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAn appeal may be brought at any time within the period of 14 days beginning with the day on which the decision was made.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e8.1.12 Note that, taken literally, this includes the earlier part of the day of the event. That may or may not matter in practice. In the case of an appeal, it is obviously impossible for the appeal to be made before the decision. If it is important to exclude earlier times, you will need to be very clear that only the remainder of the day of the event is included.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e8.1.13 If the period starts with the day of an event and is short, it may be worth considering whether as a matter of policy the number of days should be increased by one, to take account of the fact that in practice the whole of the first day may not be available.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"before-preferable-to-by-a-particular-day\"\u003e“Before” preferable to “by” a particular day\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e8.1.14 Saying that something has to be done “before” a particular day is unambiguous. Saying that it has to be done “by” a particular day may leave room for argument about whether the thing can be done on the day itself.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"working-days\"\u003eWorking days\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e8.1.15 Weekends and bank holidays will not be treated differently from other days unless you make express provision to that effect. So, if your period is expressed in days, and is very short, the policy might be only to count working days.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e8.1.16 Here are examples of definitions of “working day”, producing different policy results.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE (1)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn this section, “working day” means any day other than—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) Saturday or Sunday,\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) Christmas Day or Good Friday, or\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(c) a day which is a bank holiday under the Banking and Financial Dealings Act 1971 in England and Wales.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE (2)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn this section, “working day”, in relation to part of the United Kingdom, means a day other than—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) Saturday or Sunday, or\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) a day which is a bank holiday under the Banking and Financial Dealings Act 1971 in that or any other part of the United Kingdom.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e8.1.17 Note that under the Banking and Financial Dealings Act 1971, Christmas Day and Good Friday are “bank holidays” in Scotland but not elsewhere in the United Kingdom.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"months\"\u003eMonths\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e8.1.18 Months are a particular problem because of their varying lengths. 8.1.19 A period expressed in months beginning with a day will expire “on the eve of” (ie immediately before) the date corresponding to that with which the period begins.\u003csup id=\"fnref:22\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:22\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 22]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e For example, a period of one month beginning with 6 April will expire “on the eve of” 6 May - that is, the end of 5 May.\u003csup id=\"fnref:23\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:23\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 23]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e8.1.20 So, where a period is expressed in months, the number of days in it will vary according to which day of which month the period begins on. A period of “1 month” beginning with 6 April (and therefore ending at the end of 5 May) will be shorter than a period of “1 month” beginning with 6 May (because April is shorter than May).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e8.1.21 If variation of length in different cases is not desirable, it may be worth considering whether it would be better to express the period in weeks or days. But equality of length comes at the price of difficulty of calculation: it’s easy to see that the end of the period of 3 months beginning with 6 April ends with 5 July, but harder to determine when the period of 90 days beginning with 6 April ends.\u003c/p\u003e"
