      "@type": "Question",
      "name": "10. PART 9 SUBORDINATE LEGISLATION",
      "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/drafting-bills-for-parliament/2024-03-19-drafting-guidance#part-9-subordinate-legislation",
      "acceptedAnswer": {
        "@type": "Answer",
        "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/drafting-bills-for-parliament/2024-03-19-drafting-guidance#part-9-subordinate-legislation",
        "text": "\u003ch3 id=\"form-of-subordinate-legislation\"\u003e10.1 9.1 FORM OF SUBORDINATE LEGISLATION\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"generally-regulations-not-orders\"\u003eGenerally: regulations, not orders\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.1.1 Powers to make subordinate legislation by statutory instrument should generally take the form of powers to make regulations rather than orders.\u003csup id=\"fnref:24\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:24\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 24]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.1.2 This applies to powers to commence an Act as well as to other powers.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.1.3 It does not alter the practice of using—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• rules (for provision determining the procedure of a body or process),\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• Orders in Council, or\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• orders subject to special procedure under the Statutory Orders (Special Procedure) Act 1945.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.1.4 There are some cases where it may still be appropriate to create a new order-making power, for example when amending an old Act that contains order-making powers or when creating a new power that needs to be exercised with existing order-making powers. There is of course section 105 of the Deregulation Act 2015 (which, among other things, allows provision which may be made by order to be made by regulations).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"commencement-powers-conferred-on-northern-ireland-departments\"\u003eCommencement powers conferred on Northern Ireland departments\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.1.5 Where a commencement power conferred on a Northern Ireland department is exercisable by statutory rule, it should take the form of an order-making power (rather than a regulation-making power) for consistency with the practice in Northern Ireland.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"enabling-powers\"\u003e10.2 9.2 ENABLING POWERS\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"different-provision-for-different-cases\"\u003eDifferent provision for different cases\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.2.1 There are many examples on the statute book of provisions authorising delegated powers to be exercised differently for “different cases”, “different purposes” and “different circumstances”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.2.2 First, consider whether this kind of provision is actually needed. To exercise a power so as to make different provision for cases that are materially different would not, on the whole, be surprising (one would expect like cases to be treated alike and different cases differently). So a starting point would be to consider whether, if the power were exercised to make different provision for different cases, would that be at all unexpected or unusual.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.2.3 If something further is needed, a choice then has to be made as to what exactly should be said: “cases”, “purposes”, “circumstances” or something else?\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.2.4 “Different purposes” is probably wider and more flexible than “different cases” (“different purposes” is usually considered to include “different cases”, but not vice versa). So perhaps that is the first port of call. But “different cases” is of course possible. Try to avoid both “purposes” and “cases”. “Circumstances” will rarely add anything.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.2.5 That said, it might be possible to be more specific about how the power will be used, in which case that is likely to be more helpful. For example, if there is a power to regulate football stadiums, which might need to be exercised to make different provision for different stadiums, it might be more helpful to say just that than resort to the more abstract “different cases” or “different purposes”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.2.6 “Different descriptions of case” will rarely add anything to “different cases”. In the unlikely eventuality that the subordinate legislation may need to make provision about a single case, then it would be best to make that as clear as possible rather than relying on a distinction between “different cases” and “different descriptions of case”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.2.7 For “different provision for different purposes” in the context of a commencement power, see Part 10.6.10 - 10.6.19.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"different-provision-for-different-areas\"\u003eDifferent provision for different areas\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.2.8 One would expect the law to treat people in the same way unless there is a relevant difference between them. It is not obvious that where people happen to live is, in itself, a relevant difference. So if the policy is for a power to be exercised differently in different areas within a single jurisdiction, or differently in different jurisdictions of the UK, in relation to a reserved matter, express words should be used to make that clear.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.2.9 On the whole, we do not assume that a power to make different provision for different purposes includes a power to make different provision for different areas. Forms of words which imply that differential exercise by area is just an aspect of making different provision for different purposes should be avoided.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eRegulations under section 1 may make—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) different provision for different purposes, and\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) different provision for different areas.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eNOT\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eRegulations under section 1 may make different provision for different purposes (including different provision for different areas).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"non-exercise-of-powers\"\u003eNon-exercise of powers\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.2.10 Some provisions about powers to make subordinate legislation expressly provide that it is possible for the power not to be exercised in certain cases. For example, the legislation may say that the power may be exercised “generally or only for specified cases” or “to make the full provision to which the power extends or any less provision”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.2.11 Whether this kind of provision is necessary will depend on the context. In many cases it will not be necessary. For example, if what is conferred is a power that need not be exercised at all (“The Secretary of State may make regulations…”) it may follow that, if it is exercised, it need not be exercised in all cases. On the other hand there may be cases where the context suggests that the power must be exercised for all cases or not at all. Equally, where a person has a duty to make subordinate legislation, it may seem to follow, without express wording to the contrary, that the person needs to make legislation covering the full range of possible cases.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.2.12 So do not include this kind of provision as a matter of course. If something is needed, it may be that power to make different provision for different purposes or cases will be sufficient: if different provision may be made for different cases, it may well follow that no provision need be made for some cases.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"procedure\"\u003e10.3 9.3 PROCEDURE\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"subordinate-legislation-made-by-a-minister-of-the-crown\"\u003eSubordinate legislation made by a Minister of the Crown\u003c/h4\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"making-an-instrument-a-statutory-instrument\"\u003eMaking an instrument a statutory instrument\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.1 Section 1 of the Statutory Instruments Act 1946 states—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e“Where by… any Act passed after the commencement of this Act power to make, confirm or approve orders, rules, regulations or other subordinate legislation is conferred on His Majesty in Council or on any Minister of the Crown then, if the power is expressed—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) in the case of a power conferred on His Majesty, to be exercisable by Order in Council;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) in the case of a power conferred on a Minister of the Crown, to be exercisable by statutory instrument,\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eany document by which that power is exercised shall be known as a “statutory instrument” and the provisions of this Act shall apply thereto accordingly.”\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.2 To attract section 1 of the 1946 Act it is sufficient to say—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eRegulations [or An order] [made by the relevant Minister] under this section are to be made by statutory instrument.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.3 It may sometimes be neater to roll up the attraction of section 1 with the power itself.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Secretary of State may by regulations made by statutory instrument provide…\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.4 This may in particular be neater where you have a simple power and everything can be dealt with in a single subsection. This technique is often used, for example, for commencement powers (“on such day as the Secretary of State may by regulations made by statutory instrument appoint”).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.5 If you have a number of powers to be exercised by statutory instrument, it may be best to have a single provision at the end of the Act, rather than saying the same thing several times over in different places. This is technical provision which is unlikely to be of interest to most readers.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"negative-resolution-procedure\"\u003eNegative resolution procedure\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.6 Use the following formula—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA statutory instrument containing regulations under this Act is subject to annulment in pursuance of a resolution of either House of Parliament.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.7 Note that it is the statutory instrument, rather than the regulations, which is said to be subject to annulment. This is to be consistent with section 5 of the 1946 Act. “In pursuance of” is recommended for the same reason.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"affirmative-resolution-procedure\"\u003eAffirmative resolution procedure\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.8 Use the following formula— A statutory instrument containing regulations under this Act may not be made unless a draft of the instrument has been laid before and approved by a resolution of each House of Parliament.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.9 The formula refers to a draft of the statutory instrument containing regulations, rather than a draft of the regulations themselves, for consistency with the wording of section 6 of the 1946 Act.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.10 If you need to secure that a statutory instrument subject to affirmative procedure may also contain provision that would otherwise be subject to negative procedure, make that very clear. One way in which that is sometimes done is by using the formulation in 9.3.8 with the addition of the words “(whether alone or with other provision)” after “containing”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"made-affirmative-procedure\"\u003eMade affirmative procedure\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.11 Use the following form of words as a starting point—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(1) A statutory instrument containing regulations under section [x] must be laid before Parliament after being made.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(2) Regulations contained in a statutory instrument laid before Parliament under subsection (1) cease to have effect at the end of the period of [28 days] beginning with the day on which the instrument is made unless, during that period, the instrument is approved by a resolution of each House of Parliament.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(3) In calculating the period of [28 days], no account is to be taken of any whole days that fall within a period during which—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) Parliament is dissolved or prorogued, or\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) either House of Parliament is adjourned for more than four days.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(4) If regulations cease to have effect as a result of subsection (2), that does not—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) affect the validity of anything previously done under the regulations, or\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) prevent the making of new regulations.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"wales-1\"\u003eWales\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.12 The position in relation to subordinate legislation made by the Welsh Ministers is similar to the position in relation to subordinate legislation made by a Minister of the Crown—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• section 1(1A) of the Statutory Instruments Act 1946 provides that where a power is conferred on the Welsh Ministers to make subordinate legislation and it is expressed to be exercisable by statutory instrument, the 1946 Act applies;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• section 11A of the 1946 Act modifies the Act so as to ensure that the procedural provisions work in relation to Senedd Cymru.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.13 So use the following formulations—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Welsh Ministers may by regulations made by statutory instrument provide…\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eRegulations made by the Welsh Ministers under this Act are to be made by statutory instrument.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA statutory instrument containing regulations under this Act is subject to annulment in pursuance of a resolution of Senedd Cymru.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA statutory instrument containing regulations under this Act may not be made unless a draft of the instrument has been laid before and approved by a resolution of Senedd Cymru.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"scotland-1\"\u003eScotland\u003c/h4\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"making-an-instrument-a-scottish-statutory-instrument\"\u003eMaking an instrument a Scottish statutory instrument\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.14 A power of the Scottish Ministers to make an order, regulations or rules under an enactment is generally exercisable by Scottish statutory instrument: see section 27(1) and (2)(a) of the Interpretation and Legislative Reform (Scotland) Act 2010 (asp 10). “Enactment” is defined to include Westminster Acts (see Schedule 1).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.15 Where section 27(2)(a) of the 2010 Act applies it is unnecessary to provide separately in the enabling Act that the power is exercisable by Scottish statutory instrument; the established practice is to rely on section 27. This applies to powers conferred by free-standing provision or inserted into an existing Act (as does the guidance below on attracting affirmative and negative procedures).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.16 Section 27(3) contains exceptions for cases involving a Minister of the Crown as well as the Scottish Ministers. If you are dealing with such a case you need to look at the exceptions.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"negative-and-affirmative-resolution-procedures-for-scottish-sis\"\u003eNegative and affirmative resolution procedures for Scottish SIs\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.17 The affirmative and negative resolution procedures for Scottish statutory instruments are set out in sections 28 and 29 of the Interpretation and Legislative Reform (Scotland) Act 2010 (asp 10).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.18 The procedures can be attracted by simply providing that the relevant regulations etc are subject to the negative/affirmative procedure.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eRegulations made by the Scottish Ministers under this Act are subject to the [affirmative/ negative] procedure.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.19 Note that the regulations (rather than the Scottish statutory instrument) are expressed to be subject to the relevant procedure. This is in contrast to the guidance in relation to statutory instruments under the Statutory Instruments Act 1946 and reflects the different wording of the 1946 and 2010 Acts.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.20 Section 30 of the 2010 Act provides that if neither the negative nor affirmative procedure applies to devolved subordinate legislation the Scottish statutory instrument containing it must be laid before the Scottish Parliament. If this bare laying requirement is to be disapplied, the relevant enabling power must be added to the list in section 30(4).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"signposting\"\u003eSignposting\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.21 Where relevant, it may be worth signposting the Interpretation and Legislative Reform (Scotland) Act 2010 (asp 10). A reader who has not come across “negative procedure” or “affirmative procedure” before could be puzzled and may benefit from a signpost. Taking the example in 9.3.16, one possibility would be to add “(see Part 2 of the Interpretation and Legislative Reform (Scotland) Act 2010 (asp 10))”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"northern-ireland-1\"\u003eNorthern Ireland\u003c/h4\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"making-an-instrument-a-statutory-rule\"\u003eMaking an instrument a statutory rule\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.22 A power of a Northern Ireland Department to make an order, regulations, rules or other subordinate legislation is generally exercisable by “statutory rule”: see the Statutory Rules (Northern Ireland) Order 1979 (S.I. 1979/1573 (N.I. 12)). The 1979 Order provides for the registration and numbering of statutory rules.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.23 Article 4 of the 1979 Order provides: “4. In this Order “statutory rules” means-\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) all orders, rules, regulations or byelaws having effect in Northern Ireland made after 31st December 1958 by a rule-making authority in exercise of any power of a legislative character conferred by—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e…\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(iv) any Act of the Parliament of the United Kingdom passed after 1st January 1974, if the power is expressed to be exercisable by statutory rule for the purposes of the Statutory Rules Act (Northern Ireland) 1958 or this Order.”\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.24 The 1979 Order can be attracted by providing that the power of the relevant Northern Ireland department to make regulations is exercisable by statutory rule for the purposes of the Order.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA power of [the Northern Ireland Department] to make regulations under this Act is exercisable by statutory rule for the purposes of the Statutory Rules (Northern Ireland) Order 1979 (S.I. 1979/1573 (N.I. 12)).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.25 Note that the power is expressed to be exercisable by statutory rule, which contrasts with the approach taken in relation to England or Wales where the usual approach is to provide for the regulations to be made by statutory instrument etc.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"negative-and-affirmative-procedures-for-statutory-rules\"\u003eNegative and affirmative procedures for statutory rules\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.26 For negative instruments, the usual approach in relation to Northern Ireland is to attract the definition of “subject to negative resolution” in section 41 of the Interpretation Act (Northern Ireland) 1954. The definition does not, without more, apply in relation to Westminster Acts and it extends to Northern Ireland only. To attract the definition you therefore need to refer to it expressly.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eRegulations made by [the Northern Ireland Department] under this Act are subject to negative resolution within the meaning given by section 41(6) of the Interpretation Act (Northern Ireland) 1954.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.27 For the affirmative procedure the usual approach is to adopt wording along the following lines.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eRegulations may not be made by [the Northern Ireland Department] under this Act unless a draft of the regulations has been laid before and approved by a resolution of the Northern Ireland Assembly.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.28 Although section 41 of the Interpretation Act (Northern Ireland) 1954 defines “subject to affirmative resolution”, the procedure referred to is an unusual form of affirmative procedure, so it is rare to rely on that definition.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.29 Note that in both cases, negative and affirmative, the regulations (rather than the statutory rules) are expressed to be subject to the relevant procedure. This is in contrast to the guidance in relation to statutory instruments under the Statutory Instruments Act 1946 and reflects the different wording of the Northern Ireland legislation.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"location-of-procedural-provision\"\u003eLocation of procedural provision\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.30 In some Bills, each provision which confers a power to make subordinate legislation applies any necessary parliamentary procedure. This may be helpful to readers of the Bill in Parliament, so they can see immediately what level of scrutiny is proposed.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.31 But, where a Bill confers a number of powers to make subordinate legislation, it may be more helpful to readers of the eventual Act if these matters are dealt with in general provisions situated at the back of the Act (since for most readers of the Act this is rather technical material which is unlikely to be of interest). See also paragraph 10.6.23 (separation of commencement powers from other powers).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.3.32 A “hybrid” approach is adopted in some Acts. The provision conferring the power says that it is subject to the “negative resolution procedure” or the “affirmative resolution procedure”. Then, at the end of the Act, there is a definition of “negative resolution procedure” or “affirmative resolution procedure” (or both).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"laying-documents-before-parliament\"\u003e10.4 9.4 LAYING DOCUMENTS BEFORE PARLIAMENT\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"laying-documents-before-parliament-1\"\u003eLaying documents before Parliament\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.4.1 Section 1(1) of the Laying of Documents before Parliament (Interpretation) Act 1948 provides that references to the laying of instruments and other documents “before Parliament” are to be construed as references to their laying before each House of Parliament unless the contrary intention appears.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.4.2 Section 1(1) should normally be relied on whenever it will produce the correct result. That is, normally you should say that the instrument or other document should be laid “before Parliament” rather than “before each House of Parliament”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.4.3 This does not apply to statutory instruments subject to the affirmative resolution procedure because they also have to be approved by a resolution of each House — see 9.3.8.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"amending-subordinate-legislation\"\u003e10.5 9.5 AMENDING SUBORDINATE LEGISLATION\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"amending-subordinate-legislation-1\"\u003eAmending subordinate legislation\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.5.1 A Bill is occasionally used to amend subordinate legislation.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.5.2 The question arises whether a saving is needed to allow the enabling power under which the subordinate legislation is made to be re-exercised in future to amend material inserted by the Bill. A saving should not be included as a matter of course and should be included only in the rare case where, as a matter of statutory interpretation, there is something about the context of the amendments which might cast doubt on the future exercise of the power.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e9.5.3 If proposed amendments need to go beyond the scope of the enabling power this will normally indicate that the legislative result should be achieved by some other means (for example, by free-standing provision in the Bill).\u003c/p\u003e"

        "text": "\u003ch3 id=\"introduction-3\"\u003e11.1 10.1 INTRODUCTION\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.1.1 This Part is about provisions of a general nature that appear towards the end of a Bill.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.1.2 The Appendix contains example clauses that illustrate many of the recommendations in this Part. The example clauses will not produce the right result in every case so careful thought needs to be given about how far to follow them.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"order-of-final-provisions\"\u003e11.2 10.2 ORDER OF FINAL PROVISIONS\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"running-order\"\u003eRunning order\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.2.1 Use this order as a starting point—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ePower to make consequential provision\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eRegulations (including parliamentary procedure)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eInterpretation\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eExtent\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eCommencement and transitional provision\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eShort title\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.2.2 In a very short Bill where there is no need to include a power to make transitional provision in the commencement clause it may make sense to deal with extent, commencement and short title in a single clause.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.2.3 Provision may also be needed for—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eGeneral provisions about offences (bodies corporate, unincorporated associations)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eDirections\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eNotices/service of documents\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFinancial provisions\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eCrown application\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eDevolution Application to Scillies/Isle of Man/Channel Islands\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIndex\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"heading\"\u003eHeading\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.2.4 If a single italic heading or Part heading is used to cover all the final provisions of a general nature, it should be “General” (rather than, for example, “Supplementary” or “Miscellaneous”).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"financial-provision\"\u003e11.3 10.3 FINANCIAL PROVISION\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"introduction-4\"\u003eIntroduction\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.3.1 This relates to provisions of Bills (starting in the House of Commons) which deal with effects on public expenditure.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"clause-heading\"\u003eClause heading\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.3.2 The heading for clauses dealing with effects on public expenditure should be “Financial provision[s]”, whatever the precise nature of the effects.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"form-of-provision\"\u003eForm of provision\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.3.3 It is recommended that provision dealing with such effects should refer to—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThere is to be paid out of money provided by Parliament—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) any expenditure incurred under or by virtue of the Act by [the Secretary of State], [a Minister of the Crown], [a person holding office under His Majesty] [or by a government department], and\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) any increase attributable to the Act in the sums payable under any other Act out of money so provided.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.3.4 This wording can then be reflected in the associated money resolution.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"extent\"\u003e11.4 10.4 EXTENT\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"what-is-extent\"\u003eWhat is extent?\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.4.1 A proposition about the “extent” of a statutory provision is a proposition about the jurisdictions whose law is being changed by the provision.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.4.2 The relevant jurisdictions within the United Kingdom are—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• England and Wales (note that this is a single jurisdiction);\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• Scotland;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• Northern Ireland.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.4.3 “Extent” should be distinguished from “application”, which concerns the persons and matters to which the provision relates. For example, a legal proposition may “extend” to England and Wales - that is, form part of the law of England and Wales - even though it only applies to persons in England.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"state-extent-positively\"\u003eState extent positively\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.4.4 There is a strong judicial presumption that, in the absence of provision to the contrary, Acts of the Westminster Parliament extend to each part of the UK but not beyond it (even though Parliament may legislate, in particular, for the Channel Islands, the Isle of Man and the British overseas territories).\u003csup id=\"fnref:25\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:25\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 25]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.4.5 However, the recommended approach is not to rely on that presumption but to spell out the extent of all the provisions of the Bill (including the final provisions).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.4.6 So, for an Act or a provision of an Act which extends to the whole of the UK, but not beyond, spell its extent out positively.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis Act extends to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.4.7 Where a provision extends to all three jurisdictions within the UK, it is better to refer to each of them than to “the United Kingdom” as such.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.4.8 Equally, for an Act which extends to one or two jurisdictions within the UK, spell that out positively.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLES\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis Act extends to England and Wales.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis Act extends to England and Wales and Scotland.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.4.9 There may of course be cases where it is not convenient, or not helpful, to state extent expressly, even if the Act is thought to extend only to the UK: for example, where an Act simply amends an existing Act which itself has no specific extent provision.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.4.10 A different approach will also be needed for an Act which extends, or might extend, beyond the UK.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.4.11 Remember to consider the extent of amendments where providing expressly for the extent of general provisions. Normally general provisions should extend at least as far as each jurisdiction to which any provision of the Bill (including an amendment) extends.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"amendments-with-the-same-extent-as-the-amended-act\"\u003eAmendments with the same extent as the amended Act\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.4.12 Where an Act contains a number of textual amendments, and the intention is that they have the same extent as the enactments amended, it is often convenient to say just that.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLES\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAny amendment or repeal made by this Act has the same extent as the provision amended or repealed.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAny amendment, repeal or revocation made by this Act has the same extent as the provision amended, repealed or revoked.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.4.13 But watch out for cases where the catch-all wording does not produce a clear result. For example, the catch-all wording is unclear where you are inserting a new section between two sections with different extents: what is the extent of the provision amended?\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.4.14 There are also other cases where it may be more useful for the reader to be told what the extent of each amendment is, rather than just to be told that the amendment has the same extent as something else.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.4.15 Whatever approach is adopted, make sure that you know the extent of the existing provision in each case. It is possible that an existing enactment may have been extended to another jurisdiction by another enactment.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.4.16 Where you are amending an Act which also extends to the Channel Islands or the Isle of Man (whether it does so on its face or by virtue of a power to extend it there), the general kind of wording will need to be limited to the United Kingdom, so as to avoid the amendments extending to the Islands directly by operation of the Bill.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAny amendment made by this Act has the same extent within the United Kingdom as the provision amended.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"amendments-with-different-extent-from-the-amended-act\"\u003eAmendments with different extent from the amended Act\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.4.17 Try to avoid making amendments that have a more limited extent than the provision amended (for example, an amendment to a UK Act where the amendment is limited to England and Wales). Otherwise you will create parallel texts in different parts of the UK, which is confusing and a potential trap.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.4.18 One way of doing this may be to limit the application of your proposition rather than its extent (see paragraph 10.4.3).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"amendment-of-extent-provisions\"\u003eAmendment of extent provisions\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.4.19 Draft on the basis that the extent of an amendment is governed by the extent provision of the amending Act. On that basis, there is no need to amend the extent provision of the Act amended, even if the amendment has a different extent from other provisions in that Act; and doing so should be avoided.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"complex-propositions-about-extent\"\u003eComplex propositions about extent\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.4.20 An Act may well contain provisions having different extent within the UK. In such cases the extent provision is likely to be complicated. It is difficult to give any guidance in advance about the best way of designing an extent provision here. Everything depends on the particular circumstances.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.4.21 You will want to produce a provision which is itself as simple as possible. You will also want to produce a provision which allows a reader to find the extent of any given provision as easily as possible. These two aims may sometimes conflict.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.4.22 If the great majority of the Act has a particular extent, with only limited exceptions, it probably helps to start with the main case and then set out the exceptions.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.4.23 So, if the exceptions have a narrower extent than the majority of the Act, it is possible to set out the wider expression of extent and then reduce it.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(1) This Act extends to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, subject as follows.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(2) Section 77 and Schedule 6 extend to England and Wales and Northern Ireland only.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(3) Section 79 and Schedule 8 extend to England and Wales and Scotland only.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.4.24 Conversely, if the bulk of the Act has a narrow extent (say, England and Wales only), it may be best to start off with that and then build up.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(1) This Act extends to England and Wales only, subject as follows.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(2) Section 61 extends to England and Wales and Scotland.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(3) Part 5 and this Part extend to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.4.25 Do not make readers search through all the provisions of the extent clause to find out the extent of the particular provision in which they are interested.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE (to avoid)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(1) This Act extends to England and Wales only, subject as follows.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(2) Sections 12 to 15 extend also to Scotland.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(3) Sections 16 to 22 extend to Scotland only.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(4) Sections 11 to 14 extend also to Northern Ireland.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(5) Sections 31 and 78 extend to Northern Ireland only.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.4.26 The problem in that example is that to find the extent of any particular provision the reader needs first to read subsection (1) and then to look at subsection (2) to see whether it also extends to Scotland and then subsection (4) to see whether it also extends to Northern Ireland (and check subsections (3) and (5) to make sure it is not a provision extending only to Scotland or Northern Ireland). This takes time and may cause error.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.4.27 The reader is likely to want to know the jurisdictions to which any given provision extends. So rather than setting out a general provision which is then qualified, it might be better to set out what the extent of each provision of the Act is, even if it results in a longer extent provision.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(1) Parts 1 to 7 extend to England and Wales only.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(2) Part 8 extends to England and Wales and Scotland.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(3) Part 9 extends to England and Wales and Northern Ireland.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(4) This Part extends to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"powers-to-extend-to-channel-islands-and-isle-of-man\"\u003e11.5 10.5 POWERS TO EXTEND TO CHANNEL ISLANDS AND ISLE OF MAN\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"introduction-5\"\u003eIntroduction\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.5.1 This is about what to say where provision in a Bill is, by means of a power conferred on His Majesty by Order in Council, to extend to the Channel Islands and/or the Isle of Man (“the Islands”).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.5.2 A power to extend provision to the Islands should not be subject to any Parliamentary procedure.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"free-standing-provision\"\u003eFree-standing provision\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.5.3 For a power to extend free-standing provision to the Islands, the recommended form of words is—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eHis Majesty may by Order in Council provide for [any of the provisions of this Act] to extend, with or without modifications, to any of the Channel Islands or to the Isle of Man.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.5.4 If the provision to be extended is the repeal of an Act, the recommended form of words is—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eHis Majesty may by Order in Council provide for the repeal of [Act x] in [section y] to extend to any of the Channel Islands or to the Isle of Man.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"textual-amendment-of-act-which-extends-to-islands-on-its-face\"\u003eTextual amendment of Act which extends to Islands on its face\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.5.5 For a power to extend amendments to the Islands, in a case where the Act amended extends on its face to the Islands, the recommended form of words is—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eHis Majesty may by Order in Council provide for any of the amendments made by [or under] this Act of any part of [the Act being amended] to extend, with or without modifications, to any of the Channel Islands or to the Isle of Man.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.5.6 If you are also taking a power to extend free-standing provision (see Part 10.5.3), make express reference to both the free-standing provision and the textual amendments.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eHis Majesty may by Order in Council provide for—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) [sections x to y of this Act], and\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) any of the amendments made by [or under] this Act of any part of [the Act being amended], to extend, with or without modifications, to any of the Channel Islands or to the Isle of Man.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.5.7 By the way, make sure that a general proposition to the effect that amendments have the same extent as the enactments amended does not inadvertently extend the amendments to the Islands directly: see Part 10.4.16.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"textual-amendment-of-act-containing-power-to-extend-to-islands\"\u003eTextual amendment of Act containing power to extend to Islands\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.5.8 What happens where you want a power to extend amendments to the Islands, in a case where the Act amended can be or has been extended to the Islands under a power contained in that Act?\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.5.9 The recommended approach is expressly to apply the existing power to your amendments, using the following form of words—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe power under section x of [the Act being amended] may be exercised so as to extend to any of the Channel Islands or the Isle of Man any amendment or repeal made by [or under] this Act of any part of that Act (with or without modifications).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.5.10 This is recommended in preference to conferring a completely new power in the Bill to extend your amendments to the Islands; or to making the amendments and relying on silence to achieve the result that the existing power in the Act applies to that Act as amended.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.5.11 If you also have free-standing provision which is to be extended to the Islands by means of a new power, deal with that separately.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.5.12 Again, make sure that a general proposition to the effect that amendments have the same extent as the enactments amended does not extend the amendments to the Islands directly: see Part 10.4.16.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"preservation-of-powers-of-extension\"\u003ePreservation of powers of extension\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.5.13 This section is for a case where (a) you are repealing for the UK an Act which has been extended to the Islands by means of a power contained in that Act and (b) the Act needs to stay alive in the Islands after the UK repeal (whether indefinitely or until a power to extend the repeal is exercised).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.5.14 You should make it clear that the UK repeal does not affect the continuing operation of the original power of extension so far as the Islands are concerned. So say something to the effect that the repeal within the UK “does not affect any power by Order in Council to make provision extending to any of the Channel Islands”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"commencement-and-transitionals\"\u003e11.6 10.6 COMMENCEMENT AND TRANSITIONALS\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"commencement-and-coming-into-force\"\u003e“Commencement” and “coming into force”\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.6.1 Normally, when referring to the time at which a provision begins to have legal effect, use “coming into force” or “comes into force” (or “came into force”) rather than “commencement”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eRather than\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e… the period of one year beginning with the commencement of this section…\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e… applications made after the commencement of this section.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e… this section does not apply to offences committed before its commencement…\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003etry\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e… the period of one year beginning when this section comes into force…\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e… applications made after this section comes into force (or “on or after the day on which this section comes into force…”)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e… this section does not apply to offences committed before it comes into force.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.6.2 This does not prevent the use of convenient labels such as “the commencement day”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.6.3 For the sake of conformity with long-standing practice, “commencement” should also be used in the heading for the section of an Act which deals with its coming into force.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"commencement-on-royal-assent\"\u003eCommencement on Royal Assent\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.6.4 Provisions that are to come into force on Royal Assent should be identified expressly.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.6.5 The form of words used to bring such provisions into force should normally be designed to attract section 4(a) of the Interpretation Act 1978 (where provision is made for an enactment to come into force on a particular day, it comes into force at the beginning of the day).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSections X and Y and Schedule Z come into force on the day on which this Act is passed.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.6.6 Very exceptionally the desired policy may involve specifying a particular time of day.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"commencement-at-end-of-fixed-period\"\u003eCommencement at end of fixed period\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.6.7 The recommended form of words is— [This Act] comes into force at the end of the period of [two months] beginning with the day on which it is passed.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"commencement-by-regulations\"\u003eCommencement by regulations\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.6.8 In general it is clearer to say that provision is to come into force on a day appointed by regulations by a particular person, than to say that it comes into force “in accordance with” provision made by regulations. In the latter case it may not be clear whether any further power —for example, a power to make transitional provision — is also being conferred. If further power is wanted, it should be conferred expressly — see below.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.6.9 An “appointed day” provision should take the form of a positive statement.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis Act comes into force on such day as X may by regulations appoint.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003enot\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis Act does not come into force until such day as X may by regulations appoint.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"differential-commencement\"\u003eDifferential commencement\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.6.10 Sometimes where there is a power to commence it is not desired that everything should be brought into force all at once.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.6.11 Where different provisions of an Act will need to be brought into force (fully) on different days, but nothing more complicated is envisaged, it will normally be sufficient to provide that the provisions of the Act\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e“come into force on such day or days as [the Secretary of State] may by regulations appoint”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.6.12 Note that although under section 6(c) of the Interpretation Act 1978 the singular includes the plural, “day or days” is recommended to make it absolutely clear that differential commencement is envisaged.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.6.13 Where the policy is to allow one or more provisions of the Act to come into force for some purposes but not others, the commencement power will need to include wording enabling different provision for different purposes.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.6.14 If that is done, you do not need “day or days”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.6.15 Note that “different purposes” should not be used to cover “different areas” (see 9.2.8 - 9.2.9).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"power-to-make-transitional-or-saving-provision\"\u003ePower to make transitional or saving provision\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.6.16 A power to make transitional or saving provision in connection with commencement may be necessary where a Bill provides for commencement by regulations or at the end of a fixed period (eg 2 months after Royal Assent).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.6.17 A “transitional” provision manages the transition from one regime to another.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA provision that spells out how the Bill works in relation to events or matters that span the end of the old regime and the start of the new regime.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.6.18 A “saving” provision saves the operation of an existing piece of legislation or rule of law. It can do this for a temporary period or for ever, and for transitional purposes or for other purposes. It might therefore be a transitional or transitory provision but need not be so.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.6.19 A free-standing power to make transitional or saving provision should normally be included, rather than providing that transitional and saving provision may be included in commencement regulations. This ensures that the power covers transitional provision in connection with the commencement of provisions for which the a date is fixed by the Bill (eg 2 months after Royal Assent).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.6.20 There are examples of powers to make transitory provision in connection with commencement. A “transitory” provision has a limited shelf-life, such as a provision that will expire on a particular day.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA provision that references to dogs in the Dogs Act 1990 include cats until the coming into force of the Cats Act 2010.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.6.21 Transitory provision is often transitional in nature, in which case there is no need to mention it expressly since it is covered by the power to make transitional provision. The mere fact that the regulations make provision for a limited period does not require express cover. An express power to make transitory provision is therefore usually unnecessary.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"structure\"\u003eStructure\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.6.22 It can sometimes be unclear how powers conferred generally in relation to regulations under the Bill will work in relation to commencement powers and powers to make transitional and saving provision in connection with commencement.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.6.23 So it is usually best to exclude the powers relating to commencement from any general provision about what may be included in regulations and deal with everything relating to commencement separately.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.6.24 This means that the commencement clause will often include—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• a free-standing power to make transitional or saving provision;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• provision authorising commencement regulations to make differential provision;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e• provision for regulations under the clause to be made by statutory instrument.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"expiry-and-sunset\"\u003e11.7 10.7 EXPIRY AND SUNSET\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"how-to-express-temporary-effect\"\u003eHow to express temporary effect\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.7.1 To secure that legislative provision has limited duration, do one of the following—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(1) say that the enactment has effect for a certain period only\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis Act has effect for a period of 10 years beginning with [date] or\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(2) say that the enactment expires at a certain time\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis Act expires at the end of a period of 10 years beginning with [date]\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.7.2 The difference between these two is merely presentational: (1) focuses on the duration of the temporary law while (2) focuses on its expiry. Which is more appropriate in any given case will depend on the emphasis you want to give.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.7.3 If you use method (2), avoid saying that a provision expires “on” a particular day, as it may not be clear whether it expires at the beginning or end of the day (or at any other time on the day).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.7.4 Other methods have sometimes been used: for example saying that an enactment “ceases to have effect” at a certain time, or that it is “repealed” at a certain time.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.7.5 However, to say that an enactment “ceases to have effect” at a certain time is perhaps less clear than either methods (1) or (2).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.7.6 To say that an enactment is “repealed” at a certain time has no obvious advantage over methods (1) and (2) and gives rise to a possible difficulty if the enactment consists of the repeal of another enactment. Section 15 of the Interpretation Act 1978 has the effect that the repeal of a repealing enactment does not revive the repealed enactment. That is unlikely to be the result wanted. In contrast, if the repealing enactment were said to expire, the repealed provision would revive.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.7.7 So for those reasons, and in the interests of consistency, methods (1) and (2) are recommended.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"duration-to-be-separately-expressed\"\u003eDuration to be separately expressed\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.7.8 The House of Commons Standing Orders make specific provision about temporary laws. SO No. 81 (temporary laws) requires: “The precise duration of every temporary law or enactment shall be expressed in a distinct clause or subsection of the bill.”\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"effect-of-expiry\"\u003eEffect of expiry\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.7.9 Consider whether it is clear from the text and the circumstances what the effects of expiry will be.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.7.10 If a temporary enactment confers power to make subordinate legislation, any legislation made under it will cease to have effect from the time of the expiry of the enactment (but of course with the savings provided for in section 16 of the Interpretation Act 1978). So some transitional or saving provision may be needed.\u003csup id=\"fnref:26\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:26\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 26]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.7.11 Obviously, if it is appropriate to make specific savings relating to the period after the expiry of a temporary enactment or other provision about the consequences of expiry, those specific savings or other provisions should not be caught by the provision for expiry.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"short-titles\"\u003e11.8 10.8 SHORT TITLES\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"form-for-conferring-short-title\"\u003eForm for conferring short title\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e10.8.1 For consistency, always use the following formulation—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e“This Act may be cited as….”.\u003c/p\u003e"
      }

        "text": "\u003ch3 id=\"words-and-phrases\"\u003e12.1 11.1 WORDS AND PHRASES\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"affect\"\u003eaffect\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.1 The “nothing in provision A affects provision B” formula is useful if you do not know all the effects that A might have on B, or where those effects would be too numerous to mention. But if you can identify what effect it is you have in mind, that may help the reader (so, for example, “A does not limit B”).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"any\"\u003eany\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.2 Beware of a proliferation of “any”s. In many cases “a” or “an” is just as good.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.3 “Any” can be ambiguous.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Minister must consult any organisation appearing to be representative of substantial numbers of mushroom growers.\u003csup id=\"fnref:27\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:27\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 27]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIs this any one organisation or all organisations?\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.4 “Any” may be of course be useful to emphasise that something is of universal application or without qualification (but consider whether emphasis is really needed).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"apart-from\"\u003eapart from\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.5 For apart from, in the phrase apart from this section, consider but for or leaving aside.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.6 However, the awkwardness here is not so much the words themselves as the task they impose on the reader - that of working out what the situation would be without the provision in question. It might be more helpful to expand on the thought and say what you have in mind.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"description\"\u003edescription\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.7 This can seem rather vague and abstract (“animals of a description specified in regulations”). Drafters might like to consider kind, class or category (or even sort?).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.8 In the context of a regulation-making power description may emphasise that it is for the regulations to create the class in question. This may be a particular help when the thing in question already comes in obvious “kinds” or “classes” but it is desired in the regulations to categorise the thing in a different way.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"function\"\u003efunction\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.9 Draft on the basis that the natural meaning of “function” covers powers and duties. (In Hazell v Hammersmith and Fulham London Borough Council [1992] 2 A.C. 1. Lord Templeman said that the word “functions” in section 111 of the Local Government Act 1972 embraced: “all the duties and powers of a local authority; the sum total of the activities Parliament has entrusted to it.”)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.10 A definition to the effect that “functions” includes powers and duties is generally unnecessary and unhelpful. If something further is needed, consider whether it is possible to get the point across more clearly.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"prescribe\"\u003eprescribe\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.11 Prescribe is often used in the context of subordinate legislation: “regulations may prescribe…”. It avoids the need to say exactly how the subordinate legislation will proceed, and as such can be extremely useful. But a more precise word may make more impact: give, fix, set, set out, state all carry more of a punch and say what exactly the regulations will do.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eRegulations under section x may prescribe the fees that may be charged\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis could perhaps be\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eRegulations under section x may set the fees that may be charged\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.12 Prescribe is sometimes defined to mean “prescribe in regulations”. This can be a useful device to avoid lots of references to regulations. It can even be extended: section 24 of the Welfare Reform Act 2007 defines “prescribed” as “specified in, or determined in accordance with, regulations”, which avoids constant repetition of a lengthy phrase. But it is an artificial definition and consider whether it is really justified in any given case. There is clear evidence that many users of legislation find expressions like “person of a prescribed description” bewildering\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn this section, “qualifying young person” means a person of a prescribed description\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis could perhaps be\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn this section “qualifying young person” means a person of a description specified in regulations made by the Secretary of State.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"provide\"\u003eprovide\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.13 Where legislation provides for something it effects or gives rise to that thing in law. It is very useful because it does not require that the legislation should create it in any particular way.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis section applies to a pension scheme which provides for a benefit to be payable to a member where….\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eHere it does not matter, for the purposes of the section, how the pension scheme creates the benefit. It is enough that, somehow or other, the pension scheme gives rise to the benefit. Neither “permits” nor “requires” might have been right on their own (it may be that a pension scheme should be caught whether it permits or requires the payment of the benefit). One could of course have both. A possible alternative might have been “a pension scheme under which a benefit is payable….”\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(1) A person is not entitled to the benefit if the person is not in Great Britain.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(2) Regulations may provide for exceptions to subsection (1).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis doesn’t imply anything about how the regulations will be drafted, whereas specify might have given rise to an expectation that the regulations would just be a list, making more detailed provision questionable. But “create” or “make” might be possible.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.14 Sometimes make or create will allow for the same flexibility.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.15 However, consider in any given case whether it is possible to be more precise. Will the legislation enable, authorise, require, set out, stipulate a particular result? A more immediate word may also be less legalistic.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"provision\"\u003eprovision\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.16 Provision is a useful generic phrase for what legislation does, but can be legalistic and off-putting. It may be worth thinking about what the legislation actually does in the case you are concerned about: does it regulate, authorise, require?\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.17 If conferring power to make provision about or for something, consider how the power might be exercised.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLES\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eRegulations making transitional provision may, in particular—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) make provision for persons not to be treated as having any authorisation or permission;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) make provision enabling the Authority to require persons to re-apply for permission;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(c) make provision for the continuation as rules of such provisions as may be designated, including provision for the modification by the Authority of provisions designated;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(d) make provision as regards the Authority’s obligation to maintain a record.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIt might be possible, depending on the circumstances, to be more direct—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eRegulations making transitional provision may, in particular—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(a) treat persons as not having any authorisation or permission;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(b) allow the Authority to require persons to re-apply for permission;\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(c) enable the continuation of such rules as may be designated (and allow the Authority to modify them);\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(d) disapply the Authority’s obligation to maintain a record. 11.1 Words and phrases\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.18 It may be possible to avoid provision completely.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLES\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis Part of this Schedule makes further provision about….\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003emight be\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis Part of this Schedule contains more about….\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eRegulations may make provision about when an assessment period is to start.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003emight be\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eRegulations may be made about when an assessment period is to start.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.19 Wherever possible, prefer provide for to make provision for.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.20 Provisions is often used in the sense of the contents of legislation (“the provisions of this Act”). It has a great advantage in that it is not confined to any particular unit of text - a provision can be an Act, a section, a small unit of text or may not be an articulated bit of text at all. So to say that the provisions of the Act come into force by regulations might allow more latitude than to say that the sections come into force by regulations (would that allow subsections to be commenced separately?). But consider whether you can in any given context be more specific.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.21 It may be that you do not need provision in this sense at all. In particular, the phrase the provisions of is often superfluous.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis does not affect the provisions of any regulations under this section…. would mean the same without “the provisions of”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"pursuant-to-in-pursuance-of\"\u003epursuant to, in pursuance of\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.22 Where one thing follows directly from another, with no intervening cause or condition, pursuant to can often be rendered as under.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA person who has been detained continuously pursuant to two or more sentences….\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe report must include information which has been provided to the Secretary of State pursuant to regulations made under section x.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e…any services provided by another person pursuant to arrangements….\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIn all these cases “pursuant to” could perhaps have been “under”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.23 In accordance with is also possible (eg in the last two examples). Or say what you mean: as required/ authorised by….\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.24 In other cases because of would work.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf the qualification is subject to a requirement of accreditation pursuant to a determination made under section x…\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eHere “because of” would seem to work. Or better yet turn the whole thing round—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf a determination under section x means that the qualification needs to be accredited….”.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.25 Sometimes something with more colour is possible.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSuch a person is guilty of an offence if, pursuant to a request for information, he makes a statement which he knows to be false.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eHere “in response to” might be better.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.26 Pursuant to is often used to express an indirect relationship between two things, where something happens between A and B (so A is a necessary but not a sufficient condition of B).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAny transfer of land pursuant to sub-paragraph (3) is to take place on the conversion date.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eHere the point is that the sub-paragraph (3) requires the transfer of land but the transfer is actually effected by a later instrument. Here “by” or “under” would be wrong.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.27 In cases like this it may be best to describe in more detail what is going on. In the example just given “any transfer or land required by sub-paragraph (3)” might have worked.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.28 Failing that, “further to” will generally be a possible substitute. In some cases, “following” or “as a result of” or “because of” may be possible, or maybe just “after”, if the causal connection is clear.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAn Order in Council made pursuant to a recommendation….\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eHere following might be better. Or perhaps An Order in Council to give effect to a recommendation…\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"in-relation-to-in-respect-of-with-respect-to-as-respects\"\u003ein relation to, in respect of, with respect to, as respects.\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.29 These phrases are all extremely useful, and sometimes essential, in that they do not require one to specify any particular relationship. In respect of has been said to have “the widest possible meaning of any expression intended to convey some connection or relation” (Albon v Naza Motor Trading [2007] EWHC 9 (Ch) at 27).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.30 It is though tempting to use them in circumstances where a more precise relationship could be specified. In some circumstances in the case of, for, about, to or as to will do as well.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLES\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe election has effect in relation to films which commence photography in that accounting period\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe election has effect for films which….\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA transfer scheme may not make provision in relation to land\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA transfer scheme may not make provision about land\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"satisfy\"\u003esatisfy\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.31 It is enough to “meet” a condition; you don’t also need to satisfy it.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"subject-to\"\u003esubject to\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.32 “Subject to” isn’t a very precise way of describing a relationship between two propositions.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis section is subject to section x\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWhat exactly does section x do in relation to “this section”?\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSection x sets out conditions….\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSection x sets out different rules for [a particular case]\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThere are exceptions to this rule in section x\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis section does not apply to [a particular case] (see section x)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.33 If you can’t conveniently describe the relationship, “subject to” can sometimes be avoided. A signpost such as “(but see section x)” might serve to alert the reader to the fact that there are qualifications without sounding as legalistic.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.34 The relationship between the provisions may be particularly hard to follow if “subject to” is at the beginning of the sentence. It may be better to start with the main proposition and then indicate that there is a qualification, perhaps in a second sentence.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.35 “Subject to” is also not necessarily helpful if you cannot identify the provisions you are talking about. “Subject to what follows” should be avoided unless it is abundantly obvious from the context exactly which of the following provisions are being referred to. Where there is any doubt, specify exactly which provisions you mean (or express the relationship in some other way).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.36 Global cross-references such as “Subject to the provisions of the Corporation Tax Acts” are sometimes unavoidable but may not be entirely meaningful to non-expert readers. If the reference cannot be avoided, try to include a list of where the relevant other provision is made.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.37 It may be possible to dispense with “subject to” altogether, especially if the qualifying proposition is close to the proposition it qualifies — in which case the reader may be expected to grasp the relationship between the two without extra help.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.38 See also Part 3.10, Cross-references — and in particular the injunction to draft by reference to substance rather than by reference to the statutory provisions in which it is contained.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"such\"\u003esuch\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.39 Avoid “such” where possible. Often “the” or “a” will do just as well.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eInstead of\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eon such day as the Minister may specify\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eyou might say\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eon a day the Minister specifies.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"supplemental--supplementary\"\u003esupplemental / supplementary\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.40 There is no obvious difference in meaning between “supplementary” and “supplemental”. Prefer “supplementary”, as perhaps the more usual formulation.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"by-virtue-of\"\u003eby virtue of\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.41 Where a relationship is direct, there may be alternatives to the rather archaic by virtue of.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.42 Sometimes by on its own is enough. Where one thing authorises or requires another, under may be possible. Where one things causes another, or makes it possible, try as a result of or because of.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.43 That said, by virtue of can be particularly useful for indirect relationships. For example, where regulations authorise A to authorise B, it might be misleading to say that B is authorised under the regulations. Something else has to happen first.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"where--if\"\u003ewhere / if\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.44 “Where” is useful for stating a case or a set of circumstances in which a later proposition applies. “If” is used for stating a contingency.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.45 So “where” may be better for cases which inevitably will occur, “if” for conditions which may or may not be satisfied.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.46 There is of course no clear-cut distinction. In some cases, it may depend on the perspective from which you are looking at the situation.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSuppose a regulator has power to serve notices on defaulters—\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWhere the regulator serves a notice on a person, the regulator must…\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(here we are speaking of the regulator, who will frequently serve notices)\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ebut\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf the regulator serves a notice on a person, the person must…\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e(here we are speaking of the person, for whom the notice is not at all inevitable).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"without-prejudice\"\u003ewithout prejudice\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.47 Consider what the “prejudice” might be and focus on that.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLES\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWithout prejudice to the generality of section 1\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIf the fear is that the new provision might limit what section 1 says, perhaps say\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWithout limiting section 1\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWithout prejudice to the making of new regulations\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ecould be\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWithout preventing the making of new regulations\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.48 If the fear is that the new provision might affect or change the way another provision operates, perhaps say that (but see affect above).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.49 A phrase beginning without “without prejudice to…” can often be recast so as to start with the main proposition and then say how it relates to the other one.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWithout prejudice to the generality of subsection (2), the Secretary of State may issue directions under that subsection for the purposes of….\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ecan be recast as two propositions The Secretary of State may issue directions under subsection (2) for the purpose of… This does not restrict what may otherwise be done under subsection (2).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003e11.1.50 Another way of avoiding without prejudice is by in particular.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEXAMPLE\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe Secretary of State may in particular issue directions under subsection (2) for the purpose of…\u003c/p\u003e"
      }
