<p>6.2.4 Section 20(1) of the Interpretation Act 1978 states: “Where an Act describes or cites a portion of an enactment by referring to words, sections or other parts from or to which (or from and to which) the portion extends, the portion described includes the words, sections or other parts referred to unless the contrary intention appears.”</p>

<p>6.2.5 Note that this is the opposite of the practice with House amendments.</p>

<h4 id="substitution-or-insertion">Substitution or insertion?</h4>

<p>6.2.6 If you have new text that is in substance a replacement for the existing text, then put it by way of substitution, re-using the number of the existing text.</p>

<p>6.2.7 But if you want to repeal text and, at the same time, have new text to put in at the same place, where the new text is not a direct replacement for the existing text, it is better not to substitute. Instead, repeal the old text and insert the new text, without re-using the number. That way it is clearer that you are doing two separate things (so let form follow function).</p>

<h3 id="insertions">7.3 6.3 INSERTIONS</h3>

<h4 id="operative-words-2">Operative words</h4>

<p>6.3.1 Use the imperative form—</p>

<p>after x insert y</p>

<h4 id="after-or-before">After or before</h4>

<p>6.3.2 It is usual to specify that a new provision is to be inserted “after” another one.</p>

<p>6.3.3 If you are inserting something as the very first section or Schedule, you will of course need to insert it “before section 1” or “before Schedule 1”.</p>

<p>6.3.4 “Before” can also be useful in other circumstances where the new section is to be inserted at the beginning of a Part, Chapter or group of sections, where a reference to “after” the preceding section would tend to suggest that the intention was that the new section should appear at the end of the preceding Part etc.</p>

<h4 id="at-the-beginning">At the beginning</h4>

<p>6.3.5 The usual form is to say—</p>

<p>at the beginning insert x</p>

<p>rather than to say that x is inserted “before” particular words.</p>

<h4 id="at-the-end">At the end</h4>

<p>6.3.6 The usual form is to say—</p>

<p>at the end insert x</p>

<p>6.3.7 This is in contrast to House amendments to Bills, which just say “at end”.</p>

<p>6.3.8 Say “insert” rather than “add”.</p>

<h4 id="in-a-list">In a list</h4>

<p>6.3.9 Where an amendment is made to insert an entry into a list, such as a list of definitions or statutory bodies, it is sometimes framed as an amendment to insert the text “at the appropriate place” (instead of “after” something). This is appropriate where, for example, a list runs in alphabetical order.</p>

<h4 id="next-to-an-unnumbered-provision">Next to an unnumbered provision</h4>

<p>6.3.10 To add a subsection or sub-paragraph to a section or paragraph which is not already subdivided, proceed as follows—</p>

<p>• renumber the existing text—</p>

<p>In [section] [paragraph] N the existing text becomes [subsection] [sub-paragraph] (1).</p>

<p>• make any amendments to the existing text—</p>

<p>In that [subsection] [sub-paragraph], after ”x” insert…</p>

<p>• insert the new subsection or sub-paragraph—</p>

<p>After that [subsection] [sub-paragraph] insert—</p>

<p>“(2) [Text of new provision]”.</p>

<h3 id="numbering-of-inserted-provisions">7.4 6.4 NUMBERING OF INSERTED PROVISIONS</h3>

<h4 id="at-the-beginning-of-a-series">At the beginning of a series</h4>

<p>6.4.1 Number as follows when inserting a new whole provision at the beginning of an existing series of provisions (eg a subsection at the beginning of a section or a Schedule before the first Schedule).</p>

<p>• New sections inserted before the first section of an Act are preceded by a letter, starting with “A” (A1, B1, C1 and so on).</p>

<p>• The same approach is taken in relation to all other divisions of text (other than lettered paragraphs).</p>

<p>Thus the Insolvency Act 2000 inserted a Schedule A1 before Schedule 1 to the Insolvency Act 1986, and the Enterprise Act 2002 inserted a new Schedule B1 after Schedule A1.</p>

<p>• A provision inserted before “A1” (or “ai”) is “ZA1” or (“zai”).</p>

<p>• In the case of lettered paragraphs, new paragraphs inserted before paragraph (a) are (za), (zb) etc.</p>

<p>• And paragraphs inserted before (za) are (zza), (zzb) etc.</p>

<h4 id="at-the-end-of-a-series">At the end of a series</h4>

<p>6.4.2 Where adding a provision at the end of an existing series of provisions of the same kind (eg a subsection at the end of a section or a Schedule at the end of the Schedules), the numbering should continue in sequence.</p>

<h4 id="between-existing-provisions">Between existing provisions</h4>

<p>6.4.3 The following applies when inserting whole provisions between existing provisions.</p>

<p>• New provisions inserted between 1 and 2 are 1A, 1B, 1C etc.</p>

<p>• New provisions inserted between 1A and 1B are 1AA, 1AB, 1AC etc.</p>

<p>• New provisions inserted between 1 and 1A are 1ZA, 1ZB, 1ZC etc. (and not 1AA etc.)</p>

<p>• New provisions inserted between 1A and 1AA are 1AZA, 1AZB, 1AZC etc.</p>

<p>6.4.4 Do not generate a lower level identifier unless you have to.</p>

<p>• A new provision between 1AA and 1B is 1AB not 1AAA.</p>

<p>• But a new provision between 1AA and 1AB is 1AAA.</p>

<p>6.4.5 The above recommendations apply equally to sub-paragraphs with roman numerals and lettered paragraphs.</p>

<p>• New sub-paragraphs between sub-paragraphs (i) and (ii) are (ia), (ib), (ic) etc.</p>

<p>• New paragraphs between paragraphs (a) and (b) are (aa), (ab), (ac) etc.</p>

<p>• New paragraphs between paragraphs (a) and (aa) are (aza), (azb), (azc) etc.</p>

<h4 id="series-of-more-than-26">Series of more than 26</h4>

<p>6.4.6 After Z use Z1, Z2, Z3 etc. For example, after section 360Z insert sections 360Z1, 360Z2 and so on; after paragraph (z) insert paragraphs (z1), (z2), (z3).</p>

<h4 id="re-using-numbers">Re-using numbers</h4>

<p>6.4.7 If you are inserting new text at a place where there has previously been a repeal, do not re-use the number.</p>

<h3 id="identifying-text">7.5 6.5 IDENTIFYING TEXT</h3>

<h4 id="opening-or-closing-words-of-a-subsection-with-paragraphs">Opening or closing words of a subsection with paragraphs</h4>

<p>6.5.1 A subsection with paragraphs will have words before the paragraphs, and may have words after the paragraphs.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>If an inspector reasonably believes that—</p>

<p>(a) premises falling within this Part are unfit for human occupation,</p>

<p>(b) the premises are nevertheless occupied, and</p>

<p>(c) the life or health of the occupants is at risk,</p>

<p>the inspector may serve a notice under this section.</p>

<p>6.5.2 The words before the paragraphs start should be referred to as “The words before paragraph (a)” (or whatever the first paragraph is).</p>

<p>6.5.3 The words after the paragraphs should be referred to as the words “after paragraph (c)” or whatever the last paragraph is.</p>

<p>6.5.4 If you are amending words that only appear once there is no need to specify whether they appear before or after the paragraphs, but it is sometimes helpful to do so (for example, if the provision is particularly long).</p>

<h4 id="words-which-occur-more-than-once">Words which occur more than once</h4>

<p>6.5.5 Where words occur more than once in a provision, and you want to identify one instance of them, the recommended form is as follows—</p>

<p>for “x”, in the first place it occurs, substitute “y”</p>

<p>after “x”, in the second place it occurs, insert “y”</p>

<p>omit “x” in the third place it occurs.</p>

<p>6.5.6 In some cases it may be simpler to replace a slightly bigger chunk of text so as to avoid having to refer to the “first” or “second” instance of the word or phrase.</p>

<p>6.5.7 Where words occur twice and you want to catch both instances the recommended form is—</p>

<p>for “x”, in both places it occurs, substitute “y”</p>

<p>after “x”, in both places it occurs, insert “y”</p>

<p>omit “x” in both places.</p>

<p>6.5.8 Where words occur three or more times and you want to catch all instances, the recommended form is —</p>

<p>for “x”, in each place it occurs, substitute “y”</p>

<p>after “x”, in each place it occurs, insert “y”</p>

<p>omit “x” in each place.</p>

<p>6.5.9 Note that it is unnecessary to refer to “the words” x or y; or to use brackets.</p>

<p>6.5.10 If an amendment is intended to be made in a heading as well as in the body of a provision it is worth making this clear by adding “(including the heading)”.</p>

<h4 id="english-and-welsh-language-text">English and Welsh language text</h4>

<p>6.5.11 It is possible, if unusual, for a Bill to amend an Act of Senedd Cymru or an instrument made by the Welsh Ministers. Such an Act or instrument will exist in both English and Welsh. If amending both versions, refer to the “English language text” and the “Welsh language text” as opposed to the “English text” and “Welsh text” (so as not to suggest that one part of the law is “English” or “Welsh” in terms of nationality).</p>

<h3 id="amendment-of-headings">7.6 6.6 AMENDMENT OF HEADINGS</h3>

<h4 id="when-to-amend-headings">When to amend headings</h4>

<p>6.6.1 It is acceptable to amend the heading to a provision, and it may be helpful to do so - for example, if the provision is falsified by a textual amendment you are making.</p>

<p>6.6.2 There is no need to amend a heading merely because the existing heading is not quite what you would have chosen for the amended text.</p>

<h4 id="how-to-amend-headings">How to amend headings</h4>

<p>6.6.3 The wording used to amend a heading should be the same as the wording used to make other amendments (so, for these purposes, do not treat headings as different from other statutory text).</p>

<p>6.6.4 The recommended practice is not to mimic typography when amending or substituting a heading (ie do not use bold or italic font or small capitals).</p>

<p>6.6.5 However, use the appropriate typography when inserting a completely new heading (for example, a new italic heading before an existing group of sections).</p>

<h4 id="what-to-call-headings">What to call headings</h4>

<p>6.6.6 Parts and Chapters. A heading of a Part or Chapter in the body of an Act should be referred to as the “Chapter heading” or “Part heading” or “the heading of Chapter/Part X”.</p>

<p>6.6.7 Groups of sections. An italic cross-heading which precedes a group of sections in the body of an Act should be called the “italic heading before section x”.</p>

<p>6.6.8 Sections. A section heading should be referred to simply as the “heading” of the section. This applies to pre-2001 Acts as well as later Acts, even though the headings for pre2001 Acts took the form of marginal sidenotes.</p>

<p>6.6.9 Schedules. The heading of a Schedule should be referred to as such.</p>

<p>6.6.10 The heading of a Part of a Schedule should be referred to as the “Part heading” or “the heading of Part X”.</p>

<p>6.6.11 An italic heading within a Schedule should be called “the italic heading before paragraph x”.</p>

<p>6.6.12 As a matter of house style a heading is a heading “of” something, not “to” something.</p>

<h3 id="schedules-and-other-series-of-amendments">7.7 6.7 SCHEDULES AND OTHER SERIES OF AMENDMENTS</h3>

<h4 id="series-of-amendments">Series of amendments</h4>

<p>6.7.1 Although individual amendments are drafted as instructions (“insert”), series of amendments should start with “is amended”—</p>

<p>(1) The Kangaroos Act is amended [as follows] [as specified in subsections…].</p>

<p>(2) After section 1 insert….</p>

<p>(3) Omit section 2.</p>

<p>6.7.2 If you say Act X is amended “as follows”, what follows shouldn’t include an amendment to Act Y.</p>

<h4 id="format-of-amendment-schedules">Format of amendment Schedules</h4>

<p>6.7.3 Where amendments to an Act are arranged under an italic heading giving the name of the Act, the recommended style is—</p>

<p>“Counter-Terrorism Act 2008 (c. 28)</p>

<ol>
  <li>In the Counter-Terrorism Act 2008, after section N….”</li>
</ol>

<p>6.7.4 Note in particular—</p>

<p>• the short title of the Act needs to be given in the text of the amendment as well as in the heading;</p>

<p>• the chapter number should be given in the heading but does not need to be repeated in the text of the amendment.</p>

<h4 id="format-of-repeal-schedules">Format of repeal Schedules</h4>

<p>6.7.5 The format of a repeal Schedule is now fairly standard. Any repeal Schedule, or any other table of repeals, should be in that standard form.</p>

<p>6.7.6 Within each part of a Schedule or other table of repeals, the provisions affected should continue to be arranged chronologically (with chapter numbers).</p>

<p>6.7.7 Repeals and revocations may be dealt with together or in separate parts of a repeal Schedule.</p>

<h3 id="uncommenced-material">7.8 6.8 UNCOMMENCED MATERIAL</h3>

<p>6.8.1 Uncommenced legislation should be kept in a state in which it can be brought into force. So it needs to be catered for when legislating to implement new policy.</p>

<p>6.8.2 The discussion below deals with the following topics—</p>

<p>• amending uncommenced provisions;</p>

<p>• repealing uncommenced amendments;</p>

<p>• amending provisions subject to uncommenced repeals;</p>

<p>• drafting provisions that need to work with existing and prospective provisions.</p>

<h4 id="amending-uncommenced-provision">Amending uncommenced provision</h4>

<h4 id="amending-uncommenced-free-standing-provisions">Amending uncommenced free-standing provisions</h4>

<p>6.8.3 An amendment can be made to an uncommenced free-standing provision in an earlier Act in the usual way. For considerations relating to commencement, see below.</p>

<h4 id="amending-an-act-that-is-the-subject-of-earlier-uncommenced-amendments">Amending an Act that is the subject of earlier uncommenced amendments</h4>

<p>6.8.4 In the interests of simplicity, where a Bill amends an Act that is already the subject of earlier uncommenced amendments, it should operate directly on that Act (not on the intervening amending Act).</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>• Act 1 is in force.</p>

<p>• Act 2 inserts a new section 7A and the insertion is not yet in force.</p>

<p>• A Bill needs to insert a new subsection (1A) into section 7A. The amendment in the Bill should be expressed as an amendment to section 7A of Act 1 (not as an amendment to the provision of Act 2 which inserts it).</p>

<p>6.8.5 It may be helpful to include a signpost to indicate where the provision came from—</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>In section 7A of Act 1 (as inserted by section 2 of Act 2) after subsection (1) insert…</p>

<p>6.8.6 If a provision is subject to an uncommenced substitution, it may be necessary to amend the provision both in its original and in its substituted form.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE In Act 1—</p>

<p>(a) in section 1 (before its substitution by section 2 of Act 2), after “or dogs” insert “or cats”;</p>

<p>(b) in section 1 (as substituted by section 2 of Act 2), after “or dogs” insert “or cats”.</p>

<h4 id="commencement-issues">Commencement issues</h4>

<p>6.8.7 To avoid confusion, amendments should not be brought into force before the provision they amend.</p>

<p>6.8.8 The recommended approach when drafting an Act that amends earlier uncommenced provision is to—</p>

<p>(a) confer a fresh power, in the amending Act, to govern the amendments made by it (rather than expanding any power in the amended Act so that it can be used to commence the amendments), or</p>

<p>(b) if the policy is that the amended Act should never be in force without the amendments, provide for linked commencement (eg “X comes into force at the same time as Y”).</p>

<p>6.8.9 The approach in paragraph 6.8.8(a) allows flexibility as the amendments can be brought into force at the same time as or later than the provisions that they amend.</p>

<h4 id="repealing-uncommenced-amendments">Repealing uncommenced amendments</h4>

<h4 id="repeal-of-part-of-uncommenced-amendment">Repeal of part of uncommenced amendment</h4>

<p>6.8.10 Where a Bill repeals part only of an uncommenced amendment to an earlier Act, it should operate directly on that Act (not on the intervening amending Act). This is the same as the approach discussed above for amending uncommenced amendments.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>• Act 1 is in force.</p>

<p>• Act 2 inserts a new section 7A and the insertion is not yet in force.</p>

<p>• The policy underlying a Bill is to repeal subsections (3) to (6) of section 7A. The repeal should be expressed as a repeal of subsections (3) to (6) of section 7A of Act 1 (not as a partial repeal to the provision of Act 2 which inserts it).</p>

<p>6.8.11 The commencement of the repeal should be governed by the commencement provision made by the Bill; and the repeal should not be brought into force before the provision of Act 2 which inserts section 7A into Act 1.</p>

<h4 id="repeal-of-whole-of-uncommenced-amendment">Repeal of whole of uncommenced amendment</h4>

<p>6.8.12 The position is different where the policy is to repeal an uncommenced amendment in its entirety and without it ever having been brought into force. Then the repeal should operate on the Act making the uncommenced amendment (rather than the amended Act).</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>• Act 1 is in force.</p>

<p>• Act 2 inserts a new section 7A and the insertion is not yet in force.</p>

<p>• The policy underlying a Bill is to repeal section 7A. The repeal in the Bill should be expressed as a repeal of the uncommenced provision in Act 2 that inserted the new section 1A into Act 1.</p>

<p>6.8.13 The reason for adopting this approach is that the aim is to stop section 7A from operating at all, rather than altering the way in which it operates. Expressing the proposition as a repeal of section 7A of Act 1 would necessitate commencing the amendment (so that there is something to repeal) and then repealing it immediately afterwards, which is unnecessary and potentially misleading.</p>

<h4 id="amending-provisions-subject-to-an-uncommenced-repeal">Amending provisions subject to an uncommenced repeal</h4>

<p>6.8.14 A provision in an Act subject to an uncommenced repeal may need to be amended if the policy of the Bill demands a change before the repeal is to be commenced. In that case, consideration needs to be given to what will happen to the amendment.</p>

<p>6.8.15 In some cases it will be obvious that the amendment is not intended to have any effect following the commencement of the repeal (for example, where the amendment inserts a single word). An express repeal is nonetheless helpful to tidy things up.</p>

<p>6.8.16 In other cases, the intended effect may be less clear. For example, if a new section is inserted into a Part of an Act that is subject to an uncommenced repeal and the section is capable of operating in its own right, it might not always be clear to the reader that the section is intended to be repealed at the same time as the Part into which it is inserted. An express repeal of the amendment should be made to put the point beyond doubt.</p>

<p>6.8.17 An alternative approach that can sometimes be used to tackle these issues is to make transitory provision that has effect only until the repeal is commenced.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>“Until section 2 of Act 2 (which repeals section 1 of Act 1) is brought into force, section 1 of Act 1 has effect as if, after “dogs” there were inserted “and cats”.</p>

<p>6.8.18 This is likely to be of particular use in cases where the commencement of the repeal is imminent.</p>

<h4 id="drafting-a-provision-that-needs-to-work-with-existing-and-prospective-provisions">Drafting a provision that needs to work with existing and prospective provisions</h4>

<p>6.8.19 Below are examples of techniques that may be useful when drafting a provision that needs to take account of prospective amendments as well as working with the existing law.</p>

<p>6.8.20 The examples assume that—</p>

<p>• Act 1 is in force</p>

<p>• Act 2 inserts a new section 1A and is not yet in force.</p>

<p>• A Bill is inserting a new section 3A into Act 1, referring to an Authority’s functions under sections 1 and 1A.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE 1</p>

<p>(1) After section 3 of Act 1 insert—</p>

<p>“3A The Authority must publish an annual report on the exercise of its functions under section 1.”</p>

<p>(2) In section 3A of Act 1 (as inserted by subsection (1)), for “section 1” substitute “sections 1 and 1A”.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE 2</p>

<p>(1) After section 3 of Act 1 insert—</p>

<p>“3A The Authority must publish an annual report on the exercise of its functions under sections 1 and 1A.”</p>

<p>(2) Until section X of Act 2 comes [fully] into force, section 3A of Act 1 (as inserted by subsection (1)) has effect as if the reference to section 1A of Act 1 were omitted.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE 3</p>

<p>After section 3 of Act 1 insert—</p>

<p>“3A (1) The Authority must publish an annual report on the exercise of its functions under sections 1 and 1A.</p>

<p>(2) Until section X of Act 2 comes [fully] into force, subsection (1) has effect as has effect as if the reference to section 1A were omitted.”</p>

<p>6.8.21 When considering the approaches in Examples 2 and 3 consideration should be given to the trade-off between the advantages of bringing the reader’s attention to the transitional provision and the disadvantages of cluttering up the statute book in the long term.</p>

<h3 id="non-textual-modifications">7.9 6.9 NON-TEXTUAL MODIFICATIONS</h3>

<h4 id="distinguishing-between-textual-amendments-and-non-textual-modifications">Distinguishing between textual amendments and non-textual modifications</h4>

<p>6.9.1 A “non-textual modification” is a modification of an enactment that is not intended to result in a change to the text of the modified enactment when the enactment is next printed (in contrast to a textual amendment, which is).</p>

<p>6.9.2 There have been occasions where it has not been clear to departments, or to those who produce and edit statutory text, whether something is a textual amendment or a non-textual modification. Sometimes non-textual modifications have even been printed as textual amendments.</p>

<p>6.9.3 The potential for confusion arises because the word “modification” is sometimes used simply to refer to a change, whether textual or non-textual. It is therefore important to make it clear what is intended.</p>

<p>6.9.4 Sometimes non-textual modifications are drafted in essentially the same form as a textual amendment, the only difference being in the opening wording—</p>

<p>EXAMPLE (to avoid)</p>

<p>(1) Section 3 applies to fine defaulters as to offenders but with the following modifications—</p>

<p>(a) in subsection (1) for “offence” substitute “default”, and</p>

<p>(b) in subsection (2) for “6 months” substitute “3 months”.</p>

<p>6.9.5 This might readily be mistaken for a textual amendment. The opening words indicate that something other than a textual amendment is intended, but the rest is exactly the same as a textual amendment. It would be particularly easy to lose sight of the opening words if the list of substitutions and other changes were very long.</p>

<p>6.9.6 It would be clearer, in the first place, if the subjunctive mood were used to indicate that there is no intention actually to substitute the text—</p>

<p>EXAMPLE (in a simple case involving few modifications)</p>

<p>(1) Section 3 applies to fine defaulters as to offenders but as if—</p>

<p>(a) in subsection (1) for “offence” there were substituted “default”, and</p>

<p>(b) in subsection (2) for “6 months” there were substituted “3 months”.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE (in a complex case involving more modifications)</p>

<p>(1) Section 3 applies to fine defaulters as to offenders but as if it were modified as follows.</p>

<p>(2) In subsection (1) for “offence” substitute “default”.</p>

<p>(3) In subsection (2) for “6 months” substitute “3 months”.</p>

<p>(4) …</p>

<p>6.9.7 Another approach which is clear is to avoid the reference to substitution altogether—</p>

<p>EXAMPLE—</p>

<p>(1) Section 3 applies to fine defaulters as to offenders but as if—</p>

<p>(a) in subsection (1) the reference to an offence were to a default; and</p>

<p>(b) in subsection (2) the reference to 6 months were to 3 months.</p>

<h3 id="amendments-other-minor-points">7.10 6.10 AMENDMENTS: OTHER MINOR POINTS</h3>

<h4 id="parenthetical-description-of-provision-amended">Parenthetical description of provision amended</h4>

<p>6.10.1 It is common practice to give a brief description in brackets of the provision that is being amended, to give the context of the amendment and perhaps its significance. It may be particularly helpful to do so in the case of an important substantive amendment. Sometimes parenthetical descriptions may enable a reader to see exactly what an amendment is doing, though it is hard to achieve this consistently in a Bill of any length.</p>

<p>6.10.2 Include a parenthetical description only if it is useful. It may not be useful in a Schedule of consequential amendments, where there is no important substantive effect to be described (and fewer readers to describe it to). For example, if you are simply changing the name of a body in all existing legislation, there may be little point in describing every provision where you are making the change.</p>

<p>6.10.3 It is also unlikely to be worthwhile to give the description of a section after which a new section is inserted, unless there is a very close connection between the two.</p>

<p>6.10.4 The parenthetical description will often match the heading of the section or Schedule to which it relates, but it does not have to do so. It may be better, for readers of the Bill, to describe the section in a different way.</p>

<p>6.10.5 Be careful about whether you are describing a whole section or a particular provision in it. The heading of a section may be unhelpful as a description of an individual subsection. For example, if section 1 is called “cases to which Part 1 applies”, and specifies those cases, but subsection (3) sets out some exceptions, it would be misleading to say “In section 1(3) (cases to which Part 1 applies)….”</p>

<p>6.10.6 For the location of parenthetical references, see paragraph 3.10.6.</p>

<h4 id="punctuation-1">Punctuation</h4>

<p>6.10.7 Where inserted or substituted words end with a full stop before the closing quotes, do not add a further full stop after the closing quotes.</p>

<h4 id="no-need-to-amend-spent-provisions">No need to amend spent provisions</h4>

<p>6.10.8 There is no need for amendments to update a provision that is spent, whether or not subject to an uncommenced repeal. But be sure that the provision is spent — the fact that a repeal has not been commenced might indicate that the repealed provision is not (or not yet) spent.</p>

<h2 id="part-7-statutory-corporations">8. PART 7 STATUTORY CORPORATIONS</h2>

<h3 id="bodies-corporate">8.1 7.1 BODIES CORPORATE</h3>

<h4 id="form-of-words-to-establish-statutory-corporation">Form of words to establish statutory corporation</h4>

<p>7.1.1 When drafting a proposition that itself creates a statutory corporation or office, use the form of words “[Name] is established” in preference to alternatives such as “there is to be”.</p>

<p>7.1.2 This does not prevent drafters from using “there continues to be” when consolidating or re-enacting a provision that sets up a statutory corporation or office or when turning an existing non-statutory body into a statutory one.</p>

<h4 id="singular-or-plural">Singular or plural?</h4>

<p>7.1.3 Statutory corporations and other bodies corporate should be treated as singular nouns.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>If the authority is satisfied that the conditions are met, it may….</p>

<p>7.1.4 When textually amending an Act that uses the plural, it may be necessary to follow suit in order to avoid confusion.</p>

<h3 id="senedd-cymru">8.2 7.2 SENEDD CYMRU</h3>

<h4 id="renaming-of-welsh-legislature">Renaming of Welsh legislature</h4>

<p>7.2.1 The Senedd and Elections (Wales) Act 2020 (“SEWA”) changed the name of the Welsh legislature (originally called the “National Assembly for Wales”).</p>

<p>7.2.2 Section 1 of the Government of Wales Act 2006 (“GOWA”), as amended by SEWA, provides that “There is to be a parliament for Wales to be known as Senedd Cymru or the Welsh Parliament (referred to in this Act as “the Senedd”)”.</p>

<p>7.2.3 Office practice for Westminster legislation is to refer to the body by its Welsh name only. This is consistent with the practice for legislation passed in Wales.</p>

<p>7.2.4 The starting point then is that the body should be referred to as “Senedd Cymru”.</p>

<p>7.2.5 Where you are referring to the body a number of times you might choose to use the form “the Senedd”, and then define that to mean “Senedd Cymru”. If you do that, there is no need to elaborate further (so do not explain that “Senedd Cymru” means Welsh Parliament).</p>

<h4 id="renaming-of-welsh-acts">Renaming of Welsh Acts</h4>

<p>7.2.6 Section 107 of GOWA provides for laws made by the Senedd to be called, in English, “Acts of Senedd Cymru” (not “Acts of the Welsh Parliament”).</p>

<p>7.2.7 Accordingly, refer to those Acts as “Acts of Senedd Cymru” (or “Acts of the Senedd” with “the Senedd” then being defined as described above).</p>

<h4 id="transitional-matters">Transitional matters</h4>

<p>7.2.8 Follow the practice described above in new text inserted into Westminster Acts which otherwise use the old names, even if this means a mixture of the old and the new names.</p>

<p>7.2.9 It is important to note that the body hasn’t changed. It just has a new name.</p>

<p>7.2.10 It is therefore possible to use the new name when referring to things done by the Welsh legislature when it had its old name.</p>

<p>7.2.11 In particular, if you are referring to Welsh legislation, and want to include Acts and Measures passed before the change of name, just refer to an Act or Measure of “Senedd Cymru” (or the Senedd). An Act passed by the body when it was called “the National Assembly for Wales” is still an Act of “Senedd Cymru”.</p>

<h2 id="part-8-periods-of-time">9. PART 8 PERIODS OF TIME</h2>

<h3 id="periods-of-time-introductory">9.1 8.1 PERIODS OF TIME Introductory</h3>

<h4 id="this-part-is-about-how-to-express-a-period-of-time-where-you-need-to-know-exactly-when-the-period-begins-or-ends17">8.1.1 This Part is about how to express a period of time where you need to know exactly when the period begins or ends.<sup id="fnref:17"><a href="#fn:17" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 17]</a></sup>
</h4>

<p>Beginnings</p>

<p>8.1.2 An unambiguous formulation is to describe the period as beginning “with” a particular day. This makes it clear that the day itself is counted within the period.<sup id="fnref:18"><a href="#fn:18" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 18]</a></sup></p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>The taxpayer must be resident in the United Kingdom throughout the period of two years beginning with the day on which the asset is acquired.</p>

<p>8.1.3 Avoid referring to a period beginning “on” a particular day. This may leave open the question of the exact time on the day in question when the period begins — and, accordingly, if the period is a whole number of days, months or years, exactly when it ends.<sup id="fnref:19"><a href="#fn:19" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 19]</a></sup></p>

<p>8.1.4 Also avoid referring to a period running “from” or “after” a particular event. This will usually be taken to exclude the day on which the event takes place.<sup id="fnref:20"><a href="#fn:20" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 20]</a></sup> But that is not invariably the case — it will depend on the context. So you will not necessarily get a certain result.</p>

<h4 id="endings">Endings</h4>

<p>8.1.5 Periods determined by reference to their end should be expressed to end “with” a particular day as opposed to “on” it, for the reasons given above.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE The taxpayer must have been resident in the United Kingdom throughout the period of two years ending with the day on which the asset was disposed of.</p>

<h4 id="within">Within</h4>

<p>8.1.6 A requirement to do something within a period is not necessarily the same as a requirement to do it before the end of the period.</p>

<p>EXAMPLES</p>

<ol>
  <li>
    <p>An appeal may be brought at any time within the period of 14 days beginning with the day after that on which the decision was made.</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>An appeal may be brought at any time before the end of the period of 14 days beginning with the day after that on which the decision was made.</p>
  </li>
</ol>

<p>8.1.7 If “within” is used (example 1), an appeal may not be brought on the day of the decision, because that is not within the period beginning the following day.</p>

<p>8.1.8 But “before the end of” (example 2) appears to leave open the possibility of action being taken on the day of the decision, because that is, literally, before the period ends. However, there is a possibility that such a proposition might be interpreted by the courts as preventing action from being taken before the day by reference to which the period is calculated (and so “before the end of” might then come to the same thing as “within”).<sup id="fnref:21"><a href="#fn:21" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 21]</a></sup></p>

<h4 id="periods-triggered-by-events">Periods triggered by events</h4>

<p>8.1.9 If an event triggers a period for something to happen — such as a decision after which there is a period for an appeal — it is a question of policy whether the day of the event should be included or not.</p>

<p>8.1.10 If you do not want to include the day of the event, it is probably best to start the period with the day after the event, and say that the action must take place within the period (as in example 1 in paragraph 8.1.6).</p>

<p>8.1.11 If you do want to include the day of the event, while following example 2 might work, it carries the risk referred to in paragraph 8.1.8. So a safer way of doing it is like this—</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>An appeal may be brought at any time within the period of 14 days beginning with the day on which the decision was made.</p>

<p>8.1.12 Note that, taken literally, this includes the earlier part of the day of the event. That may or may not matter in practice. In the case of an appeal, it is obviously impossible for the appeal to be made before the decision. If it is important to exclude earlier times, you will need to be very clear that only the remainder of the day of the event is included.</p>

<p>8.1.13 If the period starts with the day of an event and is short, it may be worth considering whether as a matter of policy the number of days should be increased by one, to take account of the fact that in practice the whole of the first day may not be available.</p>

<h4 id="before-preferable-to-by-a-particular-day">“Before” preferable to “by” a particular day</h4>

<p>8.1.14 Saying that something has to be done “before” a particular day is unambiguous. Saying that it has to be done “by” a particular day may leave room for argument about whether the thing can be done on the day itself.</p>

<h4 id="working-days">Working days</h4>

<p>8.1.15 Weekends and bank holidays will not be treated differently from other days unless you make express provision to that effect. So, if your period is expressed in days, and is very short, the policy might be only to count working days.</p>

<p>8.1.16 Here are examples of definitions of “working day”, producing different policy results.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE (1)</p>

<p>In this section, “working day” means any day other than—</p>

<p>(a) Saturday or Sunday,</p>

<p>(b) Christmas Day or Good Friday, or</p>

<p>(c) a day which is a bank holiday under the Banking and Financial Dealings Act 1971 in England and Wales.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE (2)</p>

<p>In this section, “working day”, in relation to part of the United Kingdom, means a day other than—</p>

<p>(a) Saturday or Sunday, or</p>

<p>(b) a day which is a bank holiday under the Banking and Financial Dealings Act 1971 in that or any other part of the United Kingdom.</p>

<p>8.1.17 Note that under the Banking and Financial Dealings Act 1971, Christmas Day and Good Friday are “bank holidays” in Scotland but not elsewhere in the United Kingdom.</p>

<h4 id="months">Months</h4>

<p>8.1.18 Months are a particular problem because of their varying lengths. 8.1.19 A period expressed in months beginning with a day will expire “on the eve of” (ie immediately before) the date corresponding to that with which the period begins.<sup id="fnref:22"><a href="#fn:22" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 22]</a></sup> For example, a period of one month beginning with 6 April will expire “on the eve of” 6 May - that is, the end of 5 May.<sup id="fnref:23"><a href="#fn:23" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 23]</a></sup></p>

<p>8.1.20 So, where a period is expressed in months, the number of days in it will vary according to which day of which month the period begins on. A period of “1 month” beginning with 6 April (and therefore ending at the end of 5 May) will be shorter than a period of “1 month” beginning with 6 May (because April is shorter than May).</p>

<p>8.1.21 If variation of length in different cases is not desirable, it may be worth considering whether it would be better to express the period in weeks or days. But equality of length comes at the price of difficulty of calculation: it’s easy to see that the end of the period of 3 months beginning with 6 April ends with 5 July, but harder to determine when the period of 90 days beginning with 6 April ends.</p>

<h2 id="part-9-subordinate-legislation">10. PART 9 SUBORDINATE LEGISLATION</h2>

<h3 id="form-of-subordinate-legislation">10.1 9.1 FORM OF SUBORDINATE LEGISLATION</h3>

<h4 id="generally-regulations-not-orders">Generally: regulations, not orders</h4>

<p>9.1.1 Powers to make subordinate legislation by statutory instrument should generally take the form of powers to make regulations rather than orders.<sup id="fnref:24"><a href="#fn:24" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 24]</a></sup></p>

<p>9.1.2 This applies to powers to commence an Act as well as to other powers.</p>

<p>9.1.3 It does not alter the practice of using—</p>

<p>• rules (for provision determining the procedure of a body or process),</p>

<p>• Orders in Council, or</p>

<p>• orders subject to special procedure under the Statutory Orders (Special Procedure) Act 1945.</p>

<p>9.1.4 There are some cases where it may still be appropriate to create a new order-making power, for example when amending an old Act that contains order-making powers or when creating a new power that needs to be exercised with existing order-making powers. There is of course section 105 of the Deregulation Act 2015 (which, among other things, allows provision which may be made by order to be made by regulations).</p>

<h4 id="commencement-powers-conferred-on-northern-ireland-departments">Commencement powers conferred on Northern Ireland departments</h4>

<p>9.1.5 Where a commencement power conferred on a Northern Ireland department is exercisable by statutory rule, it should take the form of an order-making power (rather than a regulation-making power) for consistency with the practice in Northern Ireland.</p>

<h3 id="enabling-powers">10.2 9.2 ENABLING POWERS</h3>

<h4 id="different-provision-for-different-cases">Different provision for different cases</h4>

<p>9.2.1 There are many examples on the statute book of provisions authorising delegated powers to be exercised differently for “different cases”, “different purposes” and “different circumstances”.</p>

<p>9.2.2 First, consider whether this kind of provision is actually needed. To exercise a power so as to make different provision for cases that are materially different would not, on the whole, be surprising (one would expect like cases to be treated alike and different cases differently). So a starting point would be to consider whether, if the power were exercised to make different provision for different cases, would that be at all unexpected or unusual.</p>

<p>9.2.3 If something further is needed, a choice then has to be made as to what exactly should be said: “cases”, “purposes”, “circumstances” or something else?</p>

<p>9.2.4 “Different purposes” is probably wider and more flexible than “different cases” (“different purposes” is usually considered to include “different cases”, but not vice versa). So perhaps that is the first port of call. But “different cases” is of course possible. Try to avoid both “purposes” and “cases”. “Circumstances” will rarely add anything.</p>

<p>9.2.5 That said, it might be possible to be more specific about how the power will be used, in which case that is likely to be more helpful. For example, if there is a power to regulate football stadiums, which might need to be exercised to make different provision for different stadiums, it might be more helpful to say just that than resort to the more abstract “different cases” or “different purposes”.</p>

<p>9.2.6 “Different descriptions of case” will rarely add anything to “different cases”. In the unlikely eventuality that the subordinate legislation may need to make provision about a single case, then it would be best to make that as clear as possible rather than relying on a distinction between “different cases” and “different descriptions of case”.</p>

<p>9.2.7 For “different provision for different purposes” in the context of a commencement power, see Part 10.6.10 - 10.6.19.</p>

<h4 id="different-provision-for-different-areas">Different provision for different areas</h4>

<p>9.2.8 One would expect the law to treat people in the same way unless there is a relevant difference between them. It is not obvious that where people happen to live is, in itself, a relevant difference. So if the policy is for a power to be exercised differently in different areas within a single jurisdiction, or differently in different jurisdictions of the UK, in relation to a reserved matter, express words should be used to make that clear.</p>

<p>9.2.9 On the whole, we do not assume that a power to make different provision for different purposes includes a power to make different provision for different areas. Forms of words which imply that differential exercise by area is just an aspect of making different provision for different purposes should be avoided.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>Regulations under section 1 may make—</p>

<p>(a) different provision for different purposes, and</p>

<p>(b) different provision for different areas.</p>

<p>NOT</p>

<p>Regulations under section 1 may make different provision for different purposes (including different provision for different areas).</p>

<h4 id="non-exercise-of-powers">Non-exercise of powers</h4>

<p>9.2.10 Some provisions about powers to make subordinate legislation expressly provide that it is possible for the power not to be exercised in certain cases. For example, the legislation may say that the power may be exercised “generally or only for specified cases” or “to make the full provision to which the power extends or any less provision”.</p>

<p>9.2.11 Whether this kind of provision is necessary will depend on the context. In many cases it will not be necessary. For example, if what is conferred is a power that need not be exercised at all (“The Secretary of State may make regulations…”) it may follow that, if it is exercised, it need not be exercised in all cases. On the other hand there may be cases where the context suggests that the power must be exercised for all cases or not at all. Equally, where a person has a duty to make subordinate legislation, it may seem to follow, without express wording to the contrary, that the person needs to make legislation covering the full range of possible cases.</p>

<p>9.2.12 So do not include this kind of provision as a matter of course. If something is needed, it may be that power to make different provision for different purposes or cases will be sufficient: if different provision may be made for different cases, it may well follow that no provision need be made for some cases.</p>

<h3 id="procedure">10.3 9.3 PROCEDURE</h3>

<h4 id="subordinate-legislation-made-by-a-minister-of-the-crown">Subordinate legislation made by a Minister of the Crown</h4>

<h4 id="making-an-instrument-a-statutory-instrument">Making an instrument a statutory instrument</h4>

<p>9.3.1 Section 1 of the Statutory Instruments Act 1946 states—</p>

<p>“Where by… any Act passed after the commencement of this Act power to make, confirm or approve orders, rules, regulations or other subordinate legislation is conferred on His Majesty in Council or on any Minister of the Crown then, if the power is expressed—</p>

<p>(a) in the case of a power conferred on His Majesty, to be exercisable by Order in Council;</p>

<p>(b) in the case of a power conferred on a Minister of the Crown, to be exercisable by statutory instrument,</p>

<p>any document by which that power is exercised shall be known as a “statutory instrument” and the provisions of this Act shall apply thereto accordingly.”</p>

<p>9.3.2 To attract section 1 of the 1946 Act it is sufficient to say—</p>

<p>Regulations [or An order] [made by the relevant Minister] under this section are to be made by statutory instrument.</p>

<p>9.3.3 It may sometimes be neater to roll up the attraction of section 1 with the power itself.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>The Secretary of State may by regulations made by statutory instrument provide…</p>

<p>9.3.4 This may in particular be neater where you have a simple power and everything can be dealt with in a single subsection. This technique is often used, for example, for commencement powers (“on such day as the Secretary of State may by regulations made by statutory instrument appoint”).</p>

<p>9.3.5 If you have a number of powers to be exercised by statutory instrument, it may be best to have a single provision at the end of the Act, rather than saying the same thing several times over in different places. This is technical provision which is unlikely to be of interest to most readers.</p>

<h4 id="negative-resolution-procedure">Negative resolution procedure</h4>

<p>9.3.6 Use the following formula—</p>

<p>A statutory instrument containing regulations under this Act is subject to annulment in pursuance of a resolution of either House of Parliament.</p>

<p>9.3.7 Note that it is the statutory instrument, rather than the regulations, which is said to be subject to annulment. This is to be consistent with section 5 of the 1946 Act. “In pursuance of” is recommended for the same reason.</p>

<h4 id="affirmative-resolution-procedure">Affirmative resolution procedure</h4>

<p>9.3.8 Use the following formula— A statutory instrument containing regulations under this Act may not be made unless a draft of the instrument has been laid before and approved by a resolution of each House of Parliament.</p>

<p>9.3.9 The formula refers to a draft of the statutory instrument containing regulations, rather than a draft of the regulations themselves, for consistency with the wording of section 6 of the 1946 Act.</p>

<p>9.3.10 If you need to secure that a statutory instrument subject to affirmative procedure may also contain provision that would otherwise be subject to negative procedure, make that very clear. One way in which that is sometimes done is by using the formulation in 9.3.8 with the addition of the words “(whether alone or with other provision)” after “containing”.</p>

<h4 id="made-affirmative-procedure">Made affirmative procedure</h4>

<p>9.3.11 Use the following form of words as a starting point—</p>

<p>(1) A statutory instrument containing regulations under section [x] must be laid before Parliament after being made.</p>

<p>(2) Regulations contained in a statutory instrument laid before Parliament under subsection (1) cease to have effect at the end of the period of [28 days] beginning with the day on which the instrument is made unless, during that period, the instrument is approved by a resolution of each House of Parliament.</p>

<p>(3) In calculating the period of [28 days], no account is to be taken of any whole days that fall within a period during which—</p>

<p>(a) Parliament is dissolved or prorogued, or</p>

<p>(b) either House of Parliament is adjourned for more than four days.</p>

<p>(4) If regulations cease to have effect as a result of subsection (2), that does not—</p>

<p>(a) affect the validity of anything previously done under the regulations, or</p>

<p>(b) prevent the making of new regulations.</p>

<h4 id="wales-1">Wales</h4>

<p>9.3.12 The position in relation to subordinate legislation made by the Welsh Ministers is similar to the position in relation to subordinate legislation made by a Minister of the Crown—</p>

<p>• section 1(1A) of the Statutory Instruments Act 1946 provides that where a power is conferred on the Welsh Ministers to make subordinate legislation and it is expressed to be exercisable by statutory instrument, the 1946 Act applies;</p>

<p>• section 11A of the 1946 Act modifies the Act so as to ensure that the procedural provisions work in relation to Senedd Cymru.</p>

<p>9.3.13 So use the following formulations—</p>

<p>The Welsh Ministers may by regulations made by statutory instrument provide…</p>

<p>Regulations made by the Welsh Ministers under this Act are to be made by statutory instrument.</p>

<p>A statutory instrument containing regulations under this Act is subject to annulment in pursuance of a resolution of Senedd Cymru.</p>

<p>A statutory instrument containing regulations under this Act may not be made unless a draft of the instrument has been laid before and approved by a resolution of Senedd Cymru.</p>

<h4 id="scotland-1">Scotland</h4>

<h4 id="making-an-instrument-a-scottish-statutory-instrument">Making an instrument a Scottish statutory instrument</h4>

<p>9.3.14 A power of the Scottish Ministers to make an order, regulations or rules under an enactment is generally exercisable by Scottish statutory instrument: see section 27(1) and (2)(a) of the Interpretation and Legislative Reform (Scotland) Act 2010 (asp 10). “Enactment” is defined to include Westminster Acts (see Schedule 1).</p>

<p>9.3.15 Where section 27(2)(a) of the 2010 Act applies it is unnecessary to provide separately in the enabling Act that the power is exercisable by Scottish statutory instrument; the established practice is to rely on section 27. This applies to powers conferred by free-standing provision or inserted into an existing Act (as does the guidance below on attracting affirmative and negative procedures).</p>

<p>9.3.16 Section 27(3) contains exceptions for cases involving a Minister of the Crown as well as the Scottish Ministers. If you are dealing with such a case you need to look at the exceptions.</p>

<h4 id="negative-and-affirmative-resolution-procedures-for-scottish-sis">Negative and affirmative resolution procedures for Scottish SIs</h4>

<p>9.3.17 The affirmative and negative resolution procedures for Scottish statutory instruments are set out in sections 28 and 29 of the Interpretation and Legislative Reform (Scotland) Act 2010 (asp 10).</p>

<p>9.3.18 The procedures can be attracted by simply providing that the relevant regulations etc are subject to the negative/affirmative procedure.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>Regulations made by the Scottish Ministers under this Act are subject to the [affirmative/ negative] procedure.</p>

<p>9.3.19 Note that the regulations (rather than the Scottish statutory instrument) are expressed to be subject to the relevant procedure. This is in contrast to the guidance in relation to statutory instruments under the Statutory Instruments Act 1946 and reflects the different wording of the 1946 and 2010 Acts.</p>

<p>9.3.20 Section 30 of the 2010 Act provides that if neither the negative nor affirmative procedure applies to devolved subordinate legislation the Scottish statutory instrument containing it must be laid before the Scottish Parliament. If this bare laying requirement is to be disapplied, the relevant enabling power must be added to the list in section 30(4).</p>

<h4 id="signposting">Signposting</h4>

<p>9.3.21 Where relevant, it may be worth signposting the Interpretation and Legislative Reform (Scotland) Act 2010 (asp 10). A reader who has not come across “negative procedure” or “affirmative procedure” before could be puzzled and may benefit from a signpost. Taking the example in 9.3.16, one possibility would be to add “(see Part 2 of the Interpretation and Legislative Reform (Scotland) Act 2010 (asp 10))”.</p>

<h4 id="northern-ireland-1">Northern Ireland</h4>

<h4 id="making-an-instrument-a-statutory-rule">Making an instrument a statutory rule</h4>

<p>9.3.22 A power of a Northern Ireland Department to make an order, regulations, rules or other subordinate legislation is generally exercisable by “statutory rule”: see the Statutory Rules (Northern Ireland) Order 1979 (S.I. 1979/1573 (N.I. 12)). The 1979 Order provides for the registration and numbering of statutory rules.</p>

<p>9.3.23 Article 4 of the 1979 Order provides: “4. In this Order “statutory rules” means-</p>

<p>(a) all orders, rules, regulations or byelaws having effect in Northern Ireland made after 31st December 1958 by a rule-making authority in exercise of any power of a legislative character conferred by—</p>

<p>…</p>

<p>(iv) any Act of the Parliament of the United Kingdom passed after 1st January 1974, if the power is expressed to be exercisable by statutory rule for the purposes of the Statutory Rules Act (Northern Ireland) 1958 or this Order.”</p>

<p>9.3.24 The 1979 Order can be attracted by providing that the power of the relevant Northern Ireland department to make regulations is exercisable by statutory rule for the purposes of the Order.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>A power of [the Northern Ireland Department] to make regulations under this Act is exercisable by statutory rule for the purposes of the Statutory Rules (Northern Ireland) Order 1979 (S.I. 1979/1573 (N.I. 12)).</p>

<p>9.3.25 Note that the power is expressed to be exercisable by statutory rule, which contrasts with the approach taken in relation to England or Wales where the usual approach is to provide for the regulations to be made by statutory instrument etc.</p>

<h4 id="negative-and-affirmative-procedures-for-statutory-rules">Negative and affirmative procedures for statutory rules</h4>

<p>9.3.26 For negative instruments, the usual approach in relation to Northern Ireland is to attract the definition of “subject to negative resolution” in section 41 of the Interpretation Act (Northern Ireland) 1954. The definition does not, without more, apply in relation to Westminster Acts and it extends to Northern Ireland only. To attract the definition you therefore need to refer to it expressly.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>Regulations made by [the Northern Ireland Department] under this Act are subject to negative resolution within the meaning given by section 41(6) of the Interpretation Act (Northern Ireland) 1954.</p>

<p>9.3.27 For the affirmative procedure the usual approach is to adopt wording along the following lines.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>Regulations may not be made by [the Northern Ireland Department] under this Act unless a draft of the regulations has been laid before and approved by a resolution of the Northern Ireland Assembly.</p>

<p>9.3.28 Although section 41 of the Interpretation Act (Northern Ireland) 1954 defines “subject to affirmative resolution”, the procedure referred to is an unusual form of affirmative procedure, so it is rare to rely on that definition.</p>

<p>9.3.29 Note that in both cases, negative and affirmative, the regulations (rather than the statutory rules) are expressed to be subject to the relevant procedure. This is in contrast to the guidance in relation to statutory instruments under the Statutory Instruments Act 1946 and reflects the different wording of the Northern Ireland legislation.</p>

<h4 id="location-of-procedural-provision">Location of procedural provision</h4>

<p>9.3.30 In some Bills, each provision which confers a power to make subordinate legislation applies any necessary parliamentary procedure. This may be helpful to readers of the Bill in Parliament, so they can see immediately what level of scrutiny is proposed.</p>

<p>9.3.31 But, where a Bill confers a number of powers to make subordinate legislation, it may be more helpful to readers of the eventual Act if these matters are dealt with in general provisions situated at the back of the Act (since for most readers of the Act this is rather technical material which is unlikely to be of interest). See also paragraph 10.6.23 (separation of commencement powers from other powers).</p>

<p>9.3.32 A “hybrid” approach is adopted in some Acts. The provision conferring the power says that it is subject to the “negative resolution procedure” or the “affirmative resolution procedure”. Then, at the end of the Act, there is a definition of “negative resolution procedure” or “affirmative resolution procedure” (or both).</p>

<h3 id="laying-documents-before-parliament">10.4 9.4 LAYING DOCUMENTS BEFORE PARLIAMENT</h3>

<h4 id="laying-documents-before-parliament-1">Laying documents before Parliament</h4>

<p>9.4.1 Section 1(1) of the Laying of Documents before Parliament (Interpretation) Act 1948 provides that references to the laying of instruments and other documents “before Parliament” are to be construed as references to their laying before each House of Parliament unless the contrary intention appears.</p>

<p>9.4.2 Section 1(1) should normally be relied on whenever it will produce the correct result. That is, normally you should say that the instrument or other document should be laid “before Parliament” rather than “before each House of Parliament”.</p>

<p>9.4.3 This does not apply to statutory instruments subject to the affirmative resolution procedure because they also have to be approved by a resolution of each House — see 9.3.8.</p>

<h3 id="amending-subordinate-legislation">10.5 9.5 AMENDING SUBORDINATE LEGISLATION</h3>

<h4 id="amending-subordinate-legislation-1">Amending subordinate legislation</h4>

<p>9.5.1 A Bill is occasionally used to amend subordinate legislation.</p>

<p>9.5.2 The question arises whether a saving is needed to allow the enabling power under which the subordinate legislation is made to be re-exercised in future to amend material inserted by the Bill. A saving should not be included as a matter of course and should be included only in the rare case where, as a matter of statutory interpretation, there is something about the context of the amendments which might cast doubt on the future exercise of the power.</p>

<p>9.5.3 If proposed amendments need to go beyond the scope of the enabling power this will normally indicate that the legislative result should be achieved by some other means (for example, by free-standing provision in the Bill).</p>

<h2 id="part-10-final-provisions">11. PART 10 FINAL PROVISIONS</h2>

<h3 id="introduction-3">11.1 10.1 INTRODUCTION</h3>

<p>10.1.1 This Part is about provisions of a general nature that appear towards the end of a Bill.</p>

<p>10.1.2 The Appendix contains example clauses that illustrate many of the recommendations in this Part. The example clauses will not produce the right result in every case so careful thought needs to be given about how far to follow them.</p>

<h3 id="order-of-final-provisions">11.2 10.2 ORDER OF FINAL PROVISIONS</h3>

<h4 id="running-order">Running order</h4>

<p>10.2.1 Use this order as a starting point—</p>

<p>Power to make consequential provision</p>

<p>Regulations (including parliamentary procedure)</p>

<p>Interpretation</p>

<p>Extent</p>

<p>Commencement and transitional provision</p>

<p>Short title</p>

<p>10.2.2 In a very short Bill where there is no need to include a power to make transitional provision in the commencement clause it may make sense to deal with extent, commencement and short title in a single clause.</p>

<p>10.2.3 Provision may also be needed for—</p>

<p>General provisions about offences (bodies corporate, unincorporated associations)</p>

<p>Directions</p>

<p>Notices/service of documents</p>

<p>Financial provisions</p>

<p>Crown application</p>

<p>Devolution Application to Scillies/Isle of Man/Channel Islands</p>

<p>Index</p>

<h4 id="heading">Heading</h4>

<p>10.2.4 If a single italic heading or Part heading is used to cover all the final provisions of a general nature, it should be “General” (rather than, for example, “Supplementary” or “Miscellaneous”).</p>

<h3 id="financial-provision">11.3 10.3 FINANCIAL PROVISION</h3>

<h4 id="introduction-4">Introduction</h4>

<p>10.3.1 This relates to provisions of Bills (starting in the House of Commons) which deal with effects on public expenditure.</p>

<h4 id="clause-heading">Clause heading</h4>

<p>10.3.2 The heading for clauses dealing with effects on public expenditure should be “Financial provision[s]”, whatever the precise nature of the effects.</p>

<h4 id="form-of-provision">Form of provision</h4>

<p>10.3.3 It is recommended that provision dealing with such effects should refer to—</p>

<p>There is to be paid out of money provided by Parliament—</p>

<p>(a) any expenditure incurred under or by virtue of the Act by [the Secretary of State], [a Minister of the Crown], [a person holding office under His Majesty] [or by a government department], and</p>

<p>(b) any increase attributable to the Act in the sums payable under any other Act out of money so provided.</p>

<p>10.3.4 This wording can then be reflected in the associated money resolution.</p>

<h3 id="extent">11.4 10.4 EXTENT</h3>

<h4 id="what-is-extent">What is extent?</h4>

<p>10.4.1 A proposition about the “extent” of a statutory provision is a proposition about the jurisdictions whose law is being changed by the provision.</p>

<p>10.4.2 The relevant jurisdictions within the United Kingdom are—</p>

<p>• England and Wales (note that this is a single jurisdiction);</p>

<p>• Scotland;</p>

<p>• Northern Ireland.</p>

<p>10.4.3 “Extent” should be distinguished from “application”, which concerns the persons and matters to which the provision relates. For example, a legal proposition may “extend” to England and Wales - that is, form part of the law of England and Wales - even though it only applies to persons in England.</p>

<h4 id="state-extent-positively">State extent positively</h4>

<p>10.4.4 There is a strong judicial presumption that, in the absence of provision to the contrary, Acts of the Westminster Parliament extend to each part of the UK but not beyond it (even though Parliament may legislate, in particular, for the Channel Islands, the Isle of Man and the British overseas territories).<sup id="fnref:25"><a href="#fn:25" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 25]</a></sup></p>

<p>10.4.5 However, the recommended approach is not to rely on that presumption but to spell out the extent of all the provisions of the Bill (including the final provisions).</p>

<p>10.4.6 So, for an Act or a provision of an Act which extends to the whole of the UK, but not beyond, spell its extent out positively.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>This Act extends to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.</p>

<p>10.4.7 Where a provision extends to all three jurisdictions within the UK, it is better to refer to each of them than to “the United Kingdom” as such.</p>

<p>10.4.8 Equally, for an Act which extends to one or two jurisdictions within the UK, spell that out positively.</p>

<p>EXAMPLES</p>

<p>This Act extends to England and Wales.</p>

<p>This Act extends to England and Wales and Scotland.</p>

<p>10.4.9 There may of course be cases where it is not convenient, or not helpful, to state extent expressly, even if the Act is thought to extend only to the UK: for example, where an Act simply amends an existing Act which itself has no specific extent provision.</p>

<p>10.4.10 A different approach will also be needed for an Act which extends, or might extend, beyond the UK.</p>

<p>10.4.11 Remember to consider the extent of amendments where providing expressly for the extent of general provisions. Normally general provisions should extend at least as far as each jurisdiction to which any provision of the Bill (including an amendment) extends.</p>

<h4 id="amendments-with-the-same-extent-as-the-amended-act">Amendments with the same extent as the amended Act</h4>

<p>10.4.12 Where an Act contains a number of textual amendments, and the intention is that they have the same extent as the enactments amended, it is often convenient to say just that.</p>

<p>EXAMPLES</p>

<p>Any amendment or repeal made by this Act has the same extent as the provision amended or repealed.</p>

<p>Any amendment, repeal or revocation made by this Act has the same extent as the provision amended, repealed or revoked.</p>

<p>10.4.13 But watch out for cases where the catch-all wording does not produce a clear result. For example, the catch-all wording is unclear where you are inserting a new section between two sections with different extents: what is the extent of the provision amended?</p>

<p>10.4.14 There are also other cases where it may be more useful for the reader to be told what the extent of each amendment is, rather than just to be told that the amendment has the same extent as something else.</p>

<p>10.4.15 Whatever approach is adopted, make sure that you know the extent of the existing provision in each case. It is possible that an existing enactment may have been extended to another jurisdiction by another enactment.</p>

<p>10.4.16 Where you are amending an Act which also extends to the Channel Islands or the Isle of Man (whether it does so on its face or by virtue of a power to extend it there), the general kind of wording will need to be limited to the United Kingdom, so as to avoid the amendments extending to the Islands directly by operation of the Bill.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>Any amendment made by this Act has the same extent within the United Kingdom as the provision amended.</p>

<h4 id="amendments-with-different-extent-from-the-amended-act">Amendments with different extent from the amended Act</h4>

<p>10.4.17 Try to avoid making amendments that have a more limited extent than the provision amended (for example, an amendment to a UK Act where the amendment is limited to England and Wales). Otherwise you will create parallel texts in different parts of the UK, which is confusing and a potential trap.</p>

<p>10.4.18 One way of doing this may be to limit the application of your proposition rather than its extent (see paragraph 10.4.3).</p>

<h4 id="amendment-of-extent-provisions">Amendment of extent provisions</h4>

<p>10.4.19 Draft on the basis that the extent of an amendment is governed by the extent provision of the amending Act. On that basis, there is no need to amend the extent provision of the Act amended, even if the amendment has a different extent from other provisions in that Act; and doing so should be avoided.</p>

<h4 id="complex-propositions-about-extent">Complex propositions about extent</h4>

<p>10.4.20 An Act may well contain provisions having different extent within the UK. In such cases the extent provision is likely to be complicated. It is difficult to give any guidance in advance about the best way of designing an extent provision here. Everything depends on the particular circumstances.</p>

<p>10.4.21 You will want to produce a provision which is itself as simple as possible. You will also want to produce a provision which allows a reader to find the extent of any given provision as easily as possible. These two aims may sometimes conflict.</p>

<p>10.4.22 If the great majority of the Act has a particular extent, with only limited exceptions, it probably helps to start with the main case and then set out the exceptions.</p>

<p>10.4.23 So, if the exceptions have a narrower extent than the majority of the Act, it is possible to set out the wider expression of extent and then reduce it.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>(1) This Act extends to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, subject as follows.</p>

<p>(2) Section 77 and Schedule 6 extend to England and Wales and Northern Ireland only.</p>

<p>(3) Section 79 and Schedule 8 extend to England and Wales and Scotland only.</p>

<p>10.4.24 Conversely, if the bulk of the Act has a narrow extent (say, England and Wales only), it may be best to start off with that and then build up.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>(1) This Act extends to England and Wales only, subject as follows.</p>

<p>(2) Section 61 extends to England and Wales and Scotland.</p>

<p>(3) Part 5 and this Part extend to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.</p>

<p>10.4.25 Do not make readers search through all the provisions of the extent clause to find out the extent of the particular provision in which they are interested.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE (to avoid)</p>

<p>(1) This Act extends to England and Wales only, subject as follows.</p>

<p>(2) Sections 12 to 15 extend also to Scotland.</p>

<p>(3) Sections 16 to 22 extend to Scotland only.</p>

<p>(4) Sections 11 to 14 extend also to Northern Ireland.</p>

<p>(5) Sections 31 and 78 extend to Northern Ireland only.</p>

<p>10.4.26 The problem in that example is that to find the extent of any particular provision the reader needs first to read subsection (1) and then to look at subsection (2) to see whether it also extends to Scotland and then subsection (4) to see whether it also extends to Northern Ireland (and check subsections (3) and (5) to make sure it is not a provision extending only to Scotland or Northern Ireland). This takes time and may cause error.</p>

<p>10.4.27 The reader is likely to want to know the jurisdictions to which any given provision extends. So rather than setting out a general provision which is then qualified, it might be better to set out what the extent of each provision of the Act is, even if it results in a longer extent provision.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>(1) Parts 1 to 7 extend to England and Wales only.</p>

<p>(2) Part 8 extends to England and Wales and Scotland.</p>

<p>(3) Part 9 extends to England and Wales and Northern Ireland.</p>

<p>(4) This Part extends to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.</p>

<h3 id="powers-to-extend-to-channel-islands-and-isle-of-man">11.5 10.5 POWERS TO EXTEND TO CHANNEL ISLANDS AND ISLE OF MAN</h3>

<h4 id="introduction-5">Introduction</h4>

<p>10.5.1 This is about what to say where provision in a Bill is, by means of a power conferred on His Majesty by Order in Council, to extend to the Channel Islands and/or the Isle of Man (“the Islands”).</p>

<p>10.5.2 A power to extend provision to the Islands should not be subject to any Parliamentary procedure.</p>

<h4 id="free-standing-provision">Free-standing provision</h4>

<p>10.5.3 For a power to extend free-standing provision to the Islands, the recommended form of words is—</p>

<p>His Majesty may by Order in Council provide for [any of the provisions of this Act] to extend, with or without modifications, to any of the Channel Islands or to the Isle of Man.</p>

<p>10.5.4 If the provision to be extended is the repeal of an Act, the recommended form of words is—</p>

<p>His Majesty may by Order in Council provide for the repeal of [Act x] in [section y] to extend to any of the Channel Islands or to the Isle of Man.</p>

<h4 id="textual-amendment-of-act-which-extends-to-islands-on-its-face">Textual amendment of Act which extends to Islands on its face</h4>

<p>10.5.5 For a power to extend amendments to the Islands, in a case where the Act amended extends on its face to the Islands, the recommended form of words is—</p>

<p>His Majesty may by Order in Council provide for any of the amendments made by [or under] this Act of any part of [the Act being amended] to extend, with or without modifications, to any of the Channel Islands or to the Isle of Man.</p>

<p>10.5.6 If you are also taking a power to extend free-standing provision (see Part 10.5.3), make express reference to both the free-standing provision and the textual amendments.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>His Majesty may by Order in Council provide for—</p>

<p>(a) [sections x to y of this Act], and</p>

<p>(b) any of the amendments made by [or under] this Act of any part of [the Act being amended], to extend, with or without modifications, to any of the Channel Islands or to the Isle of Man.</p>

<p>10.5.7 By the way, make sure that a general proposition to the effect that amendments have the same extent as the enactments amended does not inadvertently extend the amendments to the Islands directly: see Part 10.4.16.</p>

<h4 id="textual-amendment-of-act-containing-power-to-extend-to-islands">Textual amendment of Act containing power to extend to Islands</h4>

<p>10.5.8 What happens where you want a power to extend amendments to the Islands, in a case where the Act amended can be or has been extended to the Islands under a power contained in that Act?</p>

<p>10.5.9 The recommended approach is expressly to apply the existing power to your amendments, using the following form of words—</p>

<p>The power under section x of [the Act being amended] may be exercised so as to extend to any of the Channel Islands or the Isle of Man any amendment or repeal made by [or under] this Act of any part of that Act (with or without modifications).</p>

<p>10.5.10 This is recommended in preference to conferring a completely new power in the Bill to extend your amendments to the Islands; or to making the amendments and relying on silence to achieve the result that the existing power in the Act applies to that Act as amended.</p>

<p>10.5.11 If you also have free-standing provision which is to be extended to the Islands by means of a new power, deal with that separately.</p>

<p>10.5.12 Again, make sure that a general proposition to the effect that amendments have the same extent as the enactments amended does not extend the amendments to the Islands directly: see Part 10.4.16.</p>

<h4 id="preservation-of-powers-of-extension">Preservation of powers of extension</h4>

<p>10.5.13 This section is for a case where (a) you are repealing for the UK an Act which has been extended to the Islands by means of a power contained in that Act and (b) the Act needs to stay alive in the Islands after the UK repeal (whether indefinitely or until a power to extend the repeal is exercised).</p>

<p>10.5.14 You should make it clear that the UK repeal does not affect the continuing operation of the original power of extension so far as the Islands are concerned. So say something to the effect that the repeal within the UK “does not affect any power by Order in Council to make provision extending to any of the Channel Islands”.</p>

<h3 id="commencement-and-transitionals">11.6 10.6 COMMENCEMENT AND TRANSITIONALS</h3>

<h4 id="commencement-and-coming-into-force">“Commencement” and “coming into force”</h4>

<p>10.6.1 Normally, when referring to the time at which a provision begins to have legal effect, use “coming into force” or “comes into force” (or “came into force”) rather than “commencement”.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>Rather than</p>

<p>… the period of one year beginning with the commencement of this section…</p>

<p>… applications made after the commencement of this section.</p>

<p>… this section does not apply to offences committed before its commencement…</p>

<p>try</p>

<p>… the period of one year beginning when this section comes into force…</p>

<p>… applications made after this section comes into force (or “on or after the day on which this section comes into force…”)</p>

<p>… this section does not apply to offences committed before it comes into force.</p>

<p>10.6.2 This does not prevent the use of convenient labels such as “the commencement day”.</p>

<p>10.6.3 For the sake of conformity with long-standing practice, “commencement” should also be used in the heading for the section of an Act which deals with its coming into force.</p>

<h4 id="commencement-on-royal-assent">Commencement on Royal Assent</h4>

<p>10.6.4 Provisions that are to come into force on Royal Assent should be identified expressly.</p>

<p>10.6.5 The form of words used to bring such provisions into force should normally be designed to attract section 4(a) of the Interpretation Act 1978 (where provision is made for an enactment to come into force on a particular day, it comes into force at the beginning of the day).</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>Sections X and Y and Schedule Z come into force on the day on which this Act is passed.</p>

<p>10.6.6 Very exceptionally the desired policy may involve specifying a particular time of day.</p>

<h4 id="commencement-at-end-of-fixed-period">Commencement at end of fixed period</h4>

<p>10.6.7 The recommended form of words is— [This Act] comes into force at the end of the period of [two months] beginning with the day on which it is passed.</p>

<h4 id="commencement-by-regulations">Commencement by regulations</h4>

<p>10.6.8 In general it is clearer to say that provision is to come into force on a day appointed by regulations by a particular person, than to say that it comes into force “in accordance with” provision made by regulations. In the latter case it may not be clear whether any further power —for example, a power to make transitional provision — is also being conferred. If further power is wanted, it should be conferred expressly — see below.</p>

<p>10.6.9 An “appointed day” provision should take the form of a positive statement.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>This Act comes into force on such day as X may by regulations appoint.</p>

<p>not</p>

<p>This Act does not come into force until such day as X may by regulations appoint.</p>

<h4 id="differential-commencement">Differential commencement</h4>

<p>10.6.10 Sometimes where there is a power to commence it is not desired that everything should be brought into force all at once.</p>

<p>10.6.11 Where different provisions of an Act will need to be brought into force (fully) on different days, but nothing more complicated is envisaged, it will normally be sufficient to provide that the provisions of the Act</p>

<p>“come into force on such day or days as [the Secretary of State] may by regulations appoint”.</p>

<p>10.6.12 Note that although under section 6(c) of the Interpretation Act 1978 the singular includes the plural, “day or days” is recommended to make it absolutely clear that differential commencement is envisaged.</p>

<p>10.6.13 Where the policy is to allow one or more provisions of the Act to come into force for some purposes but not others, the commencement power will need to include wording enabling different provision for different purposes.</p>

<p>10.6.14 If that is done, you do not need “day or days”.</p>

<p>10.6.15 Note that “different purposes” should not be used to cover “different areas” (see 9.2.8 - 9.2.9).</p>

<h4 id="power-to-make-transitional-or-saving-provision">Power to make transitional or saving provision</h4>

<p>10.6.16 A power to make transitional or saving provision in connection with commencement may be necessary where a Bill provides for commencement by regulations or at the end of a fixed period (eg 2 months after Royal Assent).</p>
