<p>10.6.17 A “transitional” provision manages the transition from one regime to another.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>A provision that spells out how the Bill works in relation to events or matters that span the end of the old regime and the start of the new regime.</p>

<p>10.6.18 A “saving” provision saves the operation of an existing piece of legislation or rule of law. It can do this for a temporary period or for ever, and for transitional purposes or for other purposes. It might therefore be a transitional or transitory provision but need not be so.</p>

<p>10.6.19 A free-standing power to make transitional or saving provision should normally be included, rather than providing that transitional and saving provision may be included in commencement regulations. This ensures that the power covers transitional provision in connection with the commencement of provisions for which the a date is fixed by the Bill (eg 2 months after Royal Assent).</p>

<p>10.6.20 There are examples of powers to make transitory provision in connection with commencement. A “transitory” provision has a limited shelf-life, such as a provision that will expire on a particular day.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>A provision that references to dogs in the Dogs Act 1990 include cats until the coming into force of the Cats Act 2010.</p>

<p>10.6.21 Transitory provision is often transitional in nature, in which case there is no need to mention it expressly since it is covered by the power to make transitional provision. The mere fact that the regulations make provision for a limited period does not require express cover. An express power to make transitory provision is therefore usually unnecessary.</p>

<h4 id="structure">Structure</h4>

<p>10.6.22 It can sometimes be unclear how powers conferred generally in relation to regulations under the Bill will work in relation to commencement powers and powers to make transitional and saving provision in connection with commencement.</p>

<p>10.6.23 So it is usually best to exclude the powers relating to commencement from any general provision about what may be included in regulations and deal with everything relating to commencement separately.</p>

<p>10.6.24 This means that the commencement clause will often include—</p>

<p>• a free-standing power to make transitional or saving provision;</p>

<p>• provision authorising commencement regulations to make differential provision;</p>

<p>• provision for regulations under the clause to be made by statutory instrument.</p>

<h3 id="expiry-and-sunset">11.7 10.7 EXPIRY AND SUNSET</h3>

<h4 id="how-to-express-temporary-effect">How to express temporary effect</h4>

<p>10.7.1 To secure that legislative provision has limited duration, do one of the following—</p>

<p>(1) say that the enactment has effect for a certain period only</p>

<p>This Act has effect for a period of 10 years beginning with [date] or</p>

<p>(2) say that the enactment expires at a certain time</p>

<p>This Act expires at the end of a period of 10 years beginning with [date]</p>

<p>10.7.2 The difference between these two is merely presentational: (1) focuses on the duration of the temporary law while (2) focuses on its expiry. Which is more appropriate in any given case will depend on the emphasis you want to give.</p>

<p>10.7.3 If you use method (2), avoid saying that a provision expires “on” a particular day, as it may not be clear whether it expires at the beginning or end of the day (or at any other time on the day).</p>

<p>10.7.4 Other methods have sometimes been used: for example saying that an enactment “ceases to have effect” at a certain time, or that it is “repealed” at a certain time.</p>

<p>10.7.5 However, to say that an enactment “ceases to have effect” at a certain time is perhaps less clear than either methods (1) or (2).</p>

<p>10.7.6 To say that an enactment is “repealed” at a certain time has no obvious advantage over methods (1) and (2) and gives rise to a possible difficulty if the enactment consists of the repeal of another enactment. Section 15 of the Interpretation Act 1978 has the effect that the repeal of a repealing enactment does not revive the repealed enactment. That is unlikely to be the result wanted. In contrast, if the repealing enactment were said to expire, the repealed provision would revive.</p>

<p>10.7.7 So for those reasons, and in the interests of consistency, methods (1) and (2) are recommended.</p>

<h4 id="duration-to-be-separately-expressed">Duration to be separately expressed</h4>

<p>10.7.8 The House of Commons Standing Orders make specific provision about temporary laws. SO No. 81 (temporary laws) requires: “The precise duration of every temporary law or enactment shall be expressed in a distinct clause or subsection of the bill.”</p>

<h4 id="effect-of-expiry">Effect of expiry</h4>

<p>10.7.9 Consider whether it is clear from the text and the circumstances what the effects of expiry will be.</p>

<p>10.7.10 If a temporary enactment confers power to make subordinate legislation, any legislation made under it will cease to have effect from the time of the expiry of the enactment (but of course with the savings provided for in section 16 of the Interpretation Act 1978). So some transitional or saving provision may be needed.<sup id="fnref:26"><a href="#fn:26" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 26]</a></sup></p>

<p>10.7.11 Obviously, if it is appropriate to make specific savings relating to the period after the expiry of a temporary enactment or other provision about the consequences of expiry, those specific savings or other provisions should not be caught by the provision for expiry.</p>

<h3 id="short-titles">11.8 10.8 SHORT TITLES</h3>

<h4 id="form-for-conferring-short-title">Form for conferring short title</h4>

<p>10.8.1 For consistency, always use the following formulation—</p>

<p>“This Act may be cited as….”.</p>

<h2 id="part-11-words-and-phrases">12. PART 11 WORDS AND PHRASES</h2>

<h3 id="words-and-phrases">12.1 11.1 WORDS AND PHRASES</h3>

<h4 id="affect">affect</h4>

<p>11.1.1 The “nothing in provision A affects provision B” formula is useful if you do not know all the effects that A might have on B, or where those effects would be too numerous to mention. But if you can identify what effect it is you have in mind, that may help the reader (so, for example, “A does not limit B”).</p>

<h4 id="any">any</h4>

<p>11.1.2 Beware of a proliferation of “any”s. In many cases “a” or “an” is just as good.</p>

<p>11.1.3 “Any” can be ambiguous.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>The Minister must consult any organisation appearing to be representative of substantial numbers of mushroom growers.<sup id="fnref:27"><a href="#fn:27" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 27]</a></sup></p>

<p>Is this any one organisation or all organisations?</p>

<p>11.1.4 “Any” may be of course be useful to emphasise that something is of universal application or without qualification (but consider whether emphasis is really needed).</p>

<h4 id="apart-from">apart from</h4>

<p>11.1.5 For apart from, in the phrase apart from this section, consider but for or leaving aside.</p>

<p>11.1.6 However, the awkwardness here is not so much the words themselves as the task they impose on the reader - that of working out what the situation would be without the provision in question. It might be more helpful to expand on the thought and say what you have in mind.</p>

<h4 id="description">description</h4>

<p>11.1.7 This can seem rather vague and abstract (“animals of a description specified in regulations”). Drafters might like to consider kind, class or category (or even sort?).</p>

<p>11.1.8 In the context of a regulation-making power description may emphasise that it is for the regulations to create the class in question. This may be a particular help when the thing in question already comes in obvious “kinds” or “classes” but it is desired in the regulations to categorise the thing in a different way.</p>

<h4 id="function">function</h4>

<p>11.1.9 Draft on the basis that the natural meaning of “function” covers powers and duties. (In Hazell v Hammersmith and Fulham London Borough Council [1992] 2 A.C. 1. Lord Templeman said that the word “functions” in section 111 of the Local Government Act 1972 embraced: “all the duties and powers of a local authority; the sum total of the activities Parliament has entrusted to it.”)</p>

<p>11.1.10 A definition to the effect that “functions” includes powers and duties is generally unnecessary and unhelpful. If something further is needed, consider whether it is possible to get the point across more clearly.</p>

<h4 id="prescribe">prescribe</h4>

<p>11.1.11 Prescribe is often used in the context of subordinate legislation: “regulations may prescribe…”. It avoids the need to say exactly how the subordinate legislation will proceed, and as such can be extremely useful. But a more precise word may make more impact: give, fix, set, set out, state all carry more of a punch and say what exactly the regulations will do.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>Regulations under section x may prescribe the fees that may be charged</p>

<p>This could perhaps be</p>

<p>Regulations under section x may set the fees that may be charged</p>

<p>11.1.12 Prescribe is sometimes defined to mean “prescribe in regulations”. This can be a useful device to avoid lots of references to regulations. It can even be extended: section 24 of the Welfare Reform Act 2007 defines “prescribed” as “specified in, or determined in accordance with, regulations”, which avoids constant repetition of a lengthy phrase. But it is an artificial definition and consider whether it is really justified in any given case. There is clear evidence that many users of legislation find expressions like “person of a prescribed description” bewildering</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>In this section, “qualifying young person” means a person of a prescribed description</p>

<p>This could perhaps be</p>

<p>In this section “qualifying young person” means a person of a description specified in regulations made by the Secretary of State.</p>

<h4 id="provide">provide</h4>

<p>11.1.13 Where legislation provides for something it effects or gives rise to that thing in law. It is very useful because it does not require that the legislation should create it in any particular way.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>This section applies to a pension scheme which provides for a benefit to be payable to a member where….</p>

<p>Here it does not matter, for the purposes of the section, how the pension scheme creates the benefit. It is enough that, somehow or other, the pension scheme gives rise to the benefit. Neither “permits” nor “requires” might have been right on their own (it may be that a pension scheme should be caught whether it permits or requires the payment of the benefit). One could of course have both. A possible alternative might have been “a pension scheme under which a benefit is payable….”</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>(1) A person is not entitled to the benefit if the person is not in Great Britain.</p>

<p>(2) Regulations may provide for exceptions to subsection (1).</p>

<p>This doesn’t imply anything about how the regulations will be drafted, whereas specify might have given rise to an expectation that the regulations would just be a list, making more detailed provision questionable. But “create” or “make” might be possible.</p>

<p>11.1.14 Sometimes make or create will allow for the same flexibility.</p>

<p>11.1.15 However, consider in any given case whether it is possible to be more precise. Will the legislation enable, authorise, require, set out, stipulate a particular result? A more immediate word may also be less legalistic.</p>

<h4 id="provision">provision</h4>

<p>11.1.16 Provision is a useful generic phrase for what legislation does, but can be legalistic and off-putting. It may be worth thinking about what the legislation actually does in the case you are concerned about: does it regulate, authorise, require?</p>

<p>11.1.17 If conferring power to make provision about or for something, consider how the power might be exercised.</p>

<p>EXAMPLES</p>

<p>Regulations making transitional provision may, in particular—</p>

<p>(a) make provision for persons not to be treated as having any authorisation or permission;</p>

<p>(b) make provision enabling the Authority to require persons to re-apply for permission;</p>

<p>(c) make provision for the continuation as rules of such provisions as may be designated, including provision for the modification by the Authority of provisions designated;</p>

<p>(d) make provision as regards the Authority’s obligation to maintain a record.</p>

<p>It might be possible, depending on the circumstances, to be more direct—</p>

<p>Regulations making transitional provision may, in particular—</p>

<p>(a) treat persons as not having any authorisation or permission;</p>

<p>(b) allow the Authority to require persons to re-apply for permission;</p>

<p>(c) enable the continuation of such rules as may be designated (and allow the Authority to modify them);</p>

<p>(d) disapply the Authority’s obligation to maintain a record. 11.1 Words and phrases</p>

<p>11.1.18 It may be possible to avoid provision completely.</p>

<p>EXAMPLES</p>

<p>This Part of this Schedule makes further provision about….</p>

<p>might be</p>

<p>This Part of this Schedule contains more about….</p>

<p>Regulations may make provision about when an assessment period is to start.</p>

<p>might be</p>

<p>Regulations may be made about when an assessment period is to start.</p>

<p>11.1.19 Wherever possible, prefer provide for to make provision for.</p>

<p>11.1.20 Provisions is often used in the sense of the contents of legislation (“the provisions of this Act”). It has a great advantage in that it is not confined to any particular unit of text - a provision can be an Act, a section, a small unit of text or may not be an articulated bit of text at all. So to say that the provisions of the Act come into force by regulations might allow more latitude than to say that the sections come into force by regulations (would that allow subsections to be commenced separately?). But consider whether you can in any given context be more specific.</p>

<p>11.1.21 It may be that you do not need provision in this sense at all. In particular, the phrase the provisions of is often superfluous.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>This does not affect the provisions of any regulations under this section…. would mean the same without “the provisions of”.</p>

<h4 id="pursuant-to-in-pursuance-of">pursuant to, in pursuance of</h4>

<p>11.1.22 Where one thing follows directly from another, with no intervening cause or condition, pursuant to can often be rendered as under.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>A person who has been detained continuously pursuant to two or more sentences….</p>

<p>The report must include information which has been provided to the Secretary of State pursuant to regulations made under section x.</p>

<p>…any services provided by another person pursuant to arrangements….</p>

<p>In all these cases “pursuant to” could perhaps have been “under”.</p>

<p>11.1.23 In accordance with is also possible (eg in the last two examples). Or say what you mean: as required/ authorised by….</p>

<p>11.1.24 In other cases because of would work.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>If the qualification is subject to a requirement of accreditation pursuant to a determination made under section x…</p>

<p>Here “because of” would seem to work. Or better yet turn the whole thing round—</p>

<p>If a determination under section x means that the qualification needs to be accredited….”.</p>

<p>11.1.25 Sometimes something with more colour is possible.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>Such a person is guilty of an offence if, pursuant to a request for information, he makes a statement which he knows to be false.</p>

<p>Here “in response to” might be better.</p>

<p>11.1.26 Pursuant to is often used to express an indirect relationship between two things, where something happens between A and B (so A is a necessary but not a sufficient condition of B).</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>Any transfer of land pursuant to sub-paragraph (3) is to take place on the conversion date.</p>

<p>Here the point is that the sub-paragraph (3) requires the transfer of land but the transfer is actually effected by a later instrument. Here “by” or “under” would be wrong.</p>

<p>11.1.27 In cases like this it may be best to describe in more detail what is going on. In the example just given “any transfer or land required by sub-paragraph (3)” might have worked.</p>

<p>11.1.28 Failing that, “further to” will generally be a possible substitute. In some cases, “following” or “as a result of” or “because of” may be possible, or maybe just “after”, if the causal connection is clear.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>An Order in Council made pursuant to a recommendation….</p>

<p>Here following might be better. Or perhaps An Order in Council to give effect to a recommendation…</p>

<h4 id="in-relation-to-in-respect-of-with-respect-to-as-respects">in relation to, in respect of, with respect to, as respects.</h4>

<p>11.1.29 These phrases are all extremely useful, and sometimes essential, in that they do not require one to specify any particular relationship. In respect of has been said to have “the widest possible meaning of any expression intended to convey some connection or relation” (Albon v Naza Motor Trading [2007] EWHC 9 (Ch) at 27).</p>

<p>11.1.30 It is though tempting to use them in circumstances where a more precise relationship could be specified. In some circumstances in the case of, for, about, to or as to will do as well.</p>

<p>EXAMPLES</p>

<p>The election has effect in relation to films which commence photography in that accounting period</p>

<p>The election has effect for films which….</p>

<p>A transfer scheme may not make provision in relation to land</p>

<p>A transfer scheme may not make provision about land</p>

<h4 id="satisfy">satisfy</h4>

<p>11.1.31 It is enough to “meet” a condition; you don’t also need to satisfy it.</p>

<h4 id="subject-to">subject to</h4>

<p>11.1.32 “Subject to” isn’t a very precise way of describing a relationship between two propositions.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>This section is subject to section x</p>

<p>What exactly does section x do in relation to “this section”?</p>

<p>Section x sets out conditions….</p>

<p>Section x sets out different rules for [a particular case]</p>

<p>There are exceptions to this rule in section x</p>

<p>This section does not apply to [a particular case] (see section x)</p>

<p>11.1.33 If you can’t conveniently describe the relationship, “subject to” can sometimes be avoided. A signpost such as “(but see section x)” might serve to alert the reader to the fact that there are qualifications without sounding as legalistic.</p>

<p>11.1.34 The relationship between the provisions may be particularly hard to follow if “subject to” is at the beginning of the sentence. It may be better to start with the main proposition and then indicate that there is a qualification, perhaps in a second sentence.</p>

<p>11.1.35 “Subject to” is also not necessarily helpful if you cannot identify the provisions you are talking about. “Subject to what follows” should be avoided unless it is abundantly obvious from the context exactly which of the following provisions are being referred to. Where there is any doubt, specify exactly which provisions you mean (or express the relationship in some other way).</p>

<p>11.1.36 Global cross-references such as “Subject to the provisions of the Corporation Tax Acts” are sometimes unavoidable but may not be entirely meaningful to non-expert readers. If the reference cannot be avoided, try to include a list of where the relevant other provision is made.</p>

<p>11.1.37 It may be possible to dispense with “subject to” altogether, especially if the qualifying proposition is close to the proposition it qualifies — in which case the reader may be expected to grasp the relationship between the two without extra help.</p>

<p>11.1.38 See also Part 3.10, Cross-references — and in particular the injunction to draft by reference to substance rather than by reference to the statutory provisions in which it is contained.</p>

<h4 id="such">such</h4>

<p>11.1.39 Avoid “such” where possible. Often “the” or “a” will do just as well.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>Instead of</p>

<p>on such day as the Minister may specify</p>

<p>you might say</p>

<p>on a day the Minister specifies.</p>

<h4 id="supplemental--supplementary">supplemental / supplementary</h4>

<p>11.1.40 There is no obvious difference in meaning between “supplementary” and “supplemental”. Prefer “supplementary”, as perhaps the more usual formulation.</p>

<h4 id="by-virtue-of">by virtue of</h4>

<p>11.1.41 Where a relationship is direct, there may be alternatives to the rather archaic by virtue of.</p>

<p>11.1.42 Sometimes by on its own is enough. Where one thing authorises or requires another, under may be possible. Where one things causes another, or makes it possible, try as a result of or because of.</p>

<p>11.1.43 That said, by virtue of can be particularly useful for indirect relationships. For example, where regulations authorise A to authorise B, it might be misleading to say that B is authorised under the regulations. Something else has to happen first.</p>

<h4 id="where--if">where / if</h4>

<p>11.1.44 “Where” is useful for stating a case or a set of circumstances in which a later proposition applies. “If” is used for stating a contingency.</p>

<p>11.1.45 So “where” may be better for cases which inevitably will occur, “if” for conditions which may or may not be satisfied.</p>

<p>11.1.46 There is of course no clear-cut distinction. In some cases, it may depend on the perspective from which you are looking at the situation.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>Suppose a regulator has power to serve notices on defaulters—</p>

<p>Where the regulator serves a notice on a person, the regulator must…</p>

<p>(here we are speaking of the regulator, who will frequently serve notices)</p>

<p>but</p>

<p>If the regulator serves a notice on a person, the person must…</p>

<p>(here we are speaking of the person, for whom the notice is not at all inevitable).</p>

<h4 id="without-prejudice">without prejudice</h4>

<p>11.1.47 Consider what the “prejudice” might be and focus on that.</p>

<p>EXAMPLES</p>

<p>Without prejudice to the generality of section 1</p>

<p>If the fear is that the new provision might limit what section 1 says, perhaps say</p>

<p>Without limiting section 1</p>

<p>Without prejudice to the making of new regulations</p>

<p>could be</p>

<p>Without preventing the making of new regulations</p>

<p>11.1.48 If the fear is that the new provision might affect or change the way another provision operates, perhaps say that (but see affect above).</p>

<p>11.1.49 A phrase beginning without “without prejudice to…” can often be recast so as to start with the main proposition and then say how it relates to the other one.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>Without prejudice to the generality of subsection (2), the Secretary of State may issue directions under that subsection for the purposes of….</p>

<p>can be recast as two propositions The Secretary of State may issue directions under subsection (2) for the purpose of… This does not restrict what may otherwise be done under subsection (2).</p>

<p>11.1.50 Another way of avoiding without prejudice is by in particular.</p>

<p>EXAMPLE</p>

<p>The Secretary of State may in particular issue directions under subsection (2) for the purpose of…</p>

<h2 id="appendix-example-end-provisions-based-on-parts-9-and-10">13. APPENDIX EXAMPLE END PROVISIONS (BASED ON PARTS 9 AND 10)</h2>

<h3 id="general">13.1 General</h3>

<h4 id="power-to-make-consequential-provision">10 Power to make consequential provision</h4>

<p>(1) The Secretary of State may by regulations make provision that is consequential on this Act.</p>

<p>(2) Regulations under this section may amend, repeal or revoke provision made by or under an Act passed—</p>

<p>(a) before this Act, or</p>

<p>(b) later in the same session of Parliament as this Act.<sup id="fnref:28"><a href="#fn:28" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 28]</a></sup></p>

<h4 id="regulations29">11 Regulations<sup id="fnref:29"><a href="#fn:29" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 29]</a></sup>
</h4>

<p>(1) A power to make regulations under any provision of this Act includes power to make—</p>

<p>(a) consequential, supplementary, incidental, transitional or saving provision;</p>

<p>(b) different provision for different purposes [or areas].</p>

<p>(2) Regulations under this Act are to be made by statutory instrument.</p>

<p>(3) A statutory instrument containing any of the following [(whether alone or with other provision)] may not be made unless a draft of the instrument has been laid before and approved by a resolution of each House of Parliament—</p>

<p>(a) regulations under section [X];</p>

<p>(b) regulations under section [Y] that amend or repeal provision made by an Act.</p>

<p>(4) Any other statutory instrument containing regulations under this Act is subject to annulment in pursuance of a resolution of either House of Parliament.</p>

<p>(5) This section does not apply to regulations under section 13.</p>

<h4 id="extent-1">12 Extent</h4>

<p>(1) Part 1 extends to England and Wales only, subject to subsection (2).</p>

<p>(2) An [amendment or repeal] [OR] [amendment, repeal or revocation] made by Part 1 has the same extent as the provision [amended or repealed] [OR] [amended, repealed or revoked].</p>

<p>(3) This Part extends to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.</p>

<h4 id="commencement">13 Commencement</h4>

<p>(1) Section 1 comes into force at the end of the period of two months beginning with the day on which this Act is passed.</p>

<p>(2) The other provisions of Part 1 come into force on such day [or days] as the Secretary of State may by regulations appoint.</p>

<p>[(3) Different days may be appointed for different purposes [or areas].]<sup id="fnref:30"><a href="#fn:30" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 30]</a></sup></p>

<p>(4) This Part comes into force on the day on which this Act is passed.</p>

<p>(5) The Secretary of State may by regulations make transitional or saving provision in connection with the coming into force of any provision of this Act.</p>

<p>(6) The power to make regulations under subsection (5) includes power to make different provision for different purposes [or areas].</p>

<p>(7) Regulations under this section are to be made by statutory instrument.</p>

<h4 id="short-title">14 Short title</h4>

<p>This Act may be cited as the End Provisions (Example) Act 2017.</p>
